#### J) Biographical Narrative · Condensed
In the late summer of 66 CE, the volatile geopolitical pressure cooker of the Levant finally exploded. Decades of crushing Roman taxation and severe domestic wealth inequality had left the Judean populace deeply radicalized. The breaking point arrived when the brutal and incompetent Roman Procurator, Gessius Florus, brazenly looted 17 talents of gold directly from the sacred Temple treasury. When the furious citizens of Jerusalem mocked him by passing a beggar's basket through the streets, Florus retaliated by unleashing his heavy infantry to massacre thousands of Jewish civilians.

This horrific urban bloodshed triggered an immediate, absolute constitutional rupture. Led by Eleazar ben Ananias, the Captain of the Temple, the Jewish priesthood executed the ultimate diplomatic maneuver: they permanently halted the daily sacrifices offered on behalf of Emperor Nero. This action was a formal, undeniable declaration of war against the Roman Empire. Simultaneously, radical Zealot and Sicarii militias seized control of the city and captured the impregnable Herodian desert fortress of Masada, securing massive caches of imperial weaponry. To visually broadcast their newfound sovereignty, the rebel government instantly minted high-purity silver shekels bearing ancient paleo-Hebrew, erasing 129 years of Roman macroeconomic dominance.

Recognizing that the critical eastern Mediterranean buffer state was in total freefall, Cestius Gallus, the Roman Legate of Syria, marched south with over 30,000 troops, including the elite 12th Legion. Reaching Jerusalem in the autumn, the Roman war machine breached the outer walls but inexplicably aborted the siege, ordering a full retreat. The Jewish militias, executing a brilliantly ruthless asymmetric counter-attack, chased the retreating Roman column into the steep, narrow ravines of the Beth Horon pass. Trapped in the treacherous topography, the heavily armored Roman infantry was annihilated by guerrilla archers and slingers. Over 5,300 Roman soldiers were slaughtered, their siege engines captured, and the sacred legionary eagle disgraced. Returning to Jerusalem covered in Roman armor, the victorious rebels believed they had secured divine liberation. In reality, their shocking, humiliating victory had merely signed the death warrant for the entire nation, guaranteeing that Emperor Nero would deploy the full, terrifying, mechanized wrath of the Roman superpower to utterly eradicate the Jewish state.

#### K) Root Excavation

The war's vocabulary is a vocabulary of blades, weights, and debts, and almost none of it begins as theology. The **sicarii** take their name from the Latin *sica*, a short curved dagger of Illyrian or Thracian origin, and the derived noun *sicarius* is not a sectarian label but a term of Roman homicide law: the Sullan statute of 81 BCE, the *lex Cornelia de sicariis et veneficis*, legislates against the dagger-man and the poisoner together. Josephus describes the practice that matches the name exactly, blades hidden under cloaks, victims struck in daylight crowds during festivals, the killer joining the outcry. The word reached Greek as a loan and appears once in the New Testament, at Acts 21:38, where a tribune asks Paul whether he is the Egyptian who led four thousand **σικαρίων** into the wilderness. A Latin legal category for a species of murderer had become, in one generation, the Greek name of a political faction.

Josephus's own habitual word for the insurgents is **λῃσταί** (*lēstai*), from **λεία** (*leia*), plunder or booty; the concrete floor is the taken thing, and the agent noun is the taker. Its Latin equivalent, *latro*, does the same work, and *latrocinium* is the administrative term by which Rome classified armed resistance as brigandage. The classification was a legal instrument, not a slur. An enemy proper, a *hostis*, possessed rights: to treat, to be taken prisoner, to be enslaved rather than executed. A *latro* possessed none, and could be crucified. The same Greek noun labels the two men crucified beside Jesus at Mark 15:27 and the man released instead of him at John 18:40, which is the imperial category under which an insurgent and a highwayman were processed identically.

Against that external naming stands the movement's self-description. Hebrew **קַנָּא** (*qannāʾ*), √**q-n-ʾ**, and its Second Temple agent form **קַנַּאי** (*qannāʾî*) render into Greek as **ζηλωτής** (*zēlōtēs*), and the Greek is the more transparent of the two. It derives from **ζέω** (*zeō*), to boil or seethe, the ordinary verb for water over a fire. Zeal at its concrete floor is a liquid at rolling boil, an internal state read off a physical process. The Hebrew root is harder: it governs the burning affect ascribed to the deity at Exodus 20:5 and to Phinehas at Numbers 25:11, and comparative lexicography has proposed a link to Arabic *qanaʾa* (قَنَأَ), to become intensely red, which would place the concrete floor at the flushed face. Whichever floor is preferred, the operative precedent is Phinehas, who kills without trial and is rewarded with a covenant of peace. The Zealot claim is not innovation. It is a legal citation.

The coinage supplies the rest. **שֶׁקֶל** (*šeqel*), √**š-q-l**, is a weight before it is a coin, cognate to Akkadian *šaqālu*, to weigh out and so to pay, and to Ugaritic *ṯql*; the concrete image is the balance-pan, and the earliest Semitic payments are weighings. **קָדוֹשׁ** (*qādôš*), √**q-d-š**, in the legend *Yerushalayim ha-qedošah*, has a concrete floor of separation and withdrawal from common use, shared with Ugaritic *qdš* and Phoenician *qdš*. The two political words are the interesting ones. **חֵרוּת** (*ḥērût*), freedom, on the year two and year three bronzes, is not biblical Hebrew; the Bible's release word is **דְּרוֹר** (*derôr*), the jubilee proclamation of Leviticus 25:10. *Ḥērût* is an abstract noun built on the *ḥōrîm*, the free-born notables of Nehemiah 2:16 and 1 Kings 21:8, and its appearance here is among its earliest datable attestations. Then, in year four, the legend changes to **לְגְאֻלַּת צִיּוֹן** (*li-geʾullat Ṣiyyon*), for the redemption of Zion, and √**g-ʾ-l** is a property word. The *gōʾēl* is the kinsman who buys back alienated land at Leviticus 25:25, who redeems a relative out of debt-slavery at 25:47, and who avenges spilled blood at Numbers 35:19. As the military position collapsed, the mint moved from a civic word to a word about land lost and blood owed.

*Warrant typing.* The derivations of *sica*, *latro*, *leia*, *zeō*, *šeqel*, *qādôš*, and *gōʾēl*, and the Akkadian and Ugaritic cognates, are Type T. The Arabic *qanaʾa* connection for √q-n-ʾ is Type C, an old lexicographic proposal that is neither established nor refuted. The reading of the year four legend change as a semantic retreat from the political to the soteriological is Type S, an inference from the legends and their dates rather than from any statement of intent.

#### L) Political Economy and Statecraft

The fiscal architecture the revolt broke had two collectors, and both were taking from the same harvest. Rome levied the *tributum soli* on land and the *tributum capitis* as a head charge, assessed by census and payable in coin, which obliged a subsistence cultivator to market grain at whatever price the season set in order to convert produce into silver. On top of that sat the Temple's half-shekel, due annually from every adult male, payable in Tyrian silver, plus tithes, firstfruits, and the priestly dues. Josephus preserves the figure that Judaea's arrears stood at forty talents when Florus took his seventeen from the treasury, which indicates a system already failing to clear before anyone was robbed.

The employment shock is the most underrated pressure in the sequence and it is documented. The Herodian Temple works were completed in the early 60s, and Josephus reports in the *Antiquities* that some eighteen thousand workmen were thereby thrown out of employment, and that Agrippa II was petitioned to find them work, which he did by paving the city with white stone. A capital that has just discharged a construction workforce of that size, in a province whose tax obligations are fixed in coin, is a capital with a large body of skilled, organised, unemployed men inside its walls. The riot that met Florus was not a spontaneous crowd.

The class dimension is legible in what the insurgents burned first. Josephus records that after firing the house of the high priest Ananias and the palaces of Agrippa and Berenice, the rebels carried the flames to the **ἀρχεῖα**, the record office, to destroy the creditors' bonds and make recovery of debt impossible. That is a targeted act against a specific archive, and it identifies the revolt's early constituency more precisely than any of Josephus's editorial characterisations: debtors moving against the instruments that recorded their debts. The high priesthood was itself a major creditor institution, which is why the aristocratic priesthood stands on the other side of the barricade from the first week.

The coinage is the sharpest instrument in the dossier and it should be read metallurgically. The Temple's half-shekel had to be paid in Tyrian silver, the shekels of Tyre bearing the head of Melqart and an eagle, tolerated because of their reliable fineness. The revolt's silver shekels are struck to that same Tyrian weight standard and at a comparably high fineness, which points to the obvious source of bullion: the accumulated Tyrian coin in the Temple treasury, melted and restruck. The rebel state's first monetary act was therefore to convert the pagan coin that Judaism had been obliged to use for its holiest tax into a coin of its own, in an archaic script deliberately chosen over the current square Aramaic hand, with a dating era running from year one. Every element is a sovereignty claim, and every element is also a technically competent piece of minting requiring the Temple's silver and, almost certainly, the Temple's priests.

Who benefits divides cleanly across two horizons. Inside the event, the beneficiaries are the factions that captured the treasury and the sacrificial apparatus, since control of the altar was control of the revenue, and the successive purges of moderate aristocrats over the following four years are a fight over that revenue as much as over strategy. In transmission, the beneficiaries are Flavian. A triumph could properly be voted only for a foreign war; suppressing a provincial rising was police work, and a dynasty without ancestors could not found its legitimacy on police work. The war therefore had to be a great war against a formidable nation, and Josephus, writing under Flavian patronage, supplies exactly that scale. The apologetic runs both ways at once, which is why it is durable: an inflated enemy magnifies Vespasian, and it also lets a defeated Jewish aristocrat tell his own people that they were beaten by an irresistible force rather than by their own factions, provided he assigns the war itself to a criminal minority. Our principal source is a man who commanded on one side and drew a pension from the other, and no reading of him is safe that forgets it.

Cestius Gallus's withdrawal deserves an account rather than the language of inexplicability. He came before Jerusalem late in the campaigning season, his communications ran back through hostile country to Caesarea, and Josephus nowhere credits him with a siege train adequate to the Antonia and the walls. A commander who has probed a fortified city, found it stronger than his intelligence indicated, and faces winter on an extended supply line has ordinary professional reasons to disengage. The catastrophe lay in the execution, not the decision: a heavy column retreating through a defile is the most vulnerable formation in ancient warfare, and the Beth Horon descent is a defile.

#### M) Archaeological Dossier

The revolt coinage is the volume's strongest evidence and it deserves precision. The silver comprises shekels, half-shekels, and quarter-shekels dated year one through year five, with year five, corresponding to 69 and 70, surviving in very small numbers, which is itself a datum about the mint's final months. The types are stable: a chalice with the year above, and a staff bearing three pomegranates, with the legends *šeqel Yisraʾel* and *Yerushalayim ha-qedošah* in paleo-Hebrew. The bronze issues of years two and three carry an amphora and a vine leaf with *ḥērût Ṣiyyon*, and the year four bronzes carry the four species, a chalice, and a palm, with *li-geʾullat Ṣiyyon*. This is Tier 1 contemporary epigraphy in the strictest sense, produced by the rebel government itself, and it is the only body of evidence for the revolt that is neither Roman nor Josephan.

A second Tier 1 item is easy to overlook. A small group of crude bronze coins struck at Gamla in the Golan carries a legend naming the redemption of Jerusalem the holy, executed in an unpractised hand on irregular flans. These are not the product of a state mint; they are a provincial town's attempt to imitate the capital's sovereignty claim with whatever die-cutter was available. They establish that the revolutionary formula travelled, and that it was reproduced locally rather than distributed centrally.

Masada's rebel phase, Tier 1, materialises the *sicarii* seizure of 66 directly. The Herodian casemate wall was subdivided into dwellings, ovens and hearths were installed in palatial spaces, ritual baths were cut or adapted, and coins of the revolt years, including years two through five, were recovered on the plateau. The occupation is unambiguous and it is domestic rather than military in character: families lived there for seven years inside a king's fortress.

The 66 events themselves, however, have almost no direct material signature, and the reason is structural rather than accidental. A riot, a massacre in a city quarter, and a running ambush along a road produce scattered, unstratified, undatable material. There is no excavated battlefield at Beth Horon and there should not be expected to be one: the Roman column built nothing, besieged nothing, and left nothing but casualties, which the victors stripped. The material record of this war begins in earnest in 67 with the siege sites, because sieges leave earthworks, and earthworks survive.

The debit side is substantial. The three thousand six hundred killed by Florus and the five thousand three hundred infantry and three hundred and eighty cavalry lost at Beth Horon are Josephus's figures, unverifiable and consistent with his general practice of round and large numbers. The loss of the legionary eagle rests on a single sentence in Suetonius and is not in Josephus, so a spectacular detail that the volume treats as established has one late witness. Most importantly, the claim that Legio XII Fulminata was annihilated is falsified by the legion's own subsequent history: the unit continued to exist, served at the siege of Jerusalem in 70, was transferred by Vespasian to Melitene in Cappadocia, and is attested there for centuries. A legion that loses five thousand men suffers a catastrophe and remains a legion. Finally, the identification of the ambush site rests entirely on Josephus's topography; the pass is real, the reasoning about it is sound, and the attribution is nonetheless textual and not stratigraphic.

#### N) Cross-Corpus Reception

Beth Horon was already a memory site before 66, and the insurgents knew it. Joshua 10:10 and 11 place the rout of the Amorite coalition on the descent of Beth Horon, with hailstones killing more than the sword did. First Maccabees 3:13 to 24 places Judas's defeat of Seron on the same descent, and 1 Maccabees 7:39 to 45 places the defeat of Nicanor at Adasa with the pursuit running through the same corridor. A Jewish force that chased a Seleucid successor down that road in 66 was not merely using good ground; it was performing a citation, and Josephus's report that the victors returned convinced that God had delivered the empire to them is entirely credible on those terms. The typology also explains the strategic paralysis that followed. A people who believe they are inside 1 Maccabees do not build for a four-year war, because in 1 Maccabees the enemy withdraws.

The zeal tradition runs on the same principle. Numbers 25 supplies Phinehas, who kills a mixed couple without judicial process and receives a covenant of perpetual priesthood for it; 1 Kings 19:10 supplies Elijah's declaration that he has been very zealous; 1 Maccabees 2:24 to 27 fuses them by having Mattathias kill at the altar and cry that whoever is zealous for the law should follow him. Sirach 45:23 had already canonised Phinehas as third in glory. The first century inherited a fully formed legal precedent for lethal private action in defence of the covenant, and the label *zēlōtēs* is a claim upon it. The New Testament preserves the label in a form that predates the organised faction: Simon is **ὁ ζηλωτής** at Luke 6:15 and Acts 1:13 and **ὁ Καναναῖος** at Mark 3:18, the second being the Aramaic *qanʾānāʾ* transliterated rather than translated. Whether it marks party membership or personal temperament is genuinely undecidable, since Josephus's organised Zealots emerge only in 67 or 68.

Gamaliel's speech at Acts 5:36 and 37 preserves the dynasty of resistance from the other side, naming Theudas and Judas the Galilean; Josephus makes Judas, who resisted the census of 6 CE, the ancestor of the line that produced Menahem, who seized Masada in 66. The revolt had a genealogy sixty years deep.

The synoptic reception rewards close comparison. Mark 13:14 warns of the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not, a Danielic cipher that requires decoding. Luke 21:20 replaces the cipher with armies encamped around Jerusalem, and Luke 19:43 adds a siege palisade, an encirclement, and the levelling of the city with its children inside. The direction of the rewriting is the argument: a cipher has been converted into siege reportage, which most scholarship takes as evidence that Luke wrote with the event behind him, though a minority holds otherwise and the question is not closed. Either way, the later evangelist supplies the technical vocabulary of circumvallation that the earlier one does not have.

Rabbinic memory converges with Josephus from an entirely independent transmission stream, and the convergence is worth more than either source alone. The Babylonian Talmud at Gittin 56a knows the *biryōnîm*, the strongmen of the city, who burned the storehouses of grain in order to force the population to fight, which is the same act Josephus reports of the factions. At Yoma 9b the tradition assigns the destruction of the second house to *sinʾat ḥinnām*, groundless hatred, which relocates the cause from Rome to internal division. That is theologically serious and it is also survivable under Roman rule, and both facts are true at once.

Against the comparative horizon the episode is less singular than it appears in its own literature. Boudica's rising of 60 or 61 and the Batavian revolt of Civilis in 69 and 70 exploited the same imperial vulnerabilities, produced comparable early successes, and ended the same way. What has no parallel is the documentary residue. No other provincial insurgency of the early principate minted a sovereign silver coinage in a deliberately archaic national script with its own dating era, and no other has left a full narrative history written from the losing side. The Qur'an preserves the outcome without the mechanics: Sūrah al-Isrāʾ 17:4 to 7 speaks of two occasions of corruption among the Banū Isrāʾīl and of servants sent who entered the place of worship as they had entered it the first time. The passage names neither Babylon nor Rome, and the identification of the second entry with 70 belongs to the exegetes rather than to the text, which is precisely how the episode survives into a later corpus: stripped of its factions, its coinage, and its debts, and retained as a pattern.


### VOLUME 83 · The Vespasian/Titus Campaign & the Galilean Subjugation

#### A) Biographical Excavation · Introduction
This episode reconstructs the terrifying, methodical counter-offensive of the Roman Empire. The targeted chronological window is the spring and summer of 67 CE. The evidentiary thesis posits that Emperor Nero, humiliated by the annihilation of the 12th Legion at Beth Horon (Volume 82), refused to let the Judean insurgency survive. He deployed his most battle-hardened, ruthlessly pragmatic general: Titus Flavius Vespasianus (Vespasian), accompanied by his son Titus. Rather than marching blindly at the heavily fortified capital of Jerusalem, Vespasian executed a textbook, mechanized Roman pacification strategy. Amassing a massive invasion force of 60,000 heavy infantry and auxiliary cavalry in Syria, he systematically rolled over the northern province of Galilee. By besieging and annihilating the rebel fortresses one by one to Jotapata, Taricheae, and Gamla to Vespasian completely severed Jerusalem’s agricultural and demographic supply lines, functionally trapping the rebel factions in the capital to starve and slaughter each other before the Roman legions ever reached the walls.

**Era Attestations:**

- **Jotapata (Yodfat) Excavations (Tier 1):** Extensive archaeological digs at the site of the ancient Galilean fortress commanded by Flavius Josephus. The site is a pristine, frozen battlefield containing a massive Roman siege ramp, hundreds of iron ballista bolts, catapult stones, and human remains displaying severe weapon trauma, physically validating the brutal 47-day Roman siege.

- **Gamla Excavations (Tier 1):** Often called the "Masada of the North," this fortified city in the Golan Heights features a massive breach in its eastern wall, perfectly matching Josephus's account of the Roman battering rams shattering the defenses, leading to the suicidal plunge of thousands of Jewish defenders into the ravine below.

- **Flavius Josephus (*The Jewish War* 3 & 4) (Tier 1):** The ultimate, controversial primary source. As the actual Jewish commanding general of the Galilee who fought Vespasian, survived a suicide pact, and subsequently defected to the Romans, Josephus provides a staggering, first-person tactical autopsy of the entire campaign.

#### B) Historiographical Artifact (Classical Record)
> *"Vespasian was very desirous of demolishing Jotapata, for he had gotten intelligence that the greatest part of the enemy had retired thither... he sent both footmen and horsemen to level the road, which was mountainous and rocky... So in four days' time they opened a broad way for the army.". Translator: William Whiston [Josephus, Jewish War 3.7.3] [Genre: Military Historiography / Siege Logistics]*
>
> *"And as the Jewish forces were now beaten... they were driven into the lake [Sea of Galilee]... the Romans leaped out of their vessels, and destroyed a great many more upon the land: one might then see the lake all bloody, and full of dead bodies, for not one of them escaped.". Translator: William Whiston [Josephus, Jewish War 3.10.9] [Genre: Military Historiography / Naval Massacre]*

**Context:** While the New Testament canon is silent on the specific tactical maneuvers of 67 CE, Josephus’s *Jewish War* serves as the undisputed historical ledger for this era. Critical historians recognize his account as highly accurate regarding Roman military topography and siege mechanics, even if his self-serving narrative regarding his own defection is heavily biased. [Scholarly Consensus]; Tier 3.

#### C) Raw Symbolism & Immediate Semiotics
- **The Paved Road:** The first action of the Roman army. Vespasian didn't attack immediately; he sent engineers to literally level the mountains so his siege towers and artillery could roll smoothly to the rebel gates. It symbolizes the inescapable, geographic dominance of the Roman war machine.

- **The Suicide Pact of Jotapata:** When the fortress fell, Josephus and 40 Jewish commanders hid in a cave and drew lots to kill each other rather than surrender. Josephus rigged the draw, surviving with one other man, and defected. It symbolizes the intense, localized fanaticism of the rebels clashing with the absolute *realpolitik* of their aristocratic leaders.

- **The Bloody Sea:** The Battle of Taricheae. Roman soldiers built rafts to pursue Jewish rebels fleeing onto the Sea of Galilee in fishing boats. The ensuing slaughter literally dyed the lake red and washed rotting corpses onto the shores, physically turning the agrarian heartland of the Jesus movement into an apocalyptic graveyard.

- **The Prophecy of Empire:** Josephus's ultimate survival tactic. Brought before Vespasian in chains, Josephus prophesied that Vespasian would soon become the Emperor of Rome. This brilliant piece of psychological manipulation saved his life and permanently embedded him in the Flavian imperial court. Scope: Mechanized siege warfare, defection, and systemic pacification.

#### D) Corroboration Anchor(s) · Same Era/Locale
- **Source: The Surrender of Sepphoris | Reference: Numismatics & Urban Arch. | Tier 1 |** Artifact datum: The largest city in the Galilee, Sepphoris, minted coins calling itself the "City of Peace" and proactively opened its gates to the Romans without firing an arrow. | **Era justification:** Proves the Jewish resistance was deeply fractured. The wealthy, urbanized Hellenistic elites recognized that fighting Vespasian was geopolitical suicide, leaving the rural, radicalized peasantry to face the legions alone.

- **Source: Roman Artillery (*Tormenta*) | Reference: Gamla/Jotapata Artifacts | Tier 1 |** Artifact datum: Thousands of carved limestone ballista balls and iron arrowheads concentrated at the precise breach points of the fortress walls. | **Era justification:** Biomechanically and technologically authenticates the Roman strategy of suppressing the defenders with massive, continuous covering fire while the battering rams (*aries*) shattered the stonework.

- **Source: Suetonius (*Life of Vespasian* 4-5) | Reference: Roman Imperial Records | Tier 1 |** Artifact datum: "He [Vespasian] was chosen as the man of all others for this expedition... he added two legions, eight squadrons of horse, and ten cohorts to the forces... and exhibited such proof of his martial skill, that in the attack on a fortress he was wounded in the knee by the stroke of a stone." | **Era justification:** Independently corroborates Josephus’s exact troop deployments and even the minor detail of Vespasian's combat injury at Jotapata.

#### E) Imagery Bridge · Canon ↔ Corroboration (and Qur’an/Hadith)
The imagery of the spring of 67 CE is one of terrifying, earth-shaking mobilization. At Ptolemais (Acre) on the Mediterranean coast, Vespasian unites his massive invasion force: three full Roman legions (the 5th, 10th, and 15th), bolstered by tens of thousands of auxiliary archers, cavalry, and Syrian mercenaries. The earth literally trembles under the boots of 60,000 professional killers.

Vespasian's strategy is a masterclass in psychological and logistical warfare. He does not march on Jerusalem. He aims directly at the agricultural heartland: the Galilee. The Galilean rebel commander is a young, aristocratic priest named Yosef ben Matityahu (Flavius Josephus). Recognizing the hopelessness of the situation, the major urban center of Sepphoris immediately surrenders, granting the Romans a massive forward operating base.

Josephus retreats to the fortified mountain town of Jotapata (Yodfat). The imagery shifts to the grueling, 47-day siege. The Romans construct massive earthen ramps. The air is black with thousands of flaming arrows and whistling 50-pound ballista stones that shatter the Jewish parapets. The Jewish defenders fight with suicidal bravery, pouring boiling oil onto the Roman legionaries under the battering rams. But the Roman mechanics are undeniable. The wall breaches. A massacre ensues. Forty thousand Jews are slaughtered or enslaved. Josephus survives a suicide pact in a hidden cave, surrenders to the Romans, and buys his life by prophesying the imperial throne for Vespasian.

The Roman steamroller pivots to the Sea of Galilee. At Taricheae, Jewish rebels take to the water in hundreds of small fishing vessels. Vespasian builds a flotilla of rafts, and his heavy infantry shoots the unarmored fishermen to pieces. The pristine lake to the former stage of Jesus's ministry to is choked with blood and rotting corpses. Finally, Vespasian marches to the Golan Heights to besiege Gamla. Built on a steep, camel-hump ridge, the fortress is breached, and 5,000 Jewish defenders throw themselves and their families into the deep ravines to avoid Roman capture. By the end of 67 CE, the northern insurgency is utterly pulverized. The Galilee is a smoking wasteland, and Vespasian turns his terrifying, methodical gaze south toward the fractured, starving capital of Jerusalem.

#### F) Chronology & Geography Lock
- **Window:** Spring to Autumn, 67 CE. Precision: Month/Season level.

- **Route:** Antioch/Ptolemais (Mobilization) -> Sepphoris (The bloodless surrender) -> Jotapata (The 47-day siege) -> Taricheae/Sea of Galilee (The naval massacre) -> Gamla (The cliffside slaughter).

- **Toponyms:** Ptolemais, Galilee, Sepphoris, Jotapata, Taricheae, Gamla.

- **Proxy Anchors:** Ptolemais (Acre). Functioning as the primary maritime staging ground, it highlights the absolute logistical superiority of the Roman Empire, which could seamlessly supply 60,000 troops via the Mediterranean while the landlocked Jewish rebels slowly starved.

#### G) Evidence Ledger
- **Emperor Nero deployed Vespasian with 60,000 troops to crush the Judean revolt. [DOCUMENTED]; Tier 1** (Tacitus, Suetonius, Josephus).

- **The Romans systematically besieged and destroyed the Galilean fortresses (Jotapata, Gamla). [DOCUMENTED]; Tier 1** (Extensively verified by modern battlefield archaeology).

- **Josephus commanded the Jewish forces, surrendered, and defected to the Romans. [DOCUMENTED]; Tier 1/2** (His own writings and his later status as a Flavian pensioner in Rome confirm his defection).

- **The Galilean campaign successfully severed Jerusalem's northern supply lines. [DOCUMENTED]; Tier 1** (A standard, highly effective Roman military pacification strategy).

- **Falsifier:** If Galilean excavations showed that Jotapata and Gamla were never attacked, continuously thriving through the 2nd century CE without any Roman ballista stones or destruction layers, the entire history of the Vespasian northern campaign would be dismantled.

#### H) Micro-Notes
- **Cross-refs (HB/NT):** The absolute destruction of the Galilean villages in 67 CE represents the physical end of the world that Jesus and his apostles inhabited. The fishing communities of Bethsaida, Capernaum, and Taricheae were wiped off the map, permanently relocating the center of both Judaism (eventually to Yavneh) and Christianity (to the Greco-Roman diaspora).

- **DSS/Second Temple:** The failure of the northern campaign exacerbated the radicalization in Jerusalem. When Galilean refugees (like the Zealot leader John of Gischala) fled south into the capital, they brought extreme, uncompromising militant ideologies that sparked a horrific, cannibalistic civil war inside Jerusalem before the Romans even arrived.

- **The "Year of the Four Emperors" (68-69 CE):** Vespasian's prophecy to Josephus came true. Shortly after pacifying the Galilee, Emperor Nero committed suicide. The Roman Empire plunged into civil war. Vespasian temporarily halted the Judean campaign, marched on Rome, and seized the imperial throne, leaving his son Titus to finish the siege of Jerusalem.

- **Outcomes:** The complete annihilation of the northern Jewish insurgency; the defection of Josephus; the trapping of the remaining rebel factions inside Jerusalem; the elevation of the Flavian dynasty.

#### J) Biographical Narrative · Condensed
In the spring of 67 CE, the Roman Empire answered the catastrophic humiliation of the Beth Horon ambush with overwhelming, mechanized wrath. Emperor Nero deployed his most battle-hardened general, Vespasian, and his son Titus, to utterly eradicate the Jewish insurgency. Assembling a massive invasion force of 60,000 heavy infantry, cavalry, and mercenaries at the coastal port of Ptolemais, Vespasian executed a textbook strategy of imperial pacification. Rather than rushing the heavily fortified capital of Jerusalem, he systematically marched into the agricultural heartland of the Galilee to sever the rebellion's supply lines.

The Jewish resistance in the north, commanded by the aristocratic priest Flavius Josephus, was deeply fractured. Recognizing the sheer demographic and technological supremacy of the Roman war machine, the wealthy urban elites in Sepphoris immediately surrendered, granting the Romans a massive, bloodless foothold. Josephus and the radicalized rural militias retreated into fortified mountain strongholds. Vespasian responded with terrifying, earth-shaking siege engineering. At Jotapata, Roman engineers leveled mountains to roll massive battering rams and artillery to the walls. After a brutal 47-day siege, the fortress was breached and 40,000 Jews were slaughtered. Josephus miraculously survived a suicide pact in a hidden cave, surrendered to the Romans, and brilliantly saved his own life by prophesying that Vespasian would soon become the Emperor of Rome.

The Roman steamroller was unstoppable. At the Battle of Taricheae, Roman heavy infantry pursued fleeing Jewish rebels onto the Sea of Galilee, slaughtering them on rafts and turning the pristine lake into a bloody graveyard. At the cliffside fortress of Gamla, thousands of defenders threw themselves into the ravines rather than face Roman capture. By the end of 67 CE, the northern insurgency was completely pulverized. The smoking, traumatized remnants of the radical Galilean militias fled south, pouring into the walls of Jerusalem. There, trapped like rats, they initiated a horrific, cannibalistic civil war against the moderate Jewish factions, doing exactly what Vespasian had calculated: bleeding the capital dry before the Roman eagles ever cast their shadow over the Temple Mount.

#### K) Root Excavation

The campaign's operative language is Latin engineering vocabulary, and every term in it is a verb of physical labour before it is a term of art. The **agger**, the siege ramp, is a noun from *aggerō*, itself *ad* plus *gerō*, to carry toward; *gerō* is the plain verb for bearing a load. An *agger* is therefore, at its floor, the heaped thing, what has been carried to a place and set down. The Greek that Josephus uses, **χῶμα** (*chōma*), from **χώννυμι** (*chōnnumi*), to throw up earth, encodes the same act. Neither word contains any notion of a siege. Both name a pile, and the military meaning is entirely a matter of where the pile is put.

**Vallum** works the same way. The base noun is *vallus*, a single stake, and the collective *vallum* is the stake-line; every legionary on the march carried *pila muralia*, sharpened stakes, so that the night camp's palisade travelled with the men who would sleep behind it. *Circumvallatio* adds only the preposition. The Roman genius in these operations is not conceptual but logistical, and the vocabulary is honest about it: an army that can carry its own fence can fortify anywhere, and an army that can heap earth faster than a garrison can eat will take any position that cannot be relieved.

The ram is named for the animal in two languages independently. Latin **aries** is the ram of the flock; Greek **κριός** (*krios*) is the same beast, and Josephus uses it throughout. The metaphor is not literary but descriptive, since the striking head was in fact cast or bound in the shape of a ram's head, and the machine's action is a butt delivered by a suspended beam swung by men in ranks. **Testudo**, tortoise, likewise names the shell rather than the animal: the interlocked shield roof and the timber shed that protected the ram crews are both *testudines*, and the related shed, the *vinea*, borrows its name from a vine arbour because its arched frame looked like one.

The most consequential term is legal rather than mechanical. **Deditio**, from *dēdō*, *dē* plus *dō*, to give away or hand over completely, is the formal act of surrender, and *deditio in fidem* places the surrendered party in the *fides*, the good faith, of the victor. This is not a treaty and confers no rights. A community that made *deditio* placed its walls, its arms, its lands, and its persons at Roman disposal and received back whatever Rome chose to return, and the surrendered were **dediticii**, a status category defined by the absence of standing. Sepphoris made *deditio* and kept its city. Jotapata and Gamla did not, and the difference in outcome is not a difference of Roman temperament but of Roman law: a place taken by storm was legally at the disposal of the storming troops.

Against that Roman vocabulary Josephus supplies one Greek word that indicts him. A deserter is an **αὐτόμολος** (*automolos*), from *autós*, self, and the aorist stem of *blōskō*, to go, so literally the one who goes across of himself. The compound is precise about agency: nobody carried him. Josephus uses the word freely of the men who slipped out of besieged cities to the Roman lines, and the reader is entitled to apply it to the author, who did the same thing at Jotapata and then took his patron's family name. Yosef ben Matityahu became **Flavius Josephus** by the ordinary Roman mechanism, in which an enfranchised or manumitted man assumes the *nomen* of the man who enfranchised him. His name is a summary of his career.

One toponym is transparent and Josephus explains it himself. **גַּמְלָא** (*Gamlāʾ*), Aramaic, is the camel, from Semitic √**g-m-l**, cognate with Hebrew *gāmāl* and Arabic *jamal* (جَمَل), and Josephus states that the place is named for the ridge's resemblance to a camel's hump with its spine. The etymology is a topographic description, and it is also a tactical brief: a settlement on a hogback is unassailable on three sides and has exactly one approach, which is where the Roman ram was placed and where the breach in the wall is still visible.

*Warrant typing.* The derivations of *agger*, *chōma*, *vallus*, *aries*, *krios*, *testudo*, *vinea*, *dēdō*, and *automolos* are Type T. The Semitic √g-m-l cognate set is Type T, and Josephus's own derivation of the toponym is a first-century witness to it. The reading of *deditio* as the legal variable explaining the divergent fates of Sepphoris and Jotapata is Type S, an inference from Roman practice rather than from any statement in the sources.

#### L) Political Economy and Statecraft

The force Vespasian assembled needs to be described accurately, because the volume's figure is right and its description of it is not. Josephus lists three legions, the Fifth Macedonica, the Tenth Fretensis, and the Fifteenth Apollinaris, together with twenty-three auxiliary cohorts, six cavalry alae, and the contingents of four client kings, Agrippa II, Antiochus of Commagene, Sohaemus of Emesa, and Malichus of Nabataea. His round total of sixty thousand is explicitly a total including servants and camp followers. The legionary heavy infantry within that number is on the order of fifteen to eighteen thousand men. The distinction is not pedantry: the ratio of auxiliaries and allied levies to citizen legionaries is the single clearest indicator that Rome fought its provincial wars substantially with provincial manpower, and that a rebellion in Galilee was suppressed in significant part by the armies of neighbouring Semitic kingdoms.

The logistical constraint that dictated the whole campaign shape is fodder, not grain. Men on the march consume something under a kilogram of wheat a day, which is a manageable tonnage; the horses, mules, and oxen that carry the siege train, the artillery, and the grain itself consume bulk forage in quantities that dwarf the human ration and cannot be carried in useful amounts. An army therefore either moves through country that can be grazed and requisitioned, or it stays within reach of water carriage. Sea transport in the Roman Mediterranean was cheaper than land transport by an order of magnitude, which is why the campaign was based on Ptolemais and later Caesarea and why it advanced from the coast inward. It is also why the operation ran in the dry months and stopped: siege works cannot be dug and ramps cannot be built in the winter mud of the Galilean hills.

The strategy of reducing the north first has a standard military rationale that the volume states only as supply interdiction. A besieging army is a stationary army with its back to whatever it has not conquered, and it can be caught between the wall in front and a relieving force behind. Rome's invariable method was to clear the countryside, take the secondary strongholds, and only then invest the capital, so that no field force remained to relieve it. Cutting Jerusalem's food supply was a consequence of that method rather than its object.

The economics of the Galilee itself explain much of the fracture the campaign exploited. The region's marketable surplus was olive oil, and Josephus's own *Life* records that John of Gischala obtained a monopoly on the oil supplied to the Jews of Caesarea Philippi and resold it at a very large multiple of the purchase price, an operation he conducted while nominally organising resistance. Sepphoris, the largest city, had already asked Cestius Gallus for a Roman garrison; Tiberias split into factions; Gischala's commander was trading with the enemy's clients. The Galilee was not a province in revolt but a set of towns with divergent interests, and Vespasian's method of reducing them one at a time was possible because they had already declined to combine.

The two horizons of benefit are unusually far apart here. Within the event, the beneficiary is Vespasian, who acquires not a province but an army: three legions personally loyal to him, a demonstrated record of competence, and, by 69, control of the Egyptian grain supply. That, and not Judaea, is the asset he converts into the principate. The oracle of a world ruler from Judaea, which Josephus, Tacitus, and Suetonius all report in circulation, is the propaganda instrument that converts a usurpation into a fulfilment, and it is a Jewish expectation captured and redirected onto a Roman general by a Jewish priest. The transaction is legible in the text: Josephus says the oracle in fact signified Vespasian.

In transmission, the beneficiary is Josephus. Jotapata must be an epic and the surrender must be providential, because the alternative reading of the same events is that a commander abandoned his men and saved himself. The cave and the lot are the hinge of his entire self-presentation, and they are the one part of the campaign for which no witness but the author could ever exist. He does not, in fact, say that he rigged the draw; he says that it fell out as it did whether by chance or by the providence of God, which is a carefully constructed sentence that permits the reader to supply either. The manipulation now routinely attributed to him is an inference from his own phrasing, and it is a reasonable one, but it is not what the text states.

Finally, the accession itself is misdescribed in the volume and the correction matters for the following volume. Vespasian did not march on Rome. He went to Alexandria and closed his hand on the grain fleet, sent Mucianus west with a field force, and was carried to power by the Danubian legions under Antonius Primus, who won the war at Cremona before Mucianus arrived. Vespasian entered Rome only in the autumn of 70, after Jerusalem had already fallen to his son. The Judaean command was a platform, and it was worked as one.

#### M) Archaeological Dossier

**Yodfat**, Tier 1, excavated in the 1990s, is the cleanest first-century battlefield in the region for a simple reason: the site was never reoccupied. The excavators recovered a defensive wall raised in haste, incorporating the outer walls of existing houses in the manner of a community fortifying itself rather than a state building a fortress; a Roman earthen ramp against the northern slope; dense concentrations of trilobate iron arrowheads and worked limestone ballista projectiles clustered where the wall was attacked; and burnt destruction deposits. Human skeletal remains were recovered from a cistern in what appears to be a secondary deposit, consistent with bodies gathered from the ruins some time after the fighting. There is also a plastered and painted room of some pretension, which tells against reading the place as a village of the desperately poor.

**Gamla**, Tier 1, excavated from 1976, is the second such site and is equally single-period. The eastern wall carries a breach; the approach is littered with ballista stones on the order of two thousand and with many hundreds of iron arrowheads, again concentrated at the point of assault; a round tower anchors the defence; and the wall itself, as at Yodfat, is largely the blocked outer line of the town's own houses. The site preserves one of the very few securely pre-70 synagogue buildings known, together with ritual baths, and it produced the small group of crude local bronzes bearing a redemption legend. The topography matches Josephus's camel-hump description exactly, which is one of the reasons his Galilean topography is rated high even where his numbers are not.

**Sepphoris**, Tier 1, supplies the collaborationist half of the picture in its own words. The city struck bronze coins dated by the regnal year of Nero and naming Vespasian, with a legend styling the place a city of peace. That is a municipal government advertising its *deditio* on the currency, and it is the exact inverse of what the Jerusalem mint was doing with the same medium in the same years.

**Magdala**, Tier 1, is included as the closest attested analogue for what the campaign destroyed rather than as a siege site. The excavated first-century synagogue there, with its carved stone table, is one of a very small number of pre-70 synagogue buildings known anywhere, and it belongs to the lakeside settlement generally identified with Taricheae. It shows what a prosperous Galilean fishing town looked like on the eve of the war.

The debit side is long and it bears on the volume's central figures. First, the forty thousand dead that Josephus reports at Jotapata cannot be reconciled with the excavated extent of the site, which supports a population in the low thousands at most; the number is a literary quantity and should be labelled as one. Second, the mass leap into the ravine at Gamla has no material confirmation: no corresponding deposit of human remains has been recovered at the foot of the ridge, and the account rests on Josephus alone. Third, the cave, the lot, and the survival at Jotapata are unlocatable in principle and unverifiable in fact. Fourth, and most usefully, Josephus is a control on himself: the *Jewish War* presents him as a duly commissioned general organising and drilling a Galilean army on the Roman model, while the *Life*, written decades later against a rival's account, presents a far messier and more improvised role. The two cannot both be right, and the divergence is the best available measure of how much shaping the *War* received.

#### N) Cross-Corpus Reception

The most instructive reception of this campaign is Roman, and it concerns a single oracle. Josephus states that what most incited the Jews to war was an ambiguous prediction found in their sacred writings that at that time someone from their country would become ruler of the world, and he adds that it signified Vespasian. Tacitus, in the fifth book of the *Histories*, reports the same expectation in almost the same terms and applies it the same way. Suetonius, in the life of Vespasian, reports that an ancient and settled conviction prevailed throughout the East that men from Judaea would obtain universal dominion, and that this was understood of Vespasian and Titus. Three writers, two of them Roman and hostile, transmit a Jewish messianic expectation and hand it to a Flavian. Whatever the historical value of Josephus's prison prophecy, the propaganda operation is documented three times over, and it is the clearest surviving case in antiquity of a subject people's eschatology being captured and mounted on the throne that defeated them.

The rabbinic tradition preserves the same story with a different protagonist. At Gittin 56a and following, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai is smuggled out of besieged Jerusalem and hails Vespasian as king, whereupon news of Nero's death arrives and the prophecy is fulfilled. This is a doublet of the Josephus episode in every structural particular: a Jewish notable, a Roman general, an accession foretold, and a personal request granted. Two entirely separate transmission streams, one Greek and Flavian, one Aramaic and rabbinic, preserve the same narrative shape. That may indicate a common event, a common circulating story, or a common need, and the honest position is that the traditions cannot be used to corroborate one another because they may be one tradition wearing two costumes.

The New Testament reception is silent about the campaign and eloquent about its setting. The towns this army moved through are the towns of the Gospel narratives, and the destruction of the Galilean lakeside is the physical terminus of that world; but no New Testament text describes the campaign, which is consistent with the composition of those texts either before it or with their interest lying elsewhere. The absence is not evidence of anything except that the Gospel writers were not writing military history.

The Qur'an and the hadith likewise contain no reception of this campaign, and the absence is expected rather than surprising. The Qur'anic engagement with the Banū Isrāʾīl operates at the level of covenant, prophecy, and consequence, and it registers the destruction of the sanctuary as a moral event, not the reduction of provincial strongpoints. A campaign remembered chiefly for engineering has nothing for that register to hold.

The comparative horizon is Roman siegecraft itself, and it is well attested on the ground elsewhere. Scipio Aemilianus's reduction of Numantia in 133 BCE, with its ring of camps joined by a circumvallation, and Caesar's double lines at Alesia in 52 BCE are both archaeologically recovered, and together with the Judaean sites they establish that what Vespasian did in Galilee was not an innovation but the execution of a doctrine that had been stable for two centuries. What is structurally distinctive about the Galilean case is not the method but the record: this is the only Roman siege campaign of antiquity narrated in detail by the commander of the defeated side, writing in the language of the empire, under the family name of the man who had captured him, about towns that were never rebuilt. The sites are silent, the coins are laconic, and the only voice is a compromised one. That is the methodological condition of the entire war, and it is stated most sharply here, at the moment the author changed sides.


### VOLUME 84 · The Destruction of the Second Temple (70 CE) & Masada (73 CE)

#### A) Biographical Excavation · Introduction
This episode reconstructs the absolute, catastrophic epicenter of ancient Jewish history: the complete incineration of the socio-theological universe of the Second Temple. The targeted chronological window spans the apex of the First Jewish-Roman War (70 CE) to its final, desolate conclusion at the Dead Sea (73 CE). The evidentiary thesis posits that while the Roman legions under General Titus executed a masterclass in mechanized siege warfare, the actual destruction of Jerusalem was exponentially accelerated by a psychotic, cannibalistic civil war among the Jewish rebel factions trapped inside the walls. By burning their own food supplies in a bid for absolute power, the Zealots did Titus's work for him. In the summer of 70 CE, the Roman war machine breached the Temple Mount, permanently destroying the Yahwistic sanctuary, liquidating the Sadducean aristocracy, and erasing the Judean state. The mop-up operation concluded three years later when the Roman Tenth Legion besieged the final Sicarii holdout at Masada, resulting in a mass suicide that denied Rome the psychological satisfaction of taking living captives.

**Era Attestations:**

- **The Arch of Titus (Tier 1):** Erected in Rome shortly after Emperor Titus's death, this massive triumphal arch physically commemorates the subjugation of Judea. Its famous relief panel clearly depicts Roman legionaries parading the sacred, solid-gold Menorah, the Table of Showbread, and the silver trumpets looted from the Jerusalem Temple through the streets of the imperial capital.

- **The Burnt House / Katros Excavations (Tier 1):** Archaeological discoveries in the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem's Old City. Excavators found the basement of a wealthy priestly family (the Katros family) covered in a thick layer of ash, containing a spear, a severed arm bone of a young woman, and coins dating exactly to the Jewish Revolt, perfectly freezing the horrific urban combat and incineration of 70 CE.

- **The Masada Siege Ramp (Tier 1):** The massive, 300-foot earthen ramp constructed by the Roman general Flavius Silva on the western face of the Masada plateau. It remains one of the most perfectly preserved, undisputed examples of Roman siege engineering in the world.

Translator: William Whiston [Josephus, Jewish War 6.5.1] [Genre: Military Historiography / Urban Annihilation]*

**Context:** The Synoptic Gospels record predictions of a classic Roman circumvallation siege, which perfectly materializes in 70 CE when Titus builds a 4.5-mile wooden wall around the city to starve it. Josephus, an eyewitness standing in the Roman camp, records the visceral, apocalyptic horror of the Temple's final moments, recognizing it as the definitive end of an era. [Scholarly Consensus]; Tier 3.

#### C) Raw Symbolism & Immediate Semiotics
- **The Burnt Food Supply:** The ultimate tragedy of extremist factionalism. Before Titus even arrived, the rival Jewish warlords (Simon bar Giora and John of Gischala) burned Jerusalem's massive, multi-year grain reserves to force the populace to fight rather than negotiate. They guaranteed their own starvation.

- **The Circumvallation Wall:** After the Jews destroyed Roman siege engines in a daring sally, Titus ordered his legions to build a massive wooden wall around the entire city in just three days. It symbolized the absolute, inescapable chokehold of the Empire; no one could enter or leave without being crucified.

- **The Fiscus Judaicus (Jewish Tax):** The ultimate imperial insult. After the Temple's destruction, Emperor Vespasian ordered that the annual half-shekel tax every Jew previously paid to Yahweh must now be paid directly to the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus in Rome.

- **The Lots of Masada:** Discovered by archaeologists, small clay ostraca bearing the names of the Sicarii leaders (including "Ben Ya'ir"). These were used to randomly select the ten men who would execute the rest of the community before turning the swords on themselves, perfectly corroborating Josephus's account of the mass suicide. Scope: Total war, factional self-destruction, and imperial triumph.

#### E) Imagery Bridge · Canon ↔ Corroboration (and Qur’an/Hadith)
The imagery of 70 CE is a descent into hell. Following a brief pause during the "Year of the Four Emperors" to when Vespasian leaves Judea to seize the imperial throne in Rome to he tasks his son, Titus, with finishing the war. Titus marches four legions (the 5th, 10th, 12th, and 15th) to the gates of Jerusalem during the Passover festival, trapping hundreds of thousands of pilgrims inside.

The imagery inside the walls is worse than the Roman threat outside. The city is fractured by a psychotic, three-way civil war. Zealot factions slaughter moderate priests, desecrate the Temple altars with the blood of their political rivals, and burn the city's massive food silos. By the time Titus initiates the siege, Jerusalem is already a starving, cannibalistic graveyard.

Titus executes a methodical, grinding siege. The Romans breach the outer "Third Wall," then the "Second Wall." Desperate Jewish defectors trying to escape are caught by Roman patrols and crucified to up to 500 a day, until the Romans literally run out of wood, creating a terrifying forest of rotting corpses facing the city walls.

In the high summer (the 9th of Av, according to tradition), the Roman battering rams shatter the defenses of the Antonia Fortress and spill into the Temple Mount. A Roman soldier throws a blazing firebrand through a golden window. The heavily timbered, magnificent sanctuary erupts into an uncontrollable inferno. The gold melts, the veil burns, and the Sadducean priests hurl themselves into the flames rather than face capture. The Roman legions set up their pagan standards in the ruined courtyard and offer sacrifices to Jupiter.

The imagery fast-forwards three years to the desolate shores of the Dead Sea. A splinter group of assassins (the Sicarii) holds the impregnable Herodian fortress of Masada. The Roman Tenth Legion, under Flavius Silva, surrounds the rock. Month after month, utilizing Jewish slave labor, the Romans build a massive earthen ramp up the 300-foot cliff. When the Roman battering ram finally breaches the wall in the spring of 73 CE, the legionaries charge in, expecting a massive battle. Instead, they are met with absolute, haunting silence. The 960 men, women, and children inside have committed mass suicide, executing a final, horrific act of defiance to deny Rome the glory of their enslavement. The Judean state is dead.
