## EXCURSUS II. The Chronology Problem: Why the Dates Will Not Settle

Every date in this work rests on a chain, and the chains are of very different strengths. Some are anchored to astronomy and are secure to the day. Some are anchored to a king list copied by a priest six centuries after the fact and are secure to within a century, if that. The reader who treats all the dates in a reference work as equally solid will be misled, and the misleading is not the fault of any individual entry but of the convention that prints numbers without their error bars. What follows is an account of how the numbers are actually made, where the joints are, and which disagreements are real disputes about evidence as against notational preferences that have hardened into camps.

The general shape of the problem is this. Absolute chronology, meaning dates in years before the common era, exists in the ancient Near East only where an astronomical observation can be tied to a named year in a documentary sequence, and where that sequence is itself continuous. Everywhere else the dating is relative, built from reign lengths, stratigraphic superposition, and ceramic typology, and it floats until it is pinned. There are very few pins. The whole edifice of second and first millennium Near Eastern chronology hangs from a small number of them, and the further a region or period is from a pin, the wider the uncertainty grows, in a way that compounds rather than averages out.

#### The Assyrian Spine

The single most important pin is Assyrian. The Assyrians named each year after an official, the *limmu* or eponym, and kept lists of these names in order, sometimes with a short note of the year's principal event. Copies of these eponym lists survive, and for the Neo-Assyrian period they form a continuous, cross-checkable sequence running from the early ninth century into the seventh. One entry, in the eponymy of Bur-Sagale of Guzana, records a revolt in the city of Ashur and, in the month Simanu, an eclipse of the sun. Total solar eclipses visible from northern Mesopotamia are rare and their circumstances are calculable backward with certainty. The eclipse in question is that of 15 June 763 BCE. That single line converts the entire relative sequence of Assyrian eponyms into absolute dates, forward and backward, for as long as the list runs continuously.

Everything else follows from this. Assyrian royal inscriptions and annals are dated by eponym, so Assyrian reigns are absolutely dated. Assyrian kings campaigned in the Levant and recorded whom they fought and who paid them, so Levantine kings acquire absolute dates by synchronism. Shalmaneser III's account of the battle at Qarqar names Ahab the Israelite among the coalition, and the battle is dated to 853 BCE. The same king's Black Obelisk records tribute from Jehu, dated to 841. Tiglath-pileser III records tribute from Menahem, and later campaigns that removed Galilee. Sennacherib's annals describe the campaign of 701 against Hezekiah in circumstantial detail, and the siege of Lachish that accompanied it is depicted on the reliefs from his palace at Nineveh and is confirmed by the destruction of Lachish Level III on the ground. Four or five hard synchronisms of this kind fix the Israelite and Judean monarchies to within a year or two across roughly a century and a half. This is why the ninth through seventh centuries are the best-dated stretch in the entire history and why the dating grows steadily worse as one moves earlier.

The Babylonian material extends the same discipline. The Babylonian Chronicle series, terse year-by-year notices of military and political events, includes the tablet that records Nebuchadnezzar's capture of Jerusalem, giving the day and month of the city's surrender; the conversion yields mid-March 597 BCE. Three exilic events, the deportation of 597, the destruction of the Temple, and the release of Jehoiachin, are therefore datable within a year, and one of them within a day. The destruction date is the one that still moves, between 587 and 586, and the reason is instructive: nothing in the Babylonian record dates it, so it must be calculated from Zedekiah's regnal years as given in Kings and Jeremiah, and the calculation depends on whether one reckons from a spring or an autumn new year and whether the accession year is counted. A one-year uncertainty at the best-documented event in the entire pre-Hellenistic history of Judah is a useful calibration of what the discipline can and cannot deliver.

#### Ptolemy, the Diaries, and the Astronomical Floor

Two further instruments carry the astronomical anchoring forward and make the later periods secure. The first is the king list conventionally called Ptolemy's Canon, a table of Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian, Ptolemaic, and Roman rulers with regnal lengths counted in Egyptian civil years of exactly 365 days, beginning with Nabonassar of Babylon in 747 BCE. Because the Egyptian civil year never intercalated, it is a perfectly regular counter, and because Ptolemy used the Canon to date the astronomical observations he cites in the *Almagest*, the list is independently checkable at many points against calculable positions of the sun, moon, and planets. It survives as an astronomer's working tool rather than a chronicler's monument, which is exactly why it is reliable: a scribe copying a propaganda list may lengthen a reign, but an astronomer computing eclipse intervals cannot afford to.

The second is the corpus of Babylonian astronomical diaries, a series of tablets recording night-by-night observations of lunar and planetary positions, eclipses, weather, the level of the Euphrates, and the market prices of six commodities, together with occasional historical notes. The series runs, with gaps, from the mid-seventh century BCE into the first century BCE. Because every tablet carries datable astronomical content, the historical notes on the same tablets are datable with it. The diaries are the reason Seleucid and late Achaemenid chronology is firm to the day, and they supply the mechanism by which several Hellenistic events in this history are placed exactly.

#### Why Egypt Is Softer

Egyptian chronology is presented in reference works with the same confident precision as Assyrian chronology and does not deserve it. Egypt produced no continuous eponym sequence, and its surviving king lists are either fragmentary, tendentious, or both. The Palermo Stone preserves Old Kingdom annals in pieces. The Turin Royal Canon, a Ramesside papyrus, gives reigns with year totals and is the closest thing to a comprehensive list, but it survives in fragments whose reassembly is itself an argument. Manetho's history, compiled in the third century BCE, is lost and known only through excerpts quoted by Josephus and by later Christian chronographers, who disagree with one another on the numbers. So Egyptian absolute chronology is built primarily by dead reckoning: summing reign lengths backward from a later fixed point, with the gaps filled by inference about coregencies and overlapping dynasties.

The attempt to pin this arithmetic astronomically rests on the heliacal rising of the star Sothis, which is Sirius. The Egyptian civil year of 365 days lost a quarter of a day annually against the solar year, so the civil calendar drifted through the seasons on a cycle of roughly 1,460 years, and a recorded observation of the Sothic rising on a given civil date theoretically fixes the year within that cycle. Two such records are load-bearing: a calendar on the verso of the Ebers Papyrus, giving a Sothic date in year nine of Amenhotep I, and a letter among the Illahun papyri predicting the rising in year seven of Senwosret III. Both have been used to anchor the New Kingdom and Middle Kingdom respectively.

The difficulty is that the calculation is highly sensitive to assumptions that cannot be independently checked. The date of the heliacal rising depends on the latitude of the observer, and the difference between observing from the Delta, from Thebes, and from Elephantine shifts the resulting absolute date by decades and, on some reconstructions, by more than a century. It is not established where either observation was made. It is not established whether the Ebers text records an observation at all rather than a schematic calendrical entry. It is not established that the arcus visionis, the sun's depression at which Sirius first becomes visible, was the value modern calculations assume. Rolf Krauss and others have argued the Sothic method through in detail and reached results that differ from the conventional scheme, and a number of specialists now prefer to anchor Egyptian chronology on lunar dates recorded in reign years, which give discrete solutions but usually several of them separated by twenty-five-year intervals.

The practical consequence is a hierarchy of confidence that should travel with every Egyptian date in this work. New Kingdom dates are good to roughly a decade or two. Middle Kingdom dates carry several decades of play. Old Kingdom dates carry a century or more. Radiocarbon programmes run on securely provenanced short-lived samples from datable Egyptian contexts have, on the whole, supported the conventional scheme rather than the radical revisions, which is a genuine and welcome result, but radiocarbon at that resolution constrains to a few decades at best and cannot adjudicate a dispute over fifteen years.

#### The Third Intermediate Period and the Shoshenq Peg

The soft spot in Egyptian chronology that matters most for this history is the Third Intermediate Period, the stretch between the end of the New Kingdom and the Kushite and Saite recoveries. Political authority in this period was fragmented: a dynasty at Tanis in the Delta, a line of Libyan-descended kings, a parallel and partly independent line of High Priests of Amun at Thebes, and later rival kings ruling simultaneously in different cities. Reign lengths are poorly attested. The standard reconstruction, worked out in painstaking detail by Kenneth Kitchen, assembles the sequence from genealogies of priestly families, from the dated burials of the Apis bulls in the Serapeum at Saqqara, and from the highest attested regnal year for each king, and it is the framework the field uses. It is also, by its own author's account, a reconstruction with places where the evidence runs out and the arithmetic is carried by assumption about how much two dynasties overlapped.

This matters because the Third Intermediate Period supplies the one synchronism that ties Egyptian chronology to the Levantine Iron Age. 1 Kings 14:25 places a campaign by Shishak against Jerusalem in the fifth year of Rehoboam. The identification of Shishak with Shoshenq I is not seriously contested, and Shoshenq I did campaign in the Levant: the Bubastite Portal at Karnak carries a relief and a topographical list of some hundred and fifty place names claimed as conquests, and a fragment of a victory stela of Shoshenq I was recovered at Megiddo, which independently confirms that his army reached the Jezreel Valley. The conventional date for the campaign is around 925 BCE.

Three cautions attach. First, the date rests on the internal Egyptian arithmetic just described, so it is not independent of the Third Intermediate Period reconstruction. Second, the Karnak list does not contain a readable entry for Jerusalem, and its geographical emphasis falls on the northern valleys and the Negev rather than on the Judean hills, which sits awkwardly with the biblical account of a raid on the Judean capital. Third, and most consequentially, Levantine archaeologists use the Shoshenq campaign as a dating instrument, attributing destruction layers to it and thereby fixing the ceramic sequence. When a destruction at a given site is dated by the Shoshenq campaign, and the Shoshenq campaign is dated by Egyptian dead reckoning, and the resulting ceramic phase is then used to date other sites, the whole structure is resting on a single peg whose own security is less than the confident round number suggests. Israel Finkelstein has questioned the attribution of particular destructions to Shoshenq, and the questioning is legitimate even where one does not accept his broader chronological programme.

#### Mesopotamia: High, Middle, Low, Ultra-Low

For the second millennium the Mesopotamian problem is of a different character, and it is the cleanest illustration in the discipline of how a single ambiguous observation can produce competing chronologies that survive for generations.

The relative sequence of Old Babylonian and Old Assyrian rulers is well established from king lists, date formulae, and the eponym sequence recovered from the Old Assyrian merchant archives at Kültepe. What is missing is an absolute pin. The candidate pin is a tablet in the celestial omen series *Enuma Anu Enlil*, conventionally Tablet 63, known as the Venus Tablet of Ammisaduqa, which records the dates of first and last visibility of Venus over twenty-one years in the reign of a king identified as Ammisaduqa, the fourth successor of Hammurabi. Venus phenomena are calculable, and the observations therefore ought to fix the reign.

They do not, because the Venus cycle repeats. The pattern of risings and settings recurs at intervals of eight years and, in a longer approximation, at intervals of fifty-six and sixty-four years, so the recorded sequence fits multiple positions in the first and second millennia. The tablet is also a late copy with textual corruption, and some of the recorded intervals are astronomically impossible as written, which forces the analyst to decide which observations to trust. Different decisions yield different solutions, and the solutions have hardened into named chronologies. On the high chronology Hammurabi reigns roughly 1848 to 1806 BCE. On the middle chronology, which is the conventional scheme used in most reference works including this one, he reigns 1792 to 1750. On the low or short chronology he reigns 1728 to 1686. On the ultra-low chronology proposed by Gasche, Armstrong, Cole, and Gurzadyan he reigns 1696 to 1654. The spread from the highest to the lowest is more than a century and a half. The Hittite sack of Babylon that ended the First Dynasty falls in 1595 on the middle chronology, 1531 on the low, and 1499 on the ultra-low.

Nothing in the historical evidence adjudicates this, which is why the debate has run for so long without resolution. What has changed recently is the introduction of independent physical evidence. Dendrochronological sequences from Anatolian sites, combined with radiocarbon determinations on wood and on short-lived material from securely stratified Middle Bronze contexts, have been argued to favour the middle chronology or something close to it, and to tell strongly against the ultra-low. That work does not close the question, but it has shifted the burden, and the ultra-low is now a minority position. The middle chronology is retained here as a convention, which is the honest reason to retain it: it is what the literature uses, and abandoning it would make this work incommensurable with everything the reader would consult next. Every second-millennium Mesopotamian date in this work should therefore be read with a silent qualifier attached, that it is a middle-chronology date and would move bodily by up to a century if the convention changed.

#### The Exodus Date

The Exodus date dispute is the point at which all these instabilities converge, and it cannot be settled because the evidence on both sides is of the wrong kind to be decisive.

The case for an early date rests on a single verse. 1 Kings 6:1 states that Solomon began building the Temple in the four hundred and eightieth year after the Israelites came out of Egypt, in the fourth year of his reign. Solomon's fourth year, working backward from the Assyrian-anchored synchronisms and the schism, falls around 967 or 966 BCE, which places the Exodus around 1446 BCE, in the Eighteenth Dynasty, with Thutmose III or Amenhotep II as the pharaoh of the oppression or the departure.

Three difficulties attach to the number itself. First, four hundred and eighty is twelve times forty, and forty is the schematic generation-figure of Hebrew narrative, used repeatedly for periods whose actual length is not being reported. A figure of twelve generations, converted to years at a notional forty per generation, is a plausible reading of what the number is doing, and if the actual generation length was closer to twenty-five years the same twelve generations yield about three hundred years and a thirteenth-century Exodus. Second, the Septuagint reads four hundred and forty at this verse, not four hundred and eighty. A figure that varies between the textual traditions is not a fixed datum. Third, the related chronological statements do not cohere. Genesis 15:13 gives four hundred years of affliction. Exodus 12:40 in the Masoretic Text gives four hundred and thirty years of sojourn in Egypt, while the Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch give four hundred and thirty years in Egypt and Canaan together, which halves the Egyptian sojourn. These are not roundings of one another; they are different schemes.

The case for a late date rests on a name. Exodus 1:11 has the Israelites building the store cities Pithom and Raamses. The city of Pi-Ramesses in the eastern Delta was founded by Ramesses II, whose reign runs from roughly 1279 to 1213 BCE, and it was abandoned when the branch of the Nile serving it silted up, after which its stone was carted to Tanis. A narrative that names it as a construction project is naming a place that existed under that name for a limited window. The consequent reconstruction puts the departure around the middle of the thirteenth century.

The counter-argument is that the name may be an updating. The same corpus refers to Zoan, which is Tanis, in contexts earlier than its foundation, and Genesis 13:10 explains a landscape by reference to a destruction that had not yet occurred in the narrative, and Genesis 14:14 uses the name Dan for a place the book of Judges says was renamed later. Scribal modernization of toponyms so that an audience can locate the story is well attested and is exactly the sort of change that leaves an anachronistic name in an otherwise older narrative. A name therefore dates a layer of the telling with confidence and dates the event only weakly.

The one hard external datum is the victory stela of Merneptah, in which the closing Canaanite stanza names Ashkelon, Gezer, Yanoam, and Israel, the last written with the determinative for a people rather than for a land or a city. The stela is dated to Merneptah's fifth year, around 1207 BCE. Israel therefore existed in Canaan, as a group Egyptian scribes classified as a people, by that date. This is a hard terminus ante quem and it constrains both models. It is comfortable for the early date, which has had two centuries to spare. It is tight for the late date, which must fit an Exodus, a wilderness period, and enough settlement in Canaan for an Egyptian king to notice and to claim a victory over, into roughly forty years.

Neither model is secure, and the reason is that the two arguments are not in contact. The early date is an argument from a schematic number in a text redacted centuries later. The late date is an argument from a toponym that may have been updated. Neither is the kind of evidence that can defeat the other. The archaeological evidence, which one might hope would arbitrate, does not, because it disconfirms both: neither 1446 nor 1250 produces a Canaan matching the conquest narrative, for reasons set out in the following excursus. A reader is entitled to hold the question open, and the honest position is that the tradition preserves a memory of departure from Egypt whose date cannot presently be fixed and may never be.

#### Judges Will Not Sum

A related failure of the internal chronology deserves separate statement, because it is often noticed and rarely followed through. The book of Judges assigns durations to oppressions and to judgeships. Added together with the wilderness period, the conquest, the years of Eli, the career of Samuel, the reign of Saul, and the forty years of David, these figures substantially exceed the four hundred and eighty years of 1 Kings 6:1, on the order of a century or more depending on how the unstated intervals are handled. The excess is not marginal and cannot be absorbed by rounding.

There are two coherent responses and they are not compatible with each other. The first is that four hundred and eighty is schematic and the Judges figures are approximately real, in which case the period is longer than Kings allows and the Exodus is earlier than either standard model. The second is that the Judges figures are themselves schematic, which their own form suggests, since a striking proportion of them are forty, eighty, or twenty, and that the judgeships were regional and partly concurrent rather than sequential and national, which the narratives themselves imply: Jephthah operates in Gilead, Samson in the Shephelah against Philistines, Deborah in the northern valleys, and there is nothing in the text requiring that a judge in Gilead and a judge in Dan held office at different times. On the second reading the durations are not a timeline at all but a rhetorical structure, and summing them is a category error. The second reading is more probable, and its consequence is that the period between the settlement and the monarchy has no internal chronology and must be dated archaeologically or not at all.

#### Kings, Chronicles, and the Thiele Solution

For the divided monarchy the situation improves dramatically, because the text supplies a dense network of cross-references and the Assyrian record supplies external pins. It also supplies a problem. Kings dates each accession by a synchronism with the reigning king of the other kingdom and then gives a reign length. On a naive reading these data are mutually inconsistent: the sums for Israel and Judah between the schism and the fall of Samaria do not match, and individual synchronisms conflict with the reign lengths on either side of them.

Edwin Thiele's reconstruction, first published in 1951 and revised over three decades, is the standard attempt to make the system cohere, and it works by proposing three mechanisms. The first is that two different systems of counting regnal years were in use. Under accession-year reckoning, also called postdating, the remainder of the calendar year in which a king takes the throne is credited to his predecessor and his own year one begins at the next new year. Under non-accession-year reckoning, or antedating, the partial year is counted as year one, so every reign is inflated by up to a year relative to the other system. Thiele argued that Judah used accession-year reckoning, that Israel used non-accession reckoning and later switched, and that Judah switched at one point too. The second mechanism is that the two kingdoms used different calendar new years, Nisan in the spring for Israel and Tishri in the autumn for Judah, so a synchronism between them can be off by a fraction of a year in either direction. The third is coregency: a son enthroned during his father's lifetime, with one source counting his years from the coregency and another from the sole reign.

With these instruments Thiele produced a scheme internally consistent and anchored to Qarqar in 853 and Jehu's tribute in 841, and it has been extremely influential; a large fraction of the monarchy dates in circulation derive from it. The criticisms are serious and should be stated. The coregencies are, with few exceptions, not reported by the text; they are inferred because the arithmetic requires them, which makes the solution unfalsifiable in the way that any scheme with enough free parameters becomes unfalsifiable. The number of coregencies required is large. Thiele himself could not reconcile the Hezekiah synchronisms with the reign of Hoshea and the fall of Samaria, and concluded that those particular verses were erroneous, which is a legitimate move but is an admission that the system does not fully close. Competing schemes by Gershon Galil, Jeremy Hughes, and others differ from Thiele and from each other by several years at various points, and there is no agreed method for choosing among them.

The practical result is that divided-monarchy dates are good to within a few years and occasionally to within one, and that the residual uncertainty is not random noise but systematic disagreement among reconstructions. Where a date in this work for an Israelite or Judean king differs by two or three years from a date the reader has seen elsewhere, the difference is almost always a choice among these schemes and not a factual dispute.

Chronicles compounds the problem in an instructive way. It reproduces much of Kings' chronological framework but alters figures at points, and its own theological programme, which requires that each reign's length and manner of ending be legible as reward or punishment, gives it a motive to adjust. The comparison is therefore useful evidence about how ancient chronological data were transmitted and edited, which is treated in the following excursus.

#### The Iron Age Low Chronology

The most consequential archaeological chronology dispute of the past three decades concerns a difference of roughly seventy-five to one hundred years in the Iron Age Levantine sequence, and it matters because the century in question is precisely the one in which a united monarchy is supposed to have existed.

The conventional scheme, established by Yigael Yadin and defended in modified form by Amihai Mazar, assigned a set of monumental buildings to the tenth century and to Solomon: the palaces and the six-chambered gate at Megiddo, the gate and casemate system at Hazor, and the six-chambered gate at Gezer, on the authority of 1 Kings 9:15, which names those three cities together as Solomonic building projects. The circularity is obvious and was noticed early: the buildings were dated by the verse and then adduced as evidence for the verse.

Israel Finkelstein's Low Chronology, argued from the mid-1990s, proposed lowering the whole Iron I and early Iron IIA sequence by seventy-five to a hundred years. Two arguments carried most of the weight. The first concerned Philistine bichrome pottery, which Finkelstein observed does not appear in strata under Egyptian control, and which he therefore dated after the Egyptian withdrawal rather than contemporary with it, pulling the beginning of the sequence down. The second concerned the pottery from the enclosure at Jezreel, a site securely attributed to the Omride dynasty by the biblical text and destroyed in the mid-ninth century, whose ceramic assemblage was found to resemble that of the Megiddo stratum conventionally assigned to Solomon. If the Megiddo assemblage is contemporary with Jezreel, the Megiddo palaces are Omride, not Solomonic. The consequence is a ninth-century date for the first monumental architecture in the north and the absence of any archaeological correlate for a tenth-century state.

The responses were substantial. Amihai Mazar proposed a Modified Conventional Chronology that lengthens Iron IIA to span roughly the tenth and ninth centuries, which absorbs much of the disagreement by declining to draw a sharp line where the low chronology needs one. Amnon Ben-Tor and Doron Ben-Ami argued from the Hazor stratigraphy for a tenth-century date for the relevant gate. Steven Ortiz and Samuel Wolff, re-excavating Gezer, argued for a tenth-century context for the six-chambered gate against the low chronology's reassignment. The dispute became, and remains, the central methodological argument in Levantine Iron Age archaeology.

Four sites are the crux. Megiddo is the crux because it has the disputed monumental buildings and a long stratified sequence, and because the renewed Tel Aviv excavation is directed by the low chronology's principal advocate, so the stratigraphic reading and the chronological proposal are entangled. Hazor and Gezer are the crux because they carry the other two of the three Solomonic cities and because their excavators reached opposite conclusions from the same class of evidence. Tel Rehov is the crux for a different reason: it produced an unusually long, well-stratified Iron Age sequence from which Amihai Mazar and his collaborators, working with Hendrik Bruins and Johannes van der Plicht, obtained a large series of radiocarbon determinations on short-lived samples, and argued that the results supported the conventional or modified conventional scheme. Finkelstein, working with Eli Piasetzky, produced competing analyses of overlapping datasets and argued that they supported a low or low-modified system.

Khirbet Qeiyafa entered the argument later and sharpened it. Excavated from 2007 by Yosef Garfinkel and Saar Ganor, it is a fortified site in the Elah Valley with a casemate wall, two gates, and a short single-phase occupation, and olive pits from destruction contexts yielded radiocarbon determinations pointing to the late eleventh or early tenth century. If the site is a Judahite foundation, it demonstrates fortified construction in the Shephelah at exactly the date the low chronology denies it. The identification is disputed: alternatives that read the site as Canaanite, Philistine, or as belonging to a northern polity have been proposed, notably by Nadav Naaman and by Finkelstein and Alexander Fantalkin, and the ostracon recovered there is written in an early alphabetic script whose reading is genuinely uncertain, so it cannot settle the ethnic attribution. What Qeiyafa established beyond dispute is that a substantial fortified site existed in the Shephelah around 1000 BCE, which was not previously demonstrable, and that its builders had the organizational capacity to raise a casemate circuit around a hilltop and to abandon it within a generation or two.

The field has converged somewhat without resolving. Most current schemes place the Iron I to Iron IIA transition in the later tenth century, which is neither the conventional date nor the low date but sits between them, and the remaining disagreement is measured in decades rather than in a century. That is real progress. It does not restore the Solomonic attribution of the northern monumental architecture, which is now widely doubted on grounds independent of the chronological dispute, and it does not vindicate the low chronology's strongest formulation either.

#### What Radiocarbon Can and Cannot Do

Because so much of the preceding turns on radiocarbon, its mechanism and its limits must be set out plainly, since it is routinely cited in popular accounts as though it delivered calendar dates directly. It does not.

The measurement yields a radiocarbon age, an expression of how much carbon-14 remains in a sample relative to a modern standard, on the assumption of a constant decay rate and a known starting concentration. The starting concentration was not constant. Atmospheric carbon-14 production varies with solar activity and the geomagnetic field, and the carbon reservoir exchanges between atmosphere, biosphere, and ocean at varying rates. Converting a radiocarbon age to a calendar date therefore requires a calibration curve built from material of independently known age, principally dendrochronologically dated tree rings, supplemented by other archives. The current international curve, IntCal20, is the product of decades of accumulated measurement.

The curve is not a straight line. It wiggles, and in places it flattens. A flat section, called a plateau, is a stretch of calendar time in which many successive years share effectively the same radiocarbon age, so that a single measurement calibrates to a very wide or multimodal calendar range. The most notorious is the Hallstatt plateau, running roughly from 800 to 400 BCE, across which radiocarbon is nearly useless for fine dating: a sample from anywhere in that four-century span can calibrate to most of it. This has direct consequences for this history. The late Iron Age, the Assyrian and Babylonian periods, the destruction of Jerusalem, and the early Persian period all fall inside or adjacent to the plateau, which is why the chronology of those centuries is carried by textual synchronism rather than by physical dating, and why radiocarbon is decisive in the tenth and ninth centuries but not in the seventh and sixth.

Bayesian modelling is the technique that has made radiocarbon useful at archaeological resolution, and it is worth understanding what it does. If a set of samples comes from a sequence of strata whose order is known, that ordering is information independent of the radiocarbon measurements, and it can be imposed as a prior constraint on the calibration. The model then finds the set of calendar dates consistent both with the individual measurements and with the required order, and the resulting posterior ranges are far tighter than any individual calibration. Software implementing this, principally OxCal, is now standard. The power is real: a stratified sequence with many determinations can constrain a transition to within a few decades even where a single date would span two centuries.

The limitation is equally real and is the source of much of the Iron Age dispute. The output depends on the model, and the model is a set of choices: which samples to include, which to exclude as outliers, where to place the phase boundaries, whether the phases are contiguous or separated by gaps, and what prior to place on the gap lengths. Two competent teams modelling overlapping data with different phase structures and different outlier treatments will produce different answers, and both will be internally valid. This is precisely what happened with the Iron Age determinations, and it is why the radiocarbon evidence did not settle the low chronology debate as both sides expected it would. A Bayesian date range is a conditional statement, and the condition is the archaeologist's stratigraphic interpretation.

Two further sample-level problems must be controlled. The first is old wood. A radiocarbon measurement on wood dates the growth of the wood, not the event that deposited it. A beam cut from the heartwood of a long-lived cedar or oak may be centuries older than the building it supports, and beams were routinely salvaged and reused, sometimes across several buildings. Determinations on structural timber therefore systematically overestimate the age of a destruction. The correction is to prefer short-lived samples: olive pits, grape pips, cereal grains, twigs, which grew within a year or a few years of their deposition. The best Levantine Iron Age sequences, including Tel Rehov and Khirbet Qeiyafa, are built on such material, which is why they carry weight.

The second is the assumption that a sample's context is what the excavator says it is. A seed in a destruction layer may have been in a jar destroyed with the building, or it may have washed in, or it may derive from earlier fill disturbed during construction. Contextual security is a stratigraphic judgment, not a laboratory measurement, and a physically impeccable determination on a badly contexted sample is worthless. There has also been discussion of whether the calibration curve, built largely from material grown in other regions and seasons, requires a regional offset for the eastern Mediterranean; the question has been raised seriously and remains open, and if an offset of even a couple of decades is established it will move Levantine radiocarbon chronology bodily.

#### What the Reader Should Do

The dates in this work are of at least four kinds, and the reader who keeps them distinct will not be misled by any of them.

Astronomically anchored dates are secure. The 763 eclipse, the surrender of Jerusalem in March 597, the campaign of 701, Qarqar in 853, and every date derived from the Babylonian diaries or Ptolemy's Canon are as firm as any date in ancient history. Where this work gives such a date without qualification, the confidence is warranted.

Synchronism-derived dates are good to within a few years. The reigns of the Israelite and Judean kings, dated by anchoring the biblical framework to the Assyrian pins, fall here. A discrepancy of two or three years against another reference work is a difference of reconstruction, not of evidence, and nothing in the historical argument turns on it.

Convention-derived dates are stable but not secure, and they can move as a body. Middle-chronology Mesopotamian dates and conventional Egyptian dates before the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty are of this kind. They are used here because they are the currency of the literature. They should be read as positions in an agreed scheme rather than as measurements, and a reader encountering a Middle Bronze date should mentally attach a range of a century.

Archaeologically derived dates are the softest and the most contested, and they are the ones where the reader should look for the argument rather than accepting the number. Any date assigned to a stratum, a destruction, or a ceramic phase is the output of a chain that runs through typology, stratigraphic interpretation, radiocarbon modelling, and often a textual synchronism, and each link can move. The Iron I to Iron IIA transition is the standing example: a genuine dispute about real evidence in which competent specialists differ, which has narrowed but has not closed.

Two habits follow. The first is to distrust precision that exceeds its warrant. A date given to the year for the second millennium is almost always a convention or a calculation, not an observation, and the appearance of exactness is an artefact of the arithmetic rather than a property of the evidence. The second is to notice when a historical argument depends on a date rather than merely mentioning one. Most narrative statements in this history survive a shift of fifty years without alteration; a small number do not, and those are the places where the chronological argument has to be made explicitly rather than assumed. Where a conclusion in this work would change if the low chronology were correct, or if the Exodus were early rather than late, or if the middle chronology were abandoned, that dependence is stated. Where it is not stated, the conclusion is robust to the dispute, and the reader may take the number as a convenience and move on.
