## EXCURSUS III. The Documentary Problem: Who Wrote This, and When, and For Whom

A historian working from the Hebrew Bible is working from a library, not a book, and the volumes of that library were written, edited, combined, and recopied over roughly a millennium by people with different purposes and different information. This is not a theological claim and it does not require any position on the origin or authority of the text. It is the ordinary condition of ancient literature. Homer, the Gilgamesh material, the Egyptian wisdom corpus, and the Zoroastrian Avesta are all composite in the same sense, and no one reads them as though a single hand produced them at a single moment. What distinguishes the biblical case is that the composition history has been studied more intensively than any other in the ancient world, that the results are contested at a level of detail no other corpus attracts, and that a great deal has been asserted about it with far more confidence than the evidence supports, in both directions.

The historian's question is narrower than the theologian's and narrower than the literary critic's. It is: given a passage, what can be inferred about when the information in it was set down, from what, and by someone answering to whom. That question can often be answered partially and is worth answering partially, because the answer changes how much weight the passage bears.

#### The Hypothesis and What It Was For

The classical Documentary Hypothesis emerged from a simple observation and grew into a system. The observation, made by Jean Astruc in 1753 and refined through the following century, was that the divine name alternates in Genesis in a way that correlates with other features: passages using the tetragrammaton tend to share a style and a theology, and passages using Elohim tend to share a different one. Wilhelm de Wette argued in 1805 that Deuteronomy stood apart from the rest of the Pentateuch and was connected to the book reportedly found in the Temple under Josiah, which remains the single most durable dating peg in the whole field. Hermann Hupfeld argued in 1853 that the Elohistic material was itself two sources rather than one. Karl Heinrich Graf and Abraham Kuenen argued that the priestly and cultic legislation, long assumed to be the oldest stratum because it was the most archaic-sounding, was in fact the latest.

Julius Wellhausen's *Prolegomena to the History of Israel* consolidated this into the form that dominated the field for a century. Four documents: J, using the divine name from the beginning, vivid and anthropomorphic; E, using Elohim until Sinai, more reticent and interested in dreams and prophets; D, essentially Deuteronomy, with its centralizing programme; and P, the Priestly source, with its genealogies, its precise dating formulae, its transcendent deity, and its elaborate cult.

The crucial move was not the identification of the sources but the ordering. By placing P last, Wellhausen inverted the traditional sequence, in which the Law was given at Sinai and the prophets subsequently called Israel back to it. On his scheme the prophets came first and the Law came last, and the elaborate priestly system was the product of the exile and after, a late crystallization rather than an original constitution. The historical narrative he built on this, in which a spontaneous early religion of the open air hardened into post-exilic legalism, is a nineteenth-century construction with a nineteenth-century shape and its own confessional and cultural commitments, and the shape has been criticized as much as the source analysis. The two should be assessed separately, because they are separable.

#### What Survived Wellhausen

Three findings have survived essentially intact and command something near consensus outside explicitly confessional scholarship.

The first is that the Pentateuch is composite. The evidence is internal and cumulative and does not depend on any particular reconstruction. There are two creation accounts with different orders of creation and different divine names. The flood narrative contains two interwoven strands with different animal counts, different durations, and different terminology, which can be separated into two continuous and internally coherent accounts. Joseph is sold by two different sets of people in adjacent verses. Moses' father-in-law bears different names. The Decalogue appears twice with a differently motivated sabbath commandment. Laws in Exodus, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy give incompatible rules for the same institutions, most conspicuously the location of slaughter and the treatment of the Passover. These are not the ordinary variations of a single author. They are the seams of combination, and they are visible without any theory.

The second is that a Priestly stratum exists and is identifiable with considerable confidence. P has a signature so distinctive that scholars who disagree about everything else generally agree on where it is. It uses a fixed set of formulae, above all the *toledot* genealogical superscription; it dates events precisely by year, month, and day; it is systematically interested in measurement, in genealogy, and in the boundaries of holiness; it holds that the divine name was not revealed to the ancestors but disclosed to Moses, so that its patriarchal narratives use different divine designations by design rather than by chance; and it has no sacrifice before Sinai, because on its scheme sacrifice requires a priesthood that does not yet exist. P is the most secure of the classical sources and the one on which historical arguments can most safely rest.

The third is that Deuteronomy is a distinct work with a programme, and that its programme is centralization: a single legitimate place of sacrifice, the abolition of the local shrines, and the consequent restructuring of slaughter, tithe, festival, and judicial procedure to accommodate the removal of local cult. De Wette's connection of that programme with the reform reported in 2 Kings 22 to 23 is an inference and not a demonstration, but it is a strong inference, because the reform as narrated does precisely what Deuteronomy legislates and nothing else in the corpus does.

#### What Did Not Survive

Two elements of the classical scheme have been substantially abandoned, and it matters which.

E as a continuous independent document is no longer widely defended. The material assigned to it is fragmentary, it does not form a narrative that stands on its own, and the criterion that identified it, the divine name, fails after Exodus 3, where by E's own account the name is revealed and both sources thereafter use it. Most current treatments regard the E material either as fragments of an alternative tradition incorporated into another source or as a supplementary layer rather than a document.

J as an early, coherent, tenth-century national epic has been under sustained attack for fifty years, chiefly from European scholarship. Gerhard von Rad's picture of a Yahwist writing in a Solomonic enlightenment now has few defenders. John Van Seters argued that the Yahwist is an exilic historian writing after and in dependence on the Deuteronomistic History, which reverses the classical order. Rolf Rendtorff and Erhard Blum dispensed with continuous sources altogether for the pre-Priestly material, arguing instead that the Pentateuch grew from originally independent blocks, a patriarchal complex, an exodus complex, a Sinai complex, which were joined by compositional layers rather than braided from parallel documents. Christoph Levin retained a Yahwist but made him a late redactor rather than an early author. The cumulative effect is that the pre-Priestly narrative material is now the least securely reconstructed part of the Pentateuch, which is the reverse of the classical picture, in which J was the foundation.

The neat arithmetic has gone with it. The classical hypothesis promised that every verse could be assigned to one of four documents. In practice the assignments required an expanding apparatus of redactors, and a method that explains any datum by positing another editor has stopped constraining anything.

#### The Current Landscape

Three broad approaches are in play, and most working scholars use elements of more than one.

The neo-documentarians, associated with Baruch Schwartz, Joel Baden, and Jeffrey Stackert and standing in a line of Israeli scholarship running back through Menahem Haran, maintain four continuous documents but reach them by a different route. They set aside divine names, vocabulary, and theology as primary criteria, on the grounds that these can be shared or imitated, and rely instead on narrative continuity and contradiction: where a text cannot be read as a single coherent sequence of events, and where separating it produces two sequences that each cohere, the separation is warranted. They are generally agnostic about absolute dating, which is a methodological virtue and a limitation for the historian.

The supplementary models envisage a base narrative successively expanded by identifiable layers, principally Deuteronomistic and Priestly, each adding material and reframing what it received. This handles the Priestly material well, since P can be read as an expansion of an existing narrative as easily as an independent one, and it handles the visible reframings of Deuteronomy well.

The fragmentary or block models, in the line of Rendtorff and Blum, treat the large traditions as originally independent and the Pentateuch as the product of their combination. This accounts elegantly for the fact that the patriarchal narratives and the exodus narrative make almost no reference to one another outside the connective passages, and that the ancestors of Genesis are not treated as an argument in the exodus material, which would be surprising if they had always been one story.

For the historian the useful residue is not a preferred model but a set of confident partial statements. The Pentateuch reached its final form in the Persian period. It contains a Priestly stratum with a distinctive and identifiable profile, whose date is disputed within a range from the late monarchy to the post-exilic period but which is certainly later than some of the material it frames. It contains a Deuteronomic core with a seventh-century profile. It contains earlier material of uncertain extent, including poetry that is linguistically archaic on independent grounds, embedded in later frames. Where a historical argument requires that a particular passage be early, that must be argued for the passage and cannot be inherited from a source-critical label.

#### The Deuteronomistic History: Noth Against Cross

For the historian of the monarchy the more consequential source-critical debate concerns not the Pentateuch but the books from Deuteronomy through Kings.

Martin Noth argued in 1943 that Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings are not separate books later collected but a single continuous work, composed by one author in the exile, who assembled diverse sources and imposed unity on them by inserting speeches and summarizing reflections at the structural joints. Joshua's farewell address, Samuel's speech at the making of the kingship, Solomon's Temple prayer, and the long theological explanation of the fall of Samaria are the load-bearing insertions, and they carry a consistent argument: the catastrophe was deserved, the warnings were given, the covenant was broken. On Noth's reading the work is a theodicy written by a man looking at ruins.

Frank Moore Cross argued in 1973 for a double redaction. The first edition, Dtr1, was Josianic, a work of the late seventh century organized around two themes running in counterpoint: the sin of Jeroboam, which condemns the northern kingdom from its foundation, and the promise to David, which sustains the southern. On this reading the work climaxes in Josiah, presented as the king who reverses Jeroboam's foundational sin by destroying the altar at Bethel, and it is a document of an active reform programme rather than a retrospective on failure. A second, exilic redaction, Dtr2, then updated it lightly, adding the material that makes Manasseh's sin unforgivable and the exile inevitable, and converting a hopeful book into an explanation of defeat. Rudolf Smend and the Göttingen school proposed a different layering, distinguishing a basic historical work from prophetic and nomistic expansions, all of them exilic or later.

The difference matters concretely for reading Kings. On Noth's model everything in the work is exilic hindsight, and the praise of Josiah is the retrospective idealization of a king under whom nothing was ultimately saved. On Cross's model there is a pre-exilic edition, and the Josianic material is contemporary political literature, produced by and for the reform party while the outcome was still open. A reader assessing the regnal evaluation formulae, the persistent complaint that the high places were not removed, or the treatment of the northern sanctuaries will weigh them very differently on the two models.

There is a textual observation that favours the double redaction, and it deserves to be stated because it is the sort of evidence that source criticism at its best produces. Josiah is praised in unqualified and superlative terms, and the praise is immediately followed by the statement that the divine anger was nonetheless not turned away, because of Manasseh. The two statements sit in adjacent verses and pull in opposite directions. A single author writing after the exile would not have constructed the eulogy he then has to cancel; an editor updating an existing eulogy would have to cancel it exactly this way. The seam is visible, and it is the kind of visible seam that carries an argument.

#### Deuteronomy and the Assyrian Treaty Form

One external control on the dating of Deuteronomy is worth stating on its own, because it is the strongest available and it does not depend on the biblical narrative.

Neo-Assyrian imperial administration used a documentary form, the loyalty oath or succession treaty, imposed on vassals and on the empire's own officials, which combined stipulations of exclusive loyalty with an extended series of curses on the disloyal. Copies of the succession treaty of Esarhaddon, which bound its subscribers to the accession of his designated heir, were recovered from Nimrud, and a further copy was found more recently at Tell Tayinat in the Amuq, showing that the document circulated in the western provinces and was deposited in a temple context there.

The structural and phraseological correspondences between that treaty form and portions of Deuteronomy are close, and they are closest in the curse sequence of Deuteronomy 28 and in the demand of Deuteronomy 13 that disloyalty be reported and punished even when the one inciting it is a brother, a child, or a wife, which is a distinctively Assyrian formulation of the informer's duty. Hans Ulrich Steymans and Bernard Levinson have worked out the correspondences in detail. The inference is not that Deuteronomy is a copy but that its authors knew the form and used it, substituting their own deity for the Assyrian king as the party to whom exclusive loyalty is owed. That substitution is a political act as well as a theological one: it takes the instrument by which the empire bound Judah and turns it against the empire.

For dating, this places the composition of the relevant material in a period when the Assyrian treaty form was current and locally known, which is the seventh century. That is an argument entirely independent of 2 Kings 22, and it converges with it.

#### The Chronicler's Controlled Experiment

The most useful single body of evidence about how ancient Israelite historiography actually worked is the relationship between Chronicles and Samuel-Kings, because it is the rare case where a source and its user both survive.

Chronicles was composed in the Persian or early Hellenistic period, several centuries after the events it narrates and at least two after the composition of much of Kings. It demonstrably used Samuel-Kings: long stretches are reproduced with only minor variation, in the same order, with the same wording. It also demonstrably altered what it used, and the alterations are systematic enough to be read as a programme.

The programme is visible in what is omitted. David's adultery and the killing of Uriah are absent. Absalom's revolt is absent. The long struggle with the house of Saul is compressed to a genealogical note and a death. Solomon's foreign wives and the apostasy attributed to them are absent. The northern kingdom, after the schism, is essentially not narrated at all except where it touches Judah. A reader with only Chronicles would not know that David committed a crime or that Solomon's reign ended in disaffection.

It is visible in what is added. Hezekiah's Passover, a substantial narrative with no parallel in Kings, is added. Manasseh, whose fifty-five year reign Kings treats as the unforgivable cause of the exile, is given a repentance: he is taken to Babylon in fetters, prays, is restored, and reforms. Uzziah's leprosy, which Kings reports without explanation, is explained as punishment for usurping a priestly function. Josiah's death at Megiddo, which Kings reports flatly, is explained as the consequence of ignoring a divine warning delivered through a foreign king.

And it is visible in the theological adjustment of details. Where 2 Samuel says that divine anger incited David to take a census, 1 Chronicles says that Satan stood against Israel and incited David, relocating the causation. The price David pays for the threshing floor differs by an order of magnitude between the two accounts, and the Chronicler's larger figure suits a site that will become the Temple. Census totals differ.

The lesson is precise and applies well beyond Chronicles. An ancient historian working from a written source could reproduce it nearly verbatim where it served him, omit what damaged his subject, add substantial narrative, and adjust theologically loaded details, all without any sense of impropriety, because the standards governing his work were not those of modern historiography. The Chronicler is not lying by his own lights; he is producing an account of the past shaped by what the past is for.

The corollary is equally important and is often missed. Some of the Chronicler's additions are independently plausible and are corroborated. His notice that Hezekiah stopped the springs and brought water inside the city coheres with the Siloam tunnel; his notice of Hezekiah's wall-building coheres with the massive fortification wall exposed in Jerusalem's Jewish Quarter; his account of Manasseh as a vassal summoned to Mesopotamia coheres with the Assyrian records that list Manasseh among tributaries. A late, tendentious source can carry accurate material from archives or traditions its earlier counterpart declined to use. Lateness is a reason for caution, not a verdict.

#### The Prophetic Books and Their Layers

The prophetic books present the composition problem in its sharpest form, because they carry material that is unambiguously datable by content alongside material that cannot be from the same hand.

Isaiah is the standing case. The first thirty-nine chapters are set in the eighth century, in a world of Assyrian pressure, and address Jerusalem and its kings. Chapters 40 onward address a community in exile, treat the fall of Jerusalem as an accomplished fact, and name Cyrus the Persian as the agent of restoration, calling him the anointed. The observation that a book cannot be addressed to a situation two centuries after its named prophet without either prediction of a highly specific kind or a second author is the origin of the division, consolidated in Bernhard Duhm's commentary of 1892, which further separated chapters 56 to 66 as addressing a restored community with a functioning but disappointing Temple. It should be noted precisely that this is an argument from content, not from manuscripts: the great Isaiah scroll from Qumran runs continuously with no break at chapter 40, so the division is a modern analytic proposal about a text that circulated as a unity from at least the second century BCE.

Jeremiah shows layering of a different kind. Poetic oracles alternate with prose sermons whose vocabulary and theology are markedly Deuteronomistic, and with third-person biographical narrative associated with the scribe Baruch. Amos shows a first-person vision sequence interrupted by a third-person narrative of confrontation with a priest at Bethel, and it closes with a restoration oracle promising the raising of the fallen booth of David, which sits oddly with the book's overwhelmingly northern and overwhelmingly negative content and is widely read as a later Judahite addition.

The general pattern is consistent across the corpus. An oracular core is preserved, arranged by editors who were not the prophet, supplied with a superscription dating it to named reigns, updated to address later situations, and in several cases fitted with a hopeful ending. The superscriptions are the historian's principal dating handle, and it should be stated plainly that they are editorial. Using a superscription to date the material it heads, and then using the dated material as evidence for the period the superscription names, is a circle. It is usually a benign circle, because the content of the core oracles generally fits the period claimed, but it is a circle and it should be visible.

#### The Text Was Not One Text

Alongside the question of composition sits the question of transmission, and here the evidence changed decisively within living memory.

Before 1947 the working assumption was that a single original text had existed and that the surviving witnesses were more or less corrupted descendants of it. The Masoretic Text, whose consonantal skeleton was stable by roughly the second century CE and whose vowels and accents were added by the Masoretes of Tiberias between the eighth and tenth centuries, was the base; the Aleppo Codex and the Leningrad Codex are its great manuscripts. The Septuagint, translated in Alexandria beginning in the third century BCE, differed from it in many places, and the differences were generally explained as translators' liberties. The Samaritan Pentateuch, with its expansions and its Gerizim readings, was explained as a sectarian revision.

The Qumran manuscripts made all three explanations untenable in their simple form. The scrolls include Hebrew manuscripts agreeing with the Septuagint against the Masoretic Text in places where the difference is substantive, which means the Greek translators were rendering a Hebrew text that genuinely differed. They include manuscripts carrying the expansionist harmonizing features of the Samaritan Pentateuch without its sectarian readings, which means the Samaritan text is a light sectarian edition of an existing Jewish text type rather than an invention. And they include manuscripts of the same book differing from one another.

Two examples carry the argument. The Septuagint of Jeremiah is roughly one-seventh shorter than the Masoretic Jeremiah, and it places the oracles against the nations in a different position in the book and in a different internal order. This was long treated as translational abbreviation. Qumran produced Hebrew fragments of Jeremiah reflecting the shorter arrangement, which establishes that two editions of the book circulated in Hebrew, one substantially longer than the other, and that the difference is editorial rather than translational. The historian's conclusion is that Jeremiah was still growing when it was being copied.

The other is a Samuel manuscript from the fourth cave, which agrees with the Septuagint against the Masoretic Text at many points, shows that the Masoretic Samuel has suffered loss through scribal error at several places, and preserves a paragraph of narrative about the Ammonite king Nahash before the account of the siege of Jabesh-Gilead which is absent from both the Masoretic Text and the Greek. Josephus knows that paragraph. Its presence in a Hebrew manuscript and in a first-century historian, and its absence from the received text, is as clear a demonstration as the field possesses that material was lost as well as added in transmission.

The resulting model is one of textual plurality: several text types circulating simultaneously in the late Second Temple period, none yet authoritative to the exclusion of the others, with standardization occurring later and for reasons that were as much social as textual. Emanuel Tov's work is the standard treatment. For the historian the practical consequence is that a variant reading is not automatically an error to be corrected toward the Masoretic Text, and that where a chronological figure, a number, or a name differs between witnesses, the difference is evidence about transmission and not merely noise.

#### The Epigraphic Control

Set against all of this is a body of evidence that is contemporary, is not literary, and was not transmitted: the Hebrew inscriptions recovered from controlled excavation. It is not large, and it is almost entirely administrative, but it establishes several things independently of any text-critical argument.

The two rolled silver plaques from a burial repository at Ketef Hinnom, on the shoulder of the Hinnom valley, carry text closely related to the priestly benediction of Numbers 6 together with the divine name. Their palaeographic date falls in the late seventh or early sixth century, and the archaeological context is a repository containing material of that period, though the date has been challenged. They are the earliest known witness to any text that became biblical, they predate the Qumran manuscripts by centuries, and their wording is close to but not identical with the received text, which is itself informative: a formula was in circulation and its wording was not yet fixed.

The ostraca from the gate guardroom at Lachish are military correspondence from the final Babylonian siege. One of them reports that the writer is watching for the fire signals of Lachish because the signals of Azekah can no longer be seen. Jeremiah names Lachish and Azekah as the last fortified cities of Judah still holding out. A letter written under siege and a prophetic book written or edited afterward converge on the same two place names in the same situation, which is the closest thing the corpus offers to independent contemporary confirmation of a narrated moment.

The ostraca from the fortress at Arad are an administrative archive: ration orders issued to a quartermaster for the supply of a mercenary contingent, references to a house of YHWH, and correspondence about a threat from Edom. They show a functioning state supply system with written orders at the level of an outpost.

The Siloam tunnel inscription, cut in the rock of the tunnel and palaeographically of the late eighth century, describes in the workmen's own voice the meeting of two teams excavating from opposite ends. It names no king, which is remarkable and is itself a datum about who commissioned inscriptions and who did not.

The inscriptions and painted plaster from the desert way station at Kuntillet Ajrud, of roughly the early eighth century, carry blessing formulae invoking YHWH of Samaria and YHWH of Teman, each with an accompanying term whose grammatical form makes it contested whether it names a goddess or a cult object. Whatever the resolution, the inscriptions establish that YHWH was invoked in localized manifestations tied to particular places, that such invocations were written down at an isolated station in the Sinai, and that whoever wrote them did not observe the theology the received corpus prescribes.

To these should be added the Samaria ostraca, dockets recording deliveries of wine and oil to the northern capital and dated by regnal year; the Mesha Stele, a Moabite royal inscription of the ninth century naming Omri, Israel, and the God of Israel from an enemy's point of view; the Aramaic stele from Tel Dan referring to the house of David; and the corpus of clay sealings from Jerusalem, including one naming Gemaryahu son of Shaphan, a man Jeremiah places in the palace, and one naming Hezekiah, both from controlled excavation. Provenance matters here more than anywhere: the unprovenanced antiquities market has produced many inscriptions bearing on these questions and some are forged, so the argument should rest on excavated material.

What all this establishes is limited and solid. Hebrew was being written in both kingdoms by the ninth century and abundantly by the eighth and seventh. It was being written for administrative, military, and commemorative purposes by people trained in a standardized script. A formula that became scriptural was in circulation before the exile. Named individuals who appear in the narrative books also appear on contemporary sealings. None of this shows that any biblical book existed in the monarchy. All of it shows that the institutional capacity to produce one did.

#### Literacy and the Archaeology of Scribal Training

The question of how widely writing was distributed bears directly on when sustained literary composition became possible, and it is answerable in outline.

Writing in Iron Age Judah was a trained craft, not a general accomplishment. The evidence is the script itself: Hebrew inscriptions of the eighth and seventh centuries show a standardized letter repertoire, consistent stance, and consistent ductus across sites hundreds of kilometres apart, and that consistency is not produced by casual imitation. It is produced by formal instruction with a curriculum. Christopher Rollston has argued this point in detail, and the standardization is the argument.

The physical traces of that instruction are the abecedaries and practice texts: an abecedary scratched on a sherd at Izbet Sartah in an Iron I context, an abecedary incised on a stone at Tel Zayit in a tenth-century context, abecedaries and repeated formulae at Kuntillet Ajrud. These are exercises. They imply teaching, and teaching implies an institution capable of supporting non-producing specialists, which means a palace or a temple.

Any specific literacy rate quoted for Iron Age Judah is an estimate built on assumptions about population and about how many of the literate would be visible archaeologically, and the honest position is that the figure is unknown and probably low. What can be argued from evidence is distribution rather than rate. An algorithmic handwriting analysis of a set of ostraca from the Arad fortress, published by a group including Shira Faigenbaum-Golovin, Arie Shaus, Eli Piasetzky, and Israel Finkelstein, concluded that the letters were written by a minimum of six distinct hands, in a remote outpost with a small garrison, which implies that literacy extended well down the military hierarchy rather than being confined to a central chancery. The figure is a statistical minimum derived from a model and has been debated, but the direction of the finding is what matters: writing was not rare among Judahite officials in the last decades of the kingdom.

For the historian this sets a constraint at each end. Sustained composition of extended prose requires a scribal establishment, which the evidence supports for the eighth century onward in Judah and for the ninth in the north. Before that the epigraphic evidence thins sharply, and the question of whether extended literary composition was occurring in the tenth century is genuinely open. Arguments have been made both ways; the material is too sparse to decide it, and any confident answer is an extrapolation.

#### Weighting a Late Text

The principle that should govern the use of all this is easy to state and hard to apply consistently.

A late text can preserve early material. Transmission is not only loss. Poetry is preserved for its form and resists modernization, which is why several biblical poems retain grammatical features that had dropped out of prose Hebrew by the monarchy and are on that ground argued to be genuinely archaic. Archives are excerpted: the lists of officials, the building notices, and the regnal formulae in Kings have the texture of chancery records and are unlike the narrative around them. Place names that ceased to matter are retained because a copyist had no motive to change them. Details with no ideological payoff survive because nobody thought to remove them. The concession that a tribe failed to take a city, the admission that a foreign king's army was in the land, the retention of a shrine at a site the final redactor's theology condemns: these are the marks of material carried through rather than composed.

An early text can lie. Contemporaneity is not veracity, and royal inscriptions are the standing demonstration. The Mesha Stele is a ninth-century inscription by a participant and it is propaganda: it attributes Israel's earlier success to a god's anger and Moab's recovery to the same god's favour, and it does not mention any Moabite reverse. The Assyrian annals are contemporary and systematically overstate; Sennacherib's account of 701 describes shutting Hezekiah up like a caged bird in his royal city, which is what a king says when he has not taken the city and needs the failure not to be legible. An Egyptian topographical list at Karnak asserts conquest of places the army may only have passed. Every royal inscription in the ancient Near East was produced to be believed by a specific audience, and none of them was produced to inform a historian.

The usable criteria are therefore not chronological. They are: does the material run against the interest of the party transmitting it; is the detail incidental, such that no ideological purpose is served by its presence; is the language or the institution described one that had ceased to exist by the time of composition, so that it could not easily have been invented; and does it converge with independent evidence of a different kind. A concession is worth more than a claim. An administrative list is worth more than a speech. An obsolete term is worth more than a familiar one. And convergence between a text and an excavated inscription that neither knew of the other is worth more than any amount of internal coherence.

Applied honestly, these criteria give a graded rather than a binary result, and the grading is the historian's actual product. It is why a work of this kind can accept the framework of the divided monarchy, treat the united monarchy's extent as an open question, use the conquest narratives as evidence about the period of their composition rather than the period they describe, and take a Persian-period source seriously where it reports a building project that has been excavated. The date of composition sets the prior. The character of the material moves it.

---

## EXCURSUS IV. The Conquest Problem: Three Models and What the Ground Actually Shows

No other question in this history has been asked so often, answered so confidently, and settled so little. The book of Joshua describes a coordinated military campaign in which a people entering from outside destroys the cities of Canaan and takes the land. The material record of Late Bronze and Iron I Canaan has been investigated for more than a century by excavators of every persuasion, and it does not show that. What it shows instead is stranger and more interesting than either the traditional account or the flat denial, and the honest presentation of it requires distinguishing carefully between what has been established, what is probable, and what remains unknown.

The stakes are not only archaeological. The conquest narrative is the charter of possession, and it has been read as such continuously for three thousand years, by the Deuteronomistic editors who compiled it, by Second Temple sectarians who applied its curses to their opponents, by the first-century movements that Rome destroyed, and by modern political programmes on more than one continent. What actually happened between roughly 1250 and 1000 BCE in the central highlands of Canaan is therefore a question with an unusual amount riding on it, which is precisely the condition under which evidence gets handled badly.

#### The Internal Evidence Comes First

Before any archaeology, the corpus contains two incompatible accounts of how Israel came to occupy the land, and they sit adjacent to one another.

The first is in Joshua 1 through 12. It is a lightning campaign: the Jordan crossed, Jericho and Ai destroyed, a southern coalition broken at Gibeon and its cities taken in sequence, a northern coalition broken at the waters of Merom and Hazor burned. The summaries are absolute. Joshua took the whole land; he left none remaining; he utterly destroyed all that breathed.

The second is in Judges 1, and it is a catalogue of failures. Judah could not dispossess the inhabitants of the plain because they had chariots of iron. Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites from Jerusalem, who dwell there to this day. Manasseh did not take Beth-Shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, or Megiddo. Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites of Gezer. Zebulun, Asher, and Naphtali all failed in their turn, and the Danites were pressed into the hills and could not come down into the valley. Joshua 13:1, in the same book as the total-conquest summaries, concedes that very much land remains to be possessed and lists it.

The list of unconquered places in Judges 1 is not random. It is precisely the fortified lowland: the coastal plain, the Jezreel and Beth-Shean valleys, and the trunk roads. What was allegedly taken is the highland. That distribution is a strong datum in its own right, and it aligns with the archaeology in a way the total-conquest summaries do not. The corpus, in other words, preserves the material for a non-conquest reconstruction inside itself, and preserved it despite the summaries that contradict it, which is the pattern of transmitted material surviving a later frame.

There is a second internal observation of equal weight. The detailed narratives of Joshua 1 through 9 are concentrated in a very small area: Jericho, Ai, Gilgal, Gibeon, and the Benjaminite plateau, all within a radius of about twenty kilometres. Beyond that the accounts become schematic lists of kings and cities without incident. Martin Noth's inference from this was that the campaign narratives began as local Benjaminite traditions attached to a sanctuary at Gilgal, explaining visible landmarks in that district, and were subsequently expanded into a national conquest. Whatever one makes of the reconstruction, the geographical concentration is a fact about the text and requires an explanation.

#### Albright and the Conquest Model

The model that dominated Anglophone scholarship from the 1930s to the 1960s was William Foxwell Albright's, developed with G. Ernest Wright and popularized in the histories of John Bright. It proposed a unified military conquest around 1250 to 1200 BCE, and its evidentiary basis was the set of Late Bronze destruction layers being uncovered across Canaan in exactly those decades. Albright pointed to burnt strata at Bethel, at Lachish, at Hazor, and at Tell Beit Mirsim, which he identified with biblical Debir. He also pointed to what appeared to be a cultural break: after the destructions came a poorer, simpler material culture, which he read as the assemblage of a newly arrived population.

The model had genuine strengths and it should not be caricatured. There were real destructions, they did cluster in the right general period, and no one had yet demonstrated that they were not related to one another. It also had a methodological advantage that later proved to be its weakness: it made a testable claim about specific sites, and the sites could be dug.

#### Why It Collapsed

It collapsed for five reasons, each independently sufficient.

The first is that the three sites the narrative treats at greatest length are exactly the three with no supporting evidence. Jericho, Ai, and Gibeon are the campaign's opening sequence and its most circumstantial narratives, and all three lack the occupation the story requires at the period the story requires it. That the failures fall precisely on the best-told episodes is not what one would expect if the tradition were reporting.

The second is that the destructions do not form a horizon. Spread across the sites where destruction is real, the dates run from the later thirteenth century into the middle of the twelfth, a span of well over a century. A single campaign leaves a single horizon. This is a sequence of events, and some of them are separated by more than a generation.

The third is that several destroyed cities were destroyed at a time or by an agent that excludes the conquest. Lachish Level VI ends in violent burning, but a bronze object bearing the cartouche of Ramesses III was recovered from the destruction debris, which places the event no earlier than the reign of that king and therefore in the middle of the twelfth century. Lachish was thus a functioning Canaanite city under Egyptian oversight for a century after the conventional conquest date.

The fourth is that the supposed cultural break turned out not to be one. The pottery of the Iron I highland villages is not intrusive. It is a simplified, impoverished continuation of Late Bronze Canaanite forms, made in the same tradition with fewer types, no decoration, and no imports. There is nothing Egyptian in it, nothing Transjordanian, nothing that points to the Sinai or to Mesopotamia. Whoever these people were, their potters had learned their craft in Canaan.

The fifth is that Albright's site identifications were in several cases wrong. Tell Beit Mirsim is no longer identified with Debir; Khirbet Rabud is the current candidate. An argument built on the correlation of destruction layers with biblical place names is only as good as the identifications, and several did not hold.

By the 1970s the conquest model had few defenders among excavators, and it is worth stating that its collapse was brought about largely by archaeologists who had expected to confirm it.

#### Alt, Noth, and Peaceful Infiltration

The principal continental alternative predated Albright's model and outlived it. Albrecht Alt argued in 1925, on the basis of territorial history and settlement geography rather than excavation, that Israel entered Canaan gradually and largely peacefully. His picture was of pastoralists moving seasonally between the steppe and the highland, grazing the hills in the dry months, and progressively settling in the sparsely occupied central hill country, which the Canaanite city-states of the plains neither controlled nor wanted. Conflict came later, when the settled groups had grown numerous enough to press on the valleys. On this reading the conquest narratives are secondary aetiologies attached to a process that was slow, undramatic, and mostly bloodless.

Martin Noth developed the model and added to it the hypothesis of an amphictyony, a sacral league of twelve tribes organized around a central sanctuary, on the analogy of the Greek and Italic leagues that maintained shared shrines. The amphictyony has been abandoned. There is no evidence for the rotating maintenance obligation that defines the Greek institution, no evidence for the institutional apparatus, and the analogy drew on much later Greek arrangements that turn out to be dissimilar in structure. The infiltration model itself, stripped of the amphictyony, survives inside the current synthesis in modified form.

Its weakness was that it assumed what the material culture would later contradict: that the settlers came from outside, as nomads from the desert fringe. The archaeological evidence points overwhelmingly to local origin. It also relied on a model of nomad-to-farmer transition drawn from modern Bedouin ethnography that specialists in pastoral economies no longer accept, in which desert nomads gradually settle in a one-way progression. Actual pastoral societies oscillate, moving toward sedentary agriculture and back toward mobility as conditions change.

#### Mendenhall, Gottwald, and the Peasant Revolt

George Mendenhall proposed in 1962 that there was no immigration at all. On his account the people who became Israel were Canaanite peasants and villagers who withdrew from the city-state system, repudiating the political and religious legitimacy of the kings who taxed them, and who were catalyzed by a small group arriving from Egypt with a covenant theology that furnished the ideological basis for the withdrawal. He drew heavily on the Amarna letters, in which fourteenth-century Canaanite kings complain repeatedly to Pharaoh about the *ʿapiru*, a term denoting people outside the state system, brigands, mercenaries, and fugitives, who destabilized the countryside and to whom subjects defected. Mendenhall's model treated the *ʿapiru* as the sociological analogue of what became Israel, not as its ethnic ancestor.

Norman Gottwald elaborated this in 1979 into a full sociological system, explicitly Marxist in its analytic vocabulary, in which early Israel was an egalitarian retribalization movement, a peasant revolution against a tributary mode of production, with Yahwism functioning as the revolutionary ideology that made the coalition possible.

The ideological context should be named because it explains the model's shape without determining its truth. The peasant revolt model was formulated during a period of decolonization and liberation theology, and its proponents were candid that contemporary movements had suggested the analogy. This is not a refutation. Every historical model is formulated somewhere, and Albright's confidence about a conquest and Alt's about gradual infiltration had contexts too.

The refutation is archaeological. A revolt should leave traces, and it does not. The highland settlements are not concentrated near destroyed cities in the way refugee settlement would be. There is no evidence of the systematic destruction of urban elite quarters that a peasant rising against city-states would produce. The cities that persisted through the transition were not sacked by their hinterlands; several were destroyed by agents plainly external, and several were not destroyed at all. Mendenhall himself repudiated Gottwald's version. What survives from the model is one genuine contribution: the insistence that the population in question was Canaanite in origin, which the material culture has since confirmed.

#### The Current Synthesis

What has replaced the three models is not a fourth model of the same kind but a reconstruction of a process, variously called ethnogenesis, symbiosis, or simply the settlement, and associated with Israel Finkelstein, William Dever, Avraham Faust, and Lawrence Stager among others, who disagree with one another on important points.

Its core claims are these. The Iron I highland population was overwhelmingly local in origin. It was composed of several elements: villagers displaced by the collapse of the lowland economy, pastoralists who had specialized in herding while an exchange economy existed to buy their animal products and sell them grain, and who were forced to grow their own grain when that economy failed, and probably some external element whose numbers cannot be estimated. It settled a landscape that had been nearly empty, and it settled it fast. It formed a distinct identity over several generations, and that identity crystallized in significant part through opposition, particularly to the Philistine polities on the western frontier, which is Faust's central argument: ethnicity is maintained at boundaries and becomes archaeologically visible when a boundary is contested.

Finkelstein added a long-term dimension that has proved durable. Surveying the highland across all periods, he found that it was settled in waves, densely in the Early Bronze Age, densely again in the Middle Bronze Age, nearly abandoned in the Late Bronze Age, and densely again in Iron I, with the population oscillating between sedentary agriculture and pastoralism in step with the fortunes of the lowland urban economy. On this reading the Iron I settlement wave is the third such cycle and not a unique event, and what requires explanation is not that people appeared in the hills but that this particular wave produced a polity and an identity that the earlier waves did not.

The disagreements within the synthesis are real. Dever insists on the term proto-Israelite and holds that a meaningful continuity with the biblical account survives. Faust argues that ethnic markers are archaeologically identifiable in the avoidance patterns of the highland assemblage. Finkelstein is markedly more sceptical of reading ethnicity from material culture at all. These positions cannot all be right, and the argument between them is the live edge of the question.

#### Jericho

Tell es-Sultan has been excavated four times: by Ernst Sellin and Carl Watzinger before the First World War, by John Garstang in the 1930s, by Kathleen Kenyon between 1952 and 1958, and by a joint Italian and Palestinian expedition from 1997.

Garstang identified a fallen double wall which he assigned to a destruction around 1400 BCE and connected directly to Joshua. Kenyon, applying the stratigraphic section method that bears her name and Mortimer Wheeler's, reached a different conclusion and it has held. The massive fortifications, comprising a stone revetment supporting a mudbrick superstructure, are Middle Bronze, and they were destroyed in the sixteenth century BCE; radiocarbon determinations on the destruction support that date and if anything pull it earlier. For the Late Bronze Age Kenyon found a small quantity of pottery and one modest building on the summit, and no city wall at all.

Bryant Wood argued in 1990 for a return to Garstang's date on ceramic grounds. The argument has not persuaded the field and it sits against the radiocarbon evidence from the destruction layer.

Two honest cautions belong here. The first is erosion. Tell es-Sultan has been dug repeatedly and its summit has suffered badly, and the uppermost strata of any tell are the first to go. A thin Late Bronze occupation could be substantially under-represented. The second is that absence of a wall is not absence of a settlement. What the evidence supports is the specific negative claim that Jericho was not a walled city in the Late Bronze Age, since the fortification line lies at the base of the mound where erosion is not the issue and where Kenyon cut her sections.

The narrative offers its own explanation of what it is doing. Joshua 6:26 lays a curse on whoever rebuilds Jericho, which is an aetiology for a mound lying unoccupied, and a story about the fall of a wall is exactly the story a visible ruin of collapsed Middle Bronze mudbrick fortification would generate in people who had no way of dating it.

#### Ai at et-Tell

The case at Ai is cleaner than at Jericho and it is, in evidentiary terms, decisive.

Et-Tell was excavated by Judith Marquet-Krause in the 1930s and by Joseph Callaway between 1964 and 1972. The results are unambiguous. There was a very large Early Bronze walled city, on the order of eleven hectares, destroyed around 2400 BCE. The site was then abandoned for approximately a thousand years. In Iron I an unwalled village was founded on the ruins, occupied for roughly a century and a half, and abandoned again. There is no Late Bronze occupation whatever. There is nothing at Ai for Joshua to destroy at any date proposed for the conquest, early or late.

The name is the crux and it should be read carefully. The Hebrew *hā-ʿAy* is a common noun with the definite article, and it means "the ruin." The place is not called Ai; it is called the Ruin. Joshua 8:28 states that Joshua made it a *tēl ʿôlām*, a permanent mound, to this day. The narrative gives an account of how a conspicuous ruin came to be a ruin, and the name of the place is a description of its condition. This is aetiology in its purest attested form, and no reconstruction of the episode need be proposed beyond it.

A minority alternative exists. Bryant Wood and the Associates for Biblical Research have excavated at Khirbet el-Maqatir since 1995 and report a small fortified site of Late Bronze I, which they propose as the true Ai on an early-date conquest model. The proposal should be reported and its weaknesses stated. The site is small; the identification depends on accepting the fifteenth-century Exodus date the identification is offered to support, which is circular; and the proposal has not been accepted outside the group advancing it. A separate proposal by David Livingston identifying Ai with Khirbet Nisya has fared no better.

#### Gibeon at el-Jib

Gibeon is the third of the narrative's opening triad, and its evidence is the most instructive because the site identification is certain while the occupation is not.

James Pritchard excavated el-Jib between 1956 and 1962. The identification rests on more than thirty jar handles inscribed with the place name *gbʿn*, several with an additional word and a personal name, recovered from the area of the great cutting. This is the only case in the conquest dossier where a site names itself, and it removes any doubt.

The site's Iron Age installations are impressive. A rock-cut circular shaft roughly eleven metres across and as deep, with a spiral stair cut into its wall, continues by a stepped tunnel to the water table some twenty-five metres below the surface; the pool of Gibeon appears in 2 Samuel 2:13. Several dozen rock-cut cellars, plastered and of uniform size, are wine-storage chambers maintaining a constant temperature, and they indicate a substantial commercial viticulture.

The problem is the date. The inscribed handles are Iron II, of the seventh century. The pool, the cellars, and the fortification wall are Iron Age. For the Late Bronze Age, Pritchard found tombs containing Late Bronze material, reused from earlier cuttings, and essentially no settlement on the site. Joshua 10:2 describes Gibeon as a great city, greater than Ai, comparable to a royal city, with mighty men. In the period the narrative requires, it is archaeologically absent.

The pattern across the three opening sites is therefore consistent and it is the most important single finding in the file: the three places where the conquest narrative is most detailed are the three places where the required occupation does not exist.

#### Hazor

Hazor is the counter-case, and it must be given its full weight.

Yigael Yadin excavated in the late 1950s and again in 1968, and Amnon Ben-Tor has directed renewed excavation since 1990. Hazor was by a wide margin the largest city in Canaan: a fortified upper mound of some six hectares and a lower enclosure of roughly seventy, an order of magnitude larger than Megiddo, Lachish, or Jerusalem. It appears in the Mari archives of the eighteenth century as a destination for consignments of tin, the limiting input in bronze production, and it is the one Canaanite city that corresponds with Mesopotamian courts as a peer.

Its final Late Bronze city ended in comprehensive violent destruction. The burnt debris is very deep, approaching or exceeding a metre in places. Mudbrick was vitrified, which requires sustained temperatures far above those of an accidental fire. The ceremonial palace with its basalt orthostats was gutted. Most striking is the treatment of the statuary: statues of Canaanite deities and of Egyptian figures were systematically decapitated and had their hands struck off. That is deliberate ritual mutilation, not collateral damage, and it identifies the destruction as an ideological act.

Two further results matter. The vast lower city, occupied since the Middle Bronze Age, was never rebuilt. And what follows on the upper mound in Iron I is not a city but a poor scatter of pits, silos, and slight structures. Whoever destroyed Hazor did not occupy it, and whoever occupied it afterward had no urban capacity at all.

Joshua 11:11 and 13 state that Hazor was burned and add, uniquely and pointedly, that Israel burned none of the other cities standing on their mounds. A text that singles out one city for burning and a site that shows exactly that is the strongest positive datum the dossier contains.

The honest fact, which must be stated as plainly as the correspondence, is that the destroyer is unidentified. A destruction layer never names its agent. Four candidates are seriously proposed: an Israelite or proto-Israelite coalition, which Ben-Tor favours; groups associated with the Sea Peoples; an Egyptian punitive expedition; and an internal uprising, argued by Sharon Zuckerman on the grounds that the destruction was selective and ritualized in a way suggesting insiders who knew what to smash. The mutilation of Egyptian statuary tells against Egypt but does not identify a positive alternative. Nothing recovered at Hazor is Israelite, and nothing recovered there refers to the events of Joshua 11.

#### Lachish, Megiddo, and Beth-Shean

Three further sites define the shape of the transition and each shows Egypt still present after any conventional conquest date.

Lachish Level VI ends in violent destruction, and the bronze object bearing the cartouche of Ramesses III in the debris fixes the event no earlier than the middle of the twelfth century. Level VI itself is a substantial Canaanite city with an Egyptianizing administrative building, and the destruction that ends it is a century after the latest conventional date for Joshua.

Megiddo Stratum VIIA, the last Canaanite city, ends around 1130 BCE. An ivory pen case bearing the cartouche of Ramesses III was recovered from the treasury of the stratum. What follows is an unwalled Iron I settlement of much reduced character. Megiddo is one of the cities Judges 1:27 concedes Manasseh did not take.

Beth-Shean is the clearest case of all. It carried a continuous Egyptian garrison through the Nineteenth and Twentieth Dynasties, attested by Egyptian-style administrative buildings, by two stelae of Seti I and one of Ramesses II, by a statue of Ramesses III, and by Egyptian-style anthropoid clay coffins. The Egyptian presence continues well into the twelfth century. Judges 1:27 concedes that Beth-Shean was not taken. This is a case where the biblical text and the excavation agree exactly, and the agreement is with the concession, not with the conquest.

Bethel is the one site where a Late Bronze destruction has been reported that would fit a conquest narrative, and it is worth noting that Joshua does not claim its capture; Judges 1:22 to 26 does, by the house of Joseph, through the betrayal of an informer, which is a different kind of story entirely. The Bethel excavations are old and poorly published by modern standards, and the identification of Beitin with Bethel, though generally accepted, has been questioned.

#### The Highland Survey

The strongest body of evidence bearing on Israelite origins is not from any single site. It is from the systematic archaeological surveys of the central hill country conducted after 1967, including Israel Finkelstein's work in Ephraim, Adam Zertal's in Manasseh, and Avi Ofer's in Judah, which walked the ground and recorded surface pottery at every identifiable site across whole regions.

The sequence they established is consistent. The Middle Bronze highland was substantially settled. The Late Bronze highland was nearly empty, with only a few dozen sites in the entire central hill country. Then in Iron I there is a wave of new foundations, on the order of two hundred and fifty to three hundred sites in the central highlands, the great majority of them small, under a hectare, unwalled, and founded on virgin ground rather than on earlier tells. In Iron II these nucleate: many small sites are abandoned and larger ones grow.

Two cautions attach to the numbers. Survey counts depend on the surveyor's criteria for what constitutes a site and on the visibility of surface pottery, which varies enormously with terrain and land use, so figures differ between surveyors and between regions. And population estimates derived from settled area by a density coefficient are inferences with wide margins, though the relative change, from near-empty to densely settled within a few generations, is not in doubt.

What the survey establishes is a real, rapid, and large-scale settlement of a landscape that had been nearly vacant, by people whose material culture came from Canaan. What it does not establish is who they were. A survey records pottery and building plans. It does not record ethnicity, language, or religion.

#### The Material Package and the Ethnic Marker Problem

The Iron I highland sites share a recognizable assemblage, and each element of it has at some point been proposed as an Israelite marker. None of them is.

The four-room house, more precisely the pillared house, is a rectangular building with three parallel long spaces divided by one or two rows of pillars and a broad room across the rear. It appears in Iron I and continues throughout Iron II, and it is genuinely characteristic of the highland. Lawrence Stager related its plan to the extended family household, and Avraham Faust has argued that its layout, in which most rooms are entered directly from the central space rather than through one another, expresses an egalitarian ethos and facilitates purity practice. But the plan also occurs in Transjordan at Ammonite and Moabite sites, occurs at sites that are certainly not Israelite, and has a straightforward functional reading as an efficient solution for a household keeping animals, storing crops, and living under one roof. A building type that occurs across a region cannot identify one population within it.

The collared-rim pithos, a large storage jar with a pronounced ridge at the neck, was treated by Albright as a diagnostic Israelite artefact. It occurs in quantity at Iron I highland sites. It also occurs in Transjordan, in the Galilee, at coastal sites, and outside any plausible Israel. Its distribution is better explained functionally: a village without market access and without a nearby perennial spring needs large-capacity storage for water and grain, and the collared rim is a structural solution to making a very large jar that can be handled. The vessel marks an economy, not a people.

Terrace agriculture, hillside cultivation retained by dry-stone walls, expands in this period and is essential to farming the steep central highland. Terraces are notoriously difficult to date, since they are repaired and rebuilt across centuries and their fill is mixed, and terracing exists both before and after. Plastered rock-cut cisterns, which permit settlement away from springs, are likewise a technology. Neither is an ethnicity.

The negative features are as characteristic as the positive: no monumental architecture, no fortification beyond the perimeter formed by the outer walls of houses in some ring-plan villages, no temples, no imported pottery, no decorated pottery, no luxury goods, no burials of any distinctive kind that can be identified.

The general problem is the one anthropology settled some time ago, following Fredrik Barth's analysis of ethnic boundaries: ethnicity is maintained at boundaries through a small number of selected markers, and it does not correspond to the whole cultural inventory of a group. Two peoples may share almost everything material and consider themselves entirely distinct; one people may vary materially across regions and consider itself one. Pots are not people. The archaeological record can demonstrate a distinct settlement system with a distinct economy, and that is a large finding. It cannot supply the system with a name.

#### The Pig-Bone Question

One dietary observation has carried more weight than any other and deserves separate handling, because it is both genuinely interesting and routinely overstated.

Faunal assemblages from Iron I highland sites show pig bones at very low frequencies or absent. Assemblages from contemporary Philistine sites on the coastal plain show substantial pig, in some cases a significant fraction of the identified remains. There is therefore a real dietary difference in Iron I between the highland and the Philistine coast, and it is not an artefact of preservation, since pig bones survive as well as any other.

What it can support is a claim about a boundary. Two adjacent populations were eating differently in a way that a person could see, and food practice is among the most common and most durable markers by which groups in contact distinguish themselves. Given that the Philistine frontier is where the settlement's western boundary was contested, a dietary marker there is exactly what boundary theory would predict.

What it cannot support is a claim about religious law, and the constraints are several. Pig husbandry is ecologically constrained: pigs require water and shade, cannot be driven long distances, and are poorly suited to a dry highland with a mobile pastoral component, so low frequencies may reflect environment rather than choice. Late Bronze Canaanite sites in the highland also show low pig, which suggests the pattern may not be new in Iron I. Transjordanian sites, which are not Israelite by anyone's account, also show low pig. And the Iron II evidence complicates the picture decisively: work by Lidar Sapir-Hen and colleagues found that pig frequencies rise in the northern kingdom during Iron II while remaining near-zero in Judah, which is incompatible with a single pan-Israelite dietary law observed from the beginning and suggests instead that the practice was regional and hardened at different times in different places.

Brian Hesse and Paula Wapnish, who did the foundational work on this material, were themselves explicitly cautious about ethnic diagnosis from pig remains, and their caution has held up better than the confident uses made of their data.

#### The Merneptah Stele

One external document names Israel in Canaan, and it is the fixed point around which the whole reconstruction has to be built.

The stela, recovered by Flinders Petrie in 1896 from Merneptah's mortuary temple at Thebes, is dated to that king's fifth year, around 1207 BCE. It is principally a victory hymn concerning a Libyan campaign, and it closes with a stanza on Canaan naming Ashkelon, Gezer, Yanoam, and Israel, of which it says that Israel is laid waste and his seed is not.

The orthography is the crux and it is precise. Ashkelon, Gezer, and Yanoam are each written with the determinative marking a foreign land or city-state. Israel is written with the determinative for a people: the throwstick together with the seated man and woman and the plural strokes. Egyptian scribes classified what they wrote about, and this scribe classified Israel differently from the three cities in the same sentence.

What the stela establishes is exact and limited. A group called Israel existed in Canaan by 1207 BCE. Egyptian administration knew of it and classified it as a people rather than as a territory or a city. An Egyptian king claimed to have damaged it, which at minimum means it was significant enough to be worth claiming a victory over. That is a great deal, and it is the earliest occurrence of the name anywhere.

What it does not establish is equally worth stating. It says nothing about this group's religion, its origin, its internal organization, or its relationship to the highland villages the surveys record. It does not locate Israel geographically beyond Canaan. It does not tell us whether the people so named are the ancestors of the Iron II kingdoms or a group whose name was later assumed by others.

Two secondary matters should be noted with their uncertainty attached. Frank Yurco proposed that a set of battle reliefs at Karnak, formerly attributed to Ramesses II, belong to Merneptah and depict this campaign, including a panel showing Israelites in Canaanite dress; Anson Rainey argued that the figures in question are Shasu. The identification is disputed and should not be used as evidence. A proposal that a name on a Berlin pedestal relief should be read as an earlier attestation of Israel has been advanced and is likewise disputed; it is not a secure datum.

#### The Enabling Condition

None of the settlement makes sense without the collapse of the system that preceded it, and that collapse is the best-documented part of the whole picture.

The Late Bronze Age Near East operated as an international system: a small number of great powers linked by diplomatic correspondence, dynastic marriage, and gift exchange, resting on long-distance trade in metals, above all Cypriot copper and tin brought from the east. The Amarna letters preserve the correspondence. The Uluburun shipwreck, which went down off the southern Turkish coast in the late fourteenth century carrying roughly ten tons of copper ingots, about a ton of tin, Canaanite jars, glass ingots, ebony, ivory, and objects originating in at least seven cultures, preserves the trade in physical form.

Between roughly 1200 and 1150 BCE that system failed. The Hittite state disappeared. Ugarit was destroyed and never reoccupied. The Mycenaean palace centres were destroyed. Cyprus was disrupted. Egypt survived but contracted sharply. The causes are debated and are almost certainly multiple: the movements grouped under the label Sea Peoples, whose coherence as a phenomenon is itself contested; drought, for which there is now real palaeoclimatic support from high-resolution pollen sequences in the Levant indicating a dry phase across roughly 1250 to 1100 BCE; seismic activity; and the intrinsic fragility of a system in which every node depended on the others.

Egypt's position in Canaan is the specific enabling condition. Egyptian imperial administration operated through garrisons at Beth-Shean, Gaza, and elsewhere, through residencies staffed by Egyptian officials, and through vassal city-kings who paid tribute and supplied corvée labour and grain. Egyptian policy deliberately kept Canaanite cities weak, which is why Late Bronze Canaan is a landscape of reduced, largely unfortified towns squatting beside decaying Middle Bronze ramparts. That system extracted surplus from the countryside and channelled it to the lowland centres and thence to Egypt, and it made the highland unattractive: a highland farmer produced a taxable surplus and received nothing.

Egypt withdrew in the middle of the twelfth century. The latest securely dated Egyptian royal objects in Canaan belong to the reigns of Ramesses III and Ramesses VI, after which the administrative presence ends. When it ended, the city-state system it had propped up lost its sponsor, the tributary extraction stopped, and the exchange economy that had allowed pastoral specialists to trade animal products for grain ceased to function. Both effects push in the same direction: the highland becomes viable because nobody is taxing it, and pastoralists must grow their own grain because nobody will sell it to them. The settlement wave follows.

#### What Can Actually Be Said

The following is established, in the sense that it would take new evidence rather than new argument to overturn it.

There was no single military conquest of Canaan of the kind Joshua 1 through 12 describes. The three sites where the narrative is most circumstantial lack the required occupation. The destructions that exist do not form a horizon and were not caused by a single agent. Several destroyed cities were under Egyptian oversight a century after the latest conventional conquest date. The Iron I highland settlement is real, rapid, large, and materially continuous with Canaanite tradition, with nothing in it pointing outside the region. A people called Israel existed in Canaan by 1207 BCE. Egypt withdrew from Canaan in the mid-twelfth century, and the Late Bronze system collapsed around it.

The following is probable, in the sense that it is the best available reading of the evidence and could be revised.

The great majority of the Iron I highland population was of local, Canaanite origin. The formation of Israel was a process running over several generations rather than an event. Some of the destructions of the later thirteenth and twelfth centuries were caused by groups that later formed part of Israel, though this cannot be demonstrated for any particular site. An external element, plausibly small, with a genuine Egyptian experience, is more likely than not, on the ground that a people does not invent for itself an origin in slavery, and that the Exodus tradition's tenacity across every later crisis is difficult to explain as invention; but this is an argument from the character of the tradition and not from any material evidence, and it should be labelled as such. The conquest narratives took shape as local Benjaminite traditions explaining visible ruins, and were expanded into a national account by editors with a centralizing programme.

The following is unknown, and describing it as unknown is not a failure of the discipline.

Who destroyed Hazor. Where Gilgal was. Whether the Exodus group existed, how large it was, and when it arrived. Whether the group Merneptah's scribe called Israel is continuous with the Iron I highland villagers, or a different body whose name was later applied to them. When the name Israel attached to the highland settlement. Whether any specific event in Joshua 1 through 12 corresponds to anything that happened. Whether the traditions preserve memory at all, or are entirely explanatory constructions built on landmarks.

The temptation at this point is to resolve the question by choosing the model that leaves the least uncomfortable residue, and it should be resisted in both directions. The evidence does not support the conquest narrative as history, and saying so is not scepticism but reporting. The evidence also does not support the reduction of Israel's origins to an undifferentiated Canaanite continuity in which nothing came from outside and nothing happened, and asserting that goes beyond what the ground shows. What the ground shows is a landscape emptied by imperial extraction, an empire withdrawing, a system collapsing, and a population moving into the hills and becoming, within a few generations, something that had a name, a boundary, and eventually a state. How much of what that population remembered about itself was true is a question the archaeology is not equipped to answer, and the honest historian records the limit rather than crossing it.
