## EXCURSUS V. The Tier Problem: An Audit of the Work's Own Evidence Scheme

#### Why this essay exists

A work that grades its evidence has done something most historical writing does not do, and it has thereby made itself checkable in a way most historical writing is not. That is a real methodological gain and it should be said before anything else. The cost of the gain is that the grading itself becomes an object of audit, and a scheme applied inconsistently is worse than no scheme at all, because it launders the inconsistency behind a number.

The preceding hundred and six volumes were audited line by line against the scheme they declare. That audit returned in excess of nine hundred findings, of which the great majority are not disputes about history but failures of the work's own stated method. They fall into a small number of recurring shapes. This essay sets out those shapes, explains the mechanism of each, and states the discipline that follows. The register of corrections at Appendix F carries the individual findings. What follows is the anatomy.

The exercise is not self-flagellation and it is not a retraction. Nearly every finding leaves the historical claim standing and changes only the warrant attached to it. A claim held at Tier 3 with honest confidence is a stronger scholarly object than the same claim held at Tier 1 with false confidence, because the first survives challenge and the second does not.

#### The declared scheme

The work grades evidence in five tiers. Tier 1 is contemporary epigraphy, undisputed archaeological stratigraphy, and palaeogenetics. Tier 2 is near-contemporary administrative archives and diplomatic correspondence. Tier 3 is canonical text aligned with a known socio-economic or regional paradigm. Tier 4 is later compilation, reception, and polemic. Tier 5 is analytical and circumstantial synthesis. A parallel vocabulary of confidence labels runs alongside: DOCUMENTED, Scholarly Consensus, DISPUTED, CIRCUMSTANTIAL, SPECULATIVE.

The scheme is sound. Two properties make it so. First, it separates the age and provenance of a source from the confidence one places in a claim, which are genuinely different variables and are routinely conflated in historical writing. Second, it forces every claim to name what carries it, which makes disagreement productive because the disagreement can be located.

The failures are not failures of the scheme. They are failures to apply it, and they are systematic rather than random, which means they can be named and prevented.

#### Fault one: the tier drift of the literary source

This is the largest single class of finding and it accounts for well over a hundred entries. Across the work, literary and historiographical sources are assigned Tier 1: Josephus, Tacitus, Suetonius, Cassius Dio, Eusebius, Ammianus Marcellinus, Procopius, Gregory of Tours, Theophanes, al-Ṭabarī, al-Balādhurī, al-Maqqarī, the Mishnah, the Talmuds, and the biblical text itself. Under the declared scheme none of these is Tier 1, because Tier 1 is defined as contemporary epigraphy and stratigraphy, and a narrative composed decades or centuries after the event by an identifiable author with an identifiable interest is a different kind of object entirely.

The distances involved are not marginal. Tacitus wrote the *Annals* around 116 CE, some fifty years after the Neronian fire and eighty after the events in Judaea he mentions in passing. Josephus wrote the *Jewish War* under Flavian patronage within a decade of the events, which is genuinely close, and the *Antiquities* around 93 or 94, which is not, and he commanded on one side of the war he narrates before being pensioned by the other. Eusebius wrote in the 320s about the 250s. Theophanes wrote around 815 about 628. Al-Ṭabarī died in 923 and wrote about 750. Al-Maqqarī died in 1632 and is cited in this work for the words of a commander in 711.

The mechanism of the drift is worth naming because it is not carelessness. It is a confusion between the importance of a source and its class. Josephus is the most important source for the first century in Judaea. He is not a contemporary inscription. The scheme measures class, not importance, and a source can be simultaneously indispensable and Tier 4. Al-Ṭabarī is the reason we know anything at all about the Abbasid revolution in narrative detail, and he is a third-century-AH compiler working from earlier transmitters whose own chains he preserves and sometimes doubts. Both statements are true and the tier records only the second.

The correction is mechanical. Literary narrative sits at Tier 2 when the author is genuinely contemporary and had access, at Tier 4 otherwise, and the tier travels with a note on the author's position and interest. The genuine Tier 1 items are then visible for what they are, and in this work they are numerous and impressive: the Merneptah Stele, the Mesha Stele, the Kurkh Monolith, the Black Obelisk, the Tel Dan Stele, the Sennacherib Prism, the Lachish reliefs and the Lachish ostraca, the Siloam inscription, the Ketef Hinnom amulets, the Babylonian Chronicles, the Jehoiachin ration tablets, the Cyrus Cylinder, the Elephantine papyri, the Pilate stele, the Temple warning inscription, the Theodotus inscription, the Gallio inscription, the revolt coinage of both Jewish wars, the Bar Kokhba letters, the Decian libelli, PERF 558, and the Dome of the Rock inscriptions. That is a formidable Tier 1 corpus and it is obscured, not strengthened, by the promotion of Josephus into it.

#### Fault two: topography as artifact

A recurring construction in the work reads: "Source: The Beth-horon Pass | Reference: Military Topography | Tier 1 | Artifact datum: the pass narrows to..." The same shape appears for the Kishon, Mount Tabor, the Michmash gorge, the Aruna Pass, the ravine north of the Temple Mount, and the terrain of Yarmūk, Tours, Nineveh, and the Zab.

Landscape is not an artifact and cannot occupy an evidence tier. It is a constraint, and constraints are extremely valuable: a pass that is four metres wide at its narrowest point genuinely does forbid the deployment of a phalanx, and that fact can rule out a reported manoeuvre. But a constraint tells you what could not have happened. It never tells you what did. Every one of the battles named above is unlocated in the sense that no battlefield has been excavated and no material assemblage has been recovered, and the topography is equally compatible with the battle having occurred there, having occurred elsewhere, or not having occurred at all.

The correction is to move terrain out of the evidence ledger and into the analysis, where it functions as a filter on reported claims rather than as support for them. A sentence of the form "the reported chariot deployment is impossible in this terrain" is strong and belongs in the argument. A sentence of the form "the terrain is Tier 1 evidence for the battle" is empty.

#### Fault three: circularity

This is the most serious fault in the set because it manufactures confidence out of nothing, and it appears at several of the work's most load-bearing points.

The clearest instance is the six-chambered gates. The gates at Megiddo, Hazor, and Gezer were assigned to the tenth century in large part because 1 Kings 9:15 says Solomon built at those three cities. The work then cites the gates as physically proving the Solomonic state described in 1 Kings 9:15. The text dated the stratum and the stratum is now confirming the text. Nothing has been added. The low-chronology debate exists precisely because that circle was noticed, and the debate is live, which means the gates cannot be presented as settled.

Tell el-Fūl is a second instance. Albright dated the fortress burn by reference to the Judges 20 narrative, and the work cites the burn as Tier 1 corroboration of Judges 20. The identification of the site with Gibeah is itself contested, only one corner tower was actually recovered, and later re-examination has questioned both date and attribution. Three uncertainties are stacked and the result is presented as Tier 1.

A subtler instance is the use of a verified fact to certify an unverified one adjacent to it. The work states that Joseph was "sold into slavery at Dothan, DOCUMENTED, Tier 3, geographically verified." Dothan is verified. The sale is not, and the verification of the setting has been silently transferred to the event. The same transfer occurs where the existence of an Egyptian institution is used to document that a specific narrated episode involving that institution took place, and where the existence of an Assyrian deportation policy is used to document the specific deportation figures reported.

The correction is a rule: no claim may be supported by evidence whose own dating or identification depends on that claim. Where the dependency exists it must be stated, and the claim then rests on the argument for the dating, not on the dating itself.

#### Fault four: the straw falsifier

Every volume in the work carries a falsifier, and this is an admirable feature that most historical writing lacks entirely. The trouble is that a large proportion of the falsifiers as written are counterfactuals that no possible discovery could satisfy, which makes them decorative.

The pattern is recognizable once named. "If eighth-century archives revealed that the Umayyads had relocated their capital to Rome and permanently banned all Persians from government, the Abbasid narrative would be falsified." "If archaeological surveys demonstrated that the central hill country was completely devoid of pastoralist activity." "If camels were absent from the Near East until the Persian or Hellenistic periods." These are not falsifiers. They are restatements of the claim with the negation attached, set at a threshold no evidence will ever reach.

A real falsifier names a discovery that is possible, that would be recognized if it occurred, and that would move the verdict. The camel case is the instructive one, because the work's stated falsifier is a straw and the real falsifier has already fired. The work asserts that domesticated camels were in use in the twelfth to eleventh centuries, matching the Midianite raiding narrative. The published copper-smelting site evidence from the Aravah places the earliest domesticated camel remains in the last third of the tenth century. The real falsifier was "if the earliest attested domesticated camels in the southern Levant postdate the narrative window by two centuries," and that is what the evidence shows. The narrative is not thereby destroyed; the camels are dated as an updating layer in the telling, exactly as the camels of Genesis 12 and 31 are. But the falsifier has to be allowed to fire, and a straw one cannot.

Other real falsifiers are available throughout and cost nothing to state. A Decian libellus issued to a self-identified Christian would falsify the standard reading of that persecution's operation. A western imperial law or coin issued after 480 would complicate the periodization at 476. Absence of Yersinia pestis ancient DNA across the geographic range reported for the Justinianic plague would falsify the identification. A datable Muslim withdrawal from Gaul in 732 rather than 759 would restore the strong reading of Tours.

#### Fault five: the warrant-tag mismatch

The confidence labels and the tiers are two axes and they are not independent in the way the work sometimes treats them. A claim cannot be [DOCUMENTED] at Tier 5, because Tier 5 is analytical synthesis and synthesis by definition documents nothing. A claim cannot be [DOCUMENTED] at Tier 3, because Tier 3 is canonical text whose alignment with a paradigm is an argument rather than a record. Yet the work carries "the golden calf was a pedestal for YHWH, DOCUMENTED, Tier 5" and "extreme cultic syncretism, DOCUMENTED, Tier 3," among others.

The rule that follows is simple and mechanical. [DOCUMENTED] is available only at Tiers 1 and 2. Tier 3 claims take [Scholarly Consensus] or [DISPUTED]. Tier 4 claims take [DISPUTED] or [CIRCUMSTANTIAL]. Tier 5 claims take [CIRCUMSTANTIAL] or [SPECULATIVE]. The work also employs hybrid tiers, "Tier 1/2" and "Tier 2/4," which appear to encode distance in time rather than class of evidence and are defined nowhere. They should be resolved to a single tier with the reservation stated in words.

#### Fault six: false independence

Convergence between two sources is powerful evidence, and it is worthless if the two are not independent. The work repeatedly treats as independent corroboration material that reaches us through a single channel.

Menander of Ephesus is cited as independently validating the Tyrian material in Kings. Menander does not survive. He reaches us through Josephus, who was harmonizing his account with the biblical narrative and quoting a Hellenistic epitomator. That is one witness in two costumes, and the correct treatment is to count it once.

The same fault appears where the Gospels are cited as multiply attesting an episode that all three Synoptics carry, without noting the literary relationship among them; where Eusebius is said to independently verify a datum he took from a source the work also cites; and where a reconstructed text is quoted as though intact. The Tel Dan Stele is the standing example of that last variant: the work quotes the royal names as though they stood on the stone, when both are substantially restored and the author's name is not preserved at all. A restoration is a scholarly proposal and must be marked as one, because a reader cannot distinguish restored text from surviving text once the brackets are dropped.

#### Fault seven: the anachronistic anchor

The corroboration sections are headed "Same Era / Locale," which is the correct discipline, and the discipline is repeatedly broken. The Mesha Stele, c. 840 BCE, is used to anchor an episode set around 1020. Nuzi, fifteenth and fourteenth century, is used to anchor patriarchal law set three or four centuries earlier. Mari, eighteenth century, is used to anchor court practice in tenth-century Jerusalem. The lmlk stamp system, late eighth century, is listed as same-era for the tenth-century schism. Ekron's olive-oil installations, seventh century, are cited as evidence of Iron I Philistine urbanism. Rekhmire, Eighteenth Dynasty, anchors a Fifteenth Dynasty vizierate. Tel Beersheba, whose sequence begins in Iron I, anchors a Middle Bronze episode.

Each of these is legitimate as an institutional analogue and illegitimate as same-era corroboration, and the difference is not pedantic. An analogue shows that a practice existed somewhere in the ancient Near East and is evidence that the practice is plausible. Same-era corroboration shows that the practice existed at this time in this place and is evidence that the narrative is anchored. Collapsing the two converts a plausibility argument into a documentation claim.

The correction is to keep the heading and enforce it, moving cross-period material to a clearly marked analogue register with the gap stated in years.

#### Fault eight: the accepted round number

Ancient quantities are treated at face value across the work: thirty thousand chariots at Michmash, four hundred thousand at Gibeah, two thousand chariots at Qarqar, twenty-five thousand at a theatre in Ephesus, thirty thousand rioters at Constantinople, twenty-five to fifty million dead of plague, two hundred and twenty thousand in the Kitos War. Excursus VIII treats the general problem. The point here is narrower and concerns tiering: a figure carried by a single literary source cannot be Tier 1, and a figure that varies between recensions of the same inscription cannot be precise.

The Samaria deportation figure is the clean illustration. Twenty-seven thousand two hundred and ninety is a specific number and it looks like a record because it is not round. It varies between Sargon's own recensions, it counts the capital and its district rather than the kingdom, and it is a fraction of a northern population running to several hundred thousand. The work describes it as the total demographic liquidation of the kingdom. The archaeology of the northern hinterland shows continued occupation. Most Israelites were not deported, and the ten lost tribes are lost mainly to a reading of one number.

#### Fault nine: the minority proposal stated as settled

A recurring construction presents a contested identification as established: Khirbet el-Maqatir as Ai, el-Ahwat as Harosheth-hagoyim, the Large Stone Structure as David's palace, the Givati remains as the Acra, the Herodium tomb as Herod's, Tell el-Fūl as Saul's palace, the Ophel complex as tenth century, the Nazareth Inscription as a Claudian response to the empty tomb. Each of these is a real proposal by a real excavator and each is contested by other specialists on stated grounds.

The correction is to name the proposer and the objection in a clause. This costs eight words and converts an assertion into a scholarly position, which is what it is.

#### What survives

An audit of this severity invites the question of what is left, and the answer is: most of it, and in better condition.

The historical spine of the work is not damaged by any of the findings above. The Omride dynasty, the Assyrian vassalage, the fall of Samaria, the Sennacherib campaign, the Babylonian destruction, the Persian restoration, the Hasmonean state, the Herodian building programme, the two revolts, the rabbinic transition, the Christianization of the empire, the Byzantine-Sassanid exhaustion, and the Arab conquests are all abundantly attested and are described in this work accurately and often with real insight. The political-economy readings, which are the work's distinctive contribution, are largely untouched by the audit, because they are analytical rather than evidentiary claims and are correctly typed as such when they are typed at all.

What the audit changes is the shape of the confidence curve across the work. It was too flat. The scheme was applied most generously exactly where the evidence is thinnest, in the patriarchal and Exodus material, and most conservatively where the evidence is strongest, in the Assyrian and Roman periods where genuine Tier 1 epigraphy is dense. Correcting the tiers steepens the curve and produces a truer picture: a narrative that is under-determined at the beginning, becomes checkable in the ninth century BCE, becomes densely documented from the eighth, and remains so.

That shape is not a defeat. It is what the evidence actually looks like, and a work that displays it honestly is doing something better than a work that flattens it. The value of a graded scheme is realized only when the grades are allowed to differ.

#### The working protocol

Ten rules follow from the foregoing and govern the corrected text.

Tier by class, not by importance. An indispensable source can be Tier 4.

Terrain is a constraint, not evidence, and belongs in the analysis rather than the ledger.

No claim may rest on evidence dated by that claim; where the dependency exists, state it.

A falsifier must name a possible discovery. If no possible discovery would move the verdict, the claim is not empirical and should be typed as structural.

[DOCUMENTED] is available at Tiers 1 and 2 only.

Sources reaching us through a single channel are counted once.

Restored text is marked as restored.

Cross-period material is an analogue, with the gap stated in years, not same-era corroboration.

A quantity carried by one literary source is not Tier 1, and a quantity that varies between recensions is not precise.

A contested identification names its proposer and its objection.

None of these rules is novel. All of them are the ordinary discipline of the field, and the work already knew them, which is why it built a tier scheme in the first place. The audit's finding is not that the method was wrong. It is that the method was not consistently run.

---

## EXCURSUS VI. Religion as Practised and Religion as Legislated

There is a gap between the religion the Hebrew Bible prescribes and the religion the ground shows people performing, and the gap is not marginal. It is not a matter of a few backsliders in the provinces, or of a syncretistic fringe at the edges of a fundamentally orthodox population. The material and epigraphic record of Iron Age Israel and Judah, read on its own terms and without the biblical frame laid over it, describes a religion that would have been unrecognizable as legitimate to the editors who assembled the corpus, and it describes it as the ordinary practice of ordinary people over several centuries in every part of the territory.

This is among the most secure findings of Levantine archaeology, and it is also among the most persistently misreported, in both directions. The confessional misreading treats the material as evidence of a corruption that the prophets successfully corrected. The debunking misreading treats it as evidence that biblical religion is a fiction. Both misread the relationship between a prescriptive text and the population it addresses. A law code is evidence of what its framers wanted, and, by the fact that they had to legislate it, evidence of what they did not have. The correct inference from a prohibition repeated across four centuries is not that the prohibited thing was rare.

#### The Shape of the Problem

The corpus is not a neutral witness to the religion of its own period. It is the product of a particular current within Judean religion, exclusivist and Jerusalem-centred, which achieved editorial control of the tradition at a late stage and reworked the inherited material to conform to its programme. The Deuteronomistic historian's organizing scheme is explicit: there was an original pure worship of YHWH alone at one legitimate sanctuary, the people repeatedly abandoned it for foreign gods, and disaster followed. Every king is graded on this axis and almost all of them fail.

That scheme has a testable implication. If the exclusivist position was original and the syncretism was intrusive, the earliest material should be the purest and the deviations should appear as identifiable foreign borrowings, concentrated at the periods and places where foreign influence was strongest. If the scheme is a late imposition, the pattern should be the reverse: the practices condemned as foreign should be indigenous, continuous, distributed everywhere, and traceable back into the Bronze Age Canaanite substrate from which the population came.

The evidence supports the second. What the prophets and the Deuteronomists denounce as foreign intrusion looks, in the ground, like the ancestral religion of the land, practised by people who had every reason to believe they were doing what their grandparents had done.

#### Kuntillet Ajrud

The single most important epigraphic site for this question sits in the northeastern Sinai, on the Darb el-Ghazza route running south from Gaza toward the Gulf of Aqaba, at a place called Kuntillet Ajrud. It was excavated by Ze'ev Meshel in 1975 and 1976. The installation is a small walled building with a bench-lined entrance chamber, occupied briefly around 800 BCE and then abandoned, and its aridity preserved what a wetter site would have destroyed.

The finds include two large storage jars, pithoi, bearing ink drawings and inscriptions, and inscriptions painted directly onto the wall plaster of the doorways. The drawings are a jumble: standing figures in the manner of the Egyptian dwarf-god Bes, a seated lyre player, a stylized tree flanked by ibexes above a striding lion, a procession of worshippers, a cow suckling a calf. Whether the drawings and the inscriptions were meant to correspond is disputed and probably unanswerable; they overlap physically without any evident compositional relationship, and the safest position is that a jar's surface functioned as available writing space rather than as a designed image.

The inscriptions are the point. Several are blessing formulas of a standard epistolary type, and two of them read, in the customary rendering, that the writer blesses the addressee by YHWH of Samaria and by his asherah, and by YHWH of Teman and by his asherah. A plaster inscription carries a related formula. The Hebrew script has features associated with the northern kingdom, and some of the ceramic and other material points north, which suggests that the site served traffic connected with Israel rather than with Judah, though it lies far to the south of both.

Two things in this are of the first importance, and they are usually collapsed into one. The second is the asherah, which is discussed below. The first, and arguably the more radical, is the localization. YHWH of Samaria and YHWH of Teman are two named local manifestations of the same deity, distinguished by place, exactly as Mesopotamian texts distinguish Ishtar of Nineveh from Ishtar of Arbela and treat them as functionally separate powers with separate cults, separate treatment in treaties, and separate offerings. A deity who exists in local instantiations is not the god of Deuteronomy 6:4, and the insistence of that verse that YHWH is one, or alone, reads very differently once it is understood as a polemic against a real practice rather than as a bare doctrinal statement.

Teman is also worth noting. It denotes the south, and specifically Edomite territory, and it belongs with the cluster of archaic poetic passages that bring YHWH from the south: from Seir and the field of Edom in Judges 5, from Sinai and Seir and Mount Paran in Deuteronomy 33, from Teman and Mount Paran in Habakkuk 3. Egyptian topographical lists at Soleb and Amara West, from the fourteenth and thirteenth centuries, record a Shasu land whose name is written with the consonants of the divine name, in a southern context. The identification of that toponym with the god is inferential and not secure, but the convergence of an eighth-century inscription, an archaic poetic tradition, and a Late Bronze Egyptian list on a southern origin for YHWH is not easily dismissed.

#### The Grammar of His Asherah

The phrase rendered "his asherah" is spelled with the consonants of the noun followed by a final he, and the grammatical question is whether that final letter is a third-person masculine singular possessive suffix. If it is, the phrase means "his asherah," and the difficulty follows immediately: in Hebrew, and in Northwest Semitic generally, proper nouns do not take pronominal suffixes. One does not say "his Baal" meaning the god Baal, any more than English says "his John." The rule is not absolute across all Semitic usage and exceptions have been proposed, but it holds strongly enough in Hebrew that a possessive suffix on the word is a serious obstacle to reading it as the name of the goddess.

Four positions have been argued and each has a real constituency. The first takes asherah here as a common noun denoting the cult object, the wooden pole or stylized living tree that the biblical texts repeatedly command to be cut down and burned, and reads the formula as invoking YHWH together with his cult symbol, which is a coherent and grammatically comfortable reading. The second accepts the suffix but denies that the rule is decisive, and reads the goddess. The third denies that the final letter is a suffix at all, taking it as part of a longer form of the name or as an archaic ending, which removes the grammatical problem but requires special pleading about the orthography. The fourth, and in the present state of the evidence the most defensible, declines the choice: it observes that in West Semitic religion the distinction between a deity, the object that instantiates the deity, and a hypostatized attribute or mediating power was neither sharp nor stable, and that a formula invoking a god along with the sanctified object through which that god's blessing was channelled is fully at home in the period and does not require a decision between goddess and pole.

What the inscriptions establish, and what does not depend on resolving the grammar, is that around 800 BCE a Hebrew-writing person performing an ordinary act of correspondence invoked YHWH together with an asherah in a formulaic blessing, without any indication that this was unusual or contested. The formula is casual. It is not a theological statement; it is the equivalent of a conventional greeting. Casual usage is stronger evidence about the state of a religion than a polemic is, because nobody argues in a greeting.

Ugaritic supplies the background that makes the whole question intelligible. In the Late Bronze pantheon of Ugarit, the aged head of the divine assembly is El, and his consort is Athirat, whose name is the same word. She is the mother of the gods and a substantial figure in the mythological texts. Israelite religion inherited El: the divine epithets scattered through Genesis are El-compounds, the name Israel is itself El-theophoric and not YHWH-theophoric, and the process by which El's characteristics, his age, his beneficence, his council, and his role as creator were absorbed into YHWH is one of the best-supported reconstructions in the field, developed at length by Mark Smith under the heading of convergence. If YHWH inherited El's attributes, the question of whether he inherited El's consort is not a strange one to ask.

#### Khirbet el-Qom

The Kuntillet Ajrud formula is not isolated. A tomb at Khirbet el-Qom, a site in the Judean hills southwest of Hebron, yielded an inscription carved into a pillar of the burial chamber, published by William Dever, dating to the later eighth century and accompanied by an incised downward-pointing hand. The letters are shallow, irregular, and in places overcut, and no two published readings agree in every particular; this is a genuinely difficult text and any confident quotation of it is overstating the case.

What is reasonably secure is that the inscription is a funerary blessing for a man named Uriyahu, that it blesses him by YHWH, and that it contains a further clause invoking an asherah in a parallel construction, with the sense that by his asherah he has been delivered from his enemies. The reading of the asherah clause is accepted by most who have worked on the stone and doubted by some. If it stands, the significance is that the Kuntillet Ajrud formula is not a northern peculiarity or a caravanserai's local habit. It is Judean, it is domestic and funerary rather than official, and it appears in the century of Isaiah, within a day's walk of Jerusalem.

#### The Judean Pillar Figurines

The most abundant class of cultic material from Iron Age Judah is a small terracotta figurine, typically ten to fifteen centimetres tall, consisting of a solid conical or pillar-shaped lower body with no legs, a flaring base, prominent breasts held or supported by the hands, and a head that is either hand-modelled with pinched features or pressed from a mould with an elaborate hairstyle. They are made of ordinary local clay, they were often whitewashed and sometimes painted, and they are not expensive objects.

They exist in enormous quantity. They are recovered by the hundred from excavations in Jerusalem alone and by the thousand across Judah as a whole, and their distribution is overwhelmingly concentrated in the eighth and seventh centuries. Crucially, the great majority come from domestic contexts, from the fills and floors of ordinary houses, and from tombs, rather than from anything identifiable as a public sanctuary. This is not a state cult. It is a household object, present in a large fraction of Judean homes, in the period of Isaiah, Micah, Hezekiah, Jeremiah, and Josiah.

The interpretations divide. One reads them as images of Asherah, which makes them the material correlate of the epigraphic formulas and of the biblical polemic in a single stroke. A second reads them as generic apotropaic or sympathetic objects associated with fertility, pregnancy, childbirth, and lactation, addressed to a general power rather than to a named goddess, and points out that the emphasis is entirely on the breasts, that there is no genital emphasis at all, and that lactation rather than sexuality appears to be the referent. A third reads them as votive representations of the female worshipper rather than of any deity. A fourth treats them as folk objects whose users may have held no articulate theology about them whatever, on the analogy of amulets and charms in later societies whose owners would have described themselves as orthodox.

The disagreement is real, and the honest position is that the figurines demonstrate a widespread domestic practice whose theological content is not recoverable from the objects. But one datum cuts through the interpretive dispute and is rarely given the weight it deserves. The figurines do not cease in the late seventh century. They continue in use up to the Babylonian destruction and then stop, which means that whatever Josiah's reform did, it did not remove them from Judean houses. The termination correlates with the end of the kingdom, not with the reform. Any reconstruction that treats the reform as an effective purge of domestic practice has to explain that, and the simplest explanation is that the reform reached the state cult and not the household.

#### The House and Its Gods

Behind the figurines stands a whole register of religion that the corpus barely legislates because it barely notices: the cult of the household, conducted by the household, without priests, at objects the household owned.

The biblical texts preserve it in fragments, and the fragments are the more valuable for being incidental. The teraphim appear in Genesis 31, where Rachel steals her father's household gods and hides them in a camel saddle, and their theft is treated as a serious property matter rather than as an act of piety or impiety. They appear in 1 Samuel 19, where Michal places one in a bed and covers it to simulate the sleeping David, which requires it to be roughly human in size or capable of being dressed to look so, a detail hard to reconcile with the small figurines and suggestive of a broader class of objects. They appear in Judges 17 and 18, in a narrative that describes a private shrine with a cast image, an ephod, teraphim, and a hired Levite as its priest, and describes it without any note of scandal until the Danites steal the whole installation. And they appear in Hosea 3:4, in a list of things Israel will be deprived of during its coming affliction: king and prince, sacrifice and pillar, ephod and teraphim. That list is a prophet's own inventory of normal religious furniture, and the teraphim are in it without comment.

The archaeology of domestic cult supports the same picture. Excavated Iron Age houses in Israel and Judah yield, in varying combinations, small limestone or ceramic incense altars and burners, chalices and offering stands, model shrines or naoi, zoomorphic and anthropomorphic vessels, rattles, and amulets, the last frequently of Egyptian derivation, with the dwarf-god Bes and the protective eye being the commonest types. Standing stones, single upright unworked stones set on end, occur at scales from the monumental down to installations that fit in a corner of a room, and the practice is continuous with the Bronze Age Canaanite substrate and continues in Transjordan and among Israel's neighbours throughout the Iron Age.

Two silver amulets recovered from a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom, on the shoulder of the Hinnom valley outside Jerusalem, excavated by Gabriel Barkay, sharpen the picture in a valuable direction. They are tiny rolled sheets of silver, worn on the person, and when unrolled and read they carry text closely related to the priestly blessing of Numbers 6, invoking YHWH's blessing and protection. Their date has been argued, with a case made for a later placement, but the pre-exilic dating around the turn of the seventh and sixth centuries is the majority position and has been reinforced by subsequent imaging work. What they show is that the apotropaic amulet, the characteristic object of popular religion everywhere in the ancient world, was in use among Judeans with a Yahwistic text on it. Popular religion did not choose between YHWH and charms. It put YHWH on the charm.

#### The High Places and the Internal Contradiction

The corpus condemns the high places, the bamot, more insistently than it condemns almost anything else. The refrain runs through the book of Kings as the standing qualification on every otherwise good king: he did what was right, only the high places were not taken away. The word itself means a height or a back or a ridge, and by extension an elevated cultic installation, which need not be on a hill and need not be elaborate.

The corpus also, without apparent embarrassment, has its own heroes use them. Samuel presides at a sacrificial meal at a high place in 1 Samuel 9. Solomon sacrifices at the great high place at Gibeon in 1 Kings 3 and receives his dream revelation there, and the text supplies an explanation for the irregularity precisely because a later editor felt the difficulty. Elijah repairs an altar on Carmel and sacrifices on it in a contest whose whole point is the legitimacy of YHWH's worship, in flat contradiction of centralization. The inconsistency is not sloppiness. It is inherited narrative resisting a later frame, and it is the corpus itself testifying that sacrifice outside Jerusalem was normal and unremarkable for most of the period the corpus covers.

#### Arad

The best-excavated Israelite or Judean sanctuary outside Jerusalem is not at a high place on a hilltop. It is inside a royal fortress. The fortress at Tel Arad, in the eastern Beersheba valley, excavated by Yohanan Aharoni, contained in its northwestern corner a small temple complex laid out in a recognizable plan: an open courtyard containing an altar of unhewn fieldstones, whose dimensions approximate the five cubits square prescribed in Exodus 27; a broad room; and, raised above it, a small niche or holy of holies reached by steps, in which were found standing stones and, flanking the entrance, two small stone incense altars.

Two features make this decisive rather than merely interesting. The first is that Arad was a state installation. It was a royal Judean fortress, garrisoned, administered, and supplied by the crown, and the sanctuary inside it was therefore an official Judean sanctuary operating outside Jerusalem, with an altar for burnt offering built to the specification the Torah gives, at a period when centralization is supposed to have been the law. The second is that it was decommissioned rather than destroyed. The altar and the inner shrine were covered over and put out of use in a controlled way, and the standing stones were laid down rather than smashed, which is the archaeological signature of a deliberate and reverent deconsecration by the authority that owned the place.

The temptation to attach that decommissioning to a named reform is very strong and has been indulged by nearly everyone who has written on it. The stratigraphy will not carry it. The sequence of the fortress's strata and the phasing of the sanctuary within them have been debated since publication, and the proposals for the date of the decommissioning range across the eighth and seventh centuries, which is to say across both Hezekiah's reign and Josiah's, and across the possibility that it had nothing to do with either. Residue analysis of the material on the two small incense altars has identified aromatic substances including frankincense, which tells us something valuable about what was burned and about the fortress's access to imported aromatics, but nothing about when the burning stopped.

#### Beersheba, Motza, and Dan

At Tel Beersheba, excavation recovered the dismantled components of a large four-horned ashlar altar, its stones found reused in the fabric of a later wall and reassembled by the excavators into a structure over a metre and a half high. No sanctuary building housing it has been identified at the site, which leaves the altar's original setting unknown. The stones were in secondary use, which establishes that an altar was taken apart and its material recycled, and that is a real datum about the fate of a monumental cult installation; the identification of the agent and the occasion is inference, and the association with Hezekiah's reform, though frequently made, rests on the coincidence of a general period rather than on stratigraphic demonstration.

At Tel Motza, a few kilometres west of Jerusalem on the road to the coast, salvage excavation uncovered a temple building of the ninth century, with a plan comparable to other Levantine temples of the period, an altar in front of it, and a favissa or deposit of cultic material including anthropomorphic and zoomorphic figurines and stands. Motza is within sight of the Judean capital. A functioning temple with figurines at that distance from the Jerusalem temple in the ninth century is the clearest possible demonstration that the Judean cultic landscape was not what the corpus describes.

At Tel Dan, in the far north, Avraham Biran's excavations exposed a large stepped platform in a walled precinct, with an adjacent altar area and associated cultic installations, in use through Iron II. Its identification with the sanctuary the corpus attributes to Jeroboam is a reasonable inference from location, scale, and date, and it is worth registering that the northern kingdom's royal sanctuary, condemned by the corpus as the founding sin of the northern monarchy, looks archaeologically like an entirely conventional Levantine state temple.

#### Elephantine

The most complete picture of a functioning Judean religious community outside the land comes from a garrison island in the Nile at the First Cataract, opposite modern Aswan, and it is preserved in Aramaic on papyrus because Upper Egypt does not rain.

A community of Judean soldiers and their families was settled on Elephantine, serving first the Egyptian and then the Persian administration. Their own documents state that their temple stood before Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525, which places its foundation in the sixth century or earlier. The archive, principally from the late fifth century, includes contracts, marriage documents, letters, and lists, and it describes a temple of YHW, spelled with three letters, with an altar at which animal sacrifice, meal offering, and incense were presented.

That is already a considerable problem for any reconstruction in which the centralization law was in force and understood as binding. It becomes a larger one in the details. A temple donation account records contributions apportioned to YHW and also to deities named Eshem-Bethel and Anath-Bethel. Legal oaths in the papyri are sworn not only by YHW but, in at least one case, by Anath-Yahu, and elsewhere by Herem-Bethel. These names are of Aramaean and Syrian derivation, and their status is disputed: they may be independent deities worshipped alongside YHW, or hypostatized aspects, or divinized cult attributes, or, in the case of the compounds with Yahu, something closer to a title. What is not disputable is that the community's own documents place them in the same religious and legal apparatus as YHW.

The temple was destroyed in 410 by the priests of the ram-god Khnum, whose own sanctuary stood on the island and whose cult had an obvious objection to a neighbouring establishment that slaughtered rams, acting with the collusion of the local Persian official Vidranga. The community's response is the most revealing document in the archive. They wrote to Bagavahya, the Persian governor of Judah, and separately to the sons of Sanballat, the governor of Samaria, requesting support for rebuilding. They mention in the letter that they had previously written to Jehohanan the high priest in Jerusalem and to others there, and had received no reply.

That silence is the datum. The Jerusalem priesthood did not authorize the Elephantine temple, and there is no indication that it ever had. But neither, so far as any surviving document shows, did it denounce it, forbid it, or treat its existence as an offence. It simply did not answer. And the Elephantine Judeans, for their part, wrote to Jerusalem as one would write to a respected senior institution whose support would be useful, not as supplicants seeking a dispensation for an irregularity. They did not think they were doing anything wrong. The eventual authorization to rebuild, preserved as a memorandum, came from the two governors and permitted meal offering and incense while omitting animal sacrifice, a restriction which may reflect Jerusalem's influence, or Persian sensitivity to the Khnum priesthood's objection, or both.

#### The Ostraca and the Default Religion

The evidence assembled so far pulls in one direction, and it would be a distortion to stop there, because a second body of epigraphic evidence pulls hard in the other and has to be given its full weight.

The Lachish letters are a group of ostraca recovered from the gate area of the city, written in the last months before the Babylonian destruction, mostly correspondence from an outpost commander named Hoshayahu to a superior named Yaush. The Arad ostraca, more than a hundred of them from the fortress discussed above, are largely administrative: ration orders instructing the quartermaster Eliashib son of Eshyahu to issue wine, bread, and oil, frequently to a group called the Kittim who were probably foreign mercenaries. A legal petition from a fort at Mesad Hashavyahu on the coast preserves a labourer's complaint that his garment was confiscated.

These are not religious documents. They are the ordinary paperwork of a state under stress. And they are saturated with Yahwism of an entirely conventional kind. The letters open with the formula that YHWH cause my lord to hear tidings of peace. Correspondents bless one another by YHWH. Oaths invoke the life of YHWH. One Arad ostracon refers to the house of YHWH. No other deity is named anywhere in this corpus. Nothing in these texts would surprise a Deuteronomist.

The correct inference is not that one body of evidence cancels the other. It is that they describe different registers of the same religion. In the public, administrative, military, and official sphere, YHWH was the god of Israel and Judah without competition, and Yahwism was the default idiom of the state and of anyone writing in a state capacity. In the household, the tomb, and the local shrine, YHWH was worshipped alongside other powers, with images, at pillars and trees, and with objects that the exclusivists condemned. Most people in most societies have held both of these at once without experiencing a contradiction, and there is no reason to think Judeans were different.

#### Theophoric Names as a Demographic Instrument

Personal names offer a way to sample a population's religious commitments at scale, and the Hebrew epigraphic corpus of seals, seal impressions, ostraca, and inscriptions supplies several thousand of them. The instrument is genuinely useful and its limits are genuinely severe, and Jeffrey Tigay's study remains the standard treatment of both.

The finding is striking. Yahwistic names, compounded with the elements yeho-, -yahu, and -yah, dominate the Judean onomasticon overwhelmingly. Names compounded with Baal are rare in Judah. In the northern kingdom the picture is different: the Samaria ostraca, administrative dockets of the early eighth century recording shipments of wine and oil to the capital, contain both Yahwistic and Baalistic names in a proportion that has been much argued over, and Baal names are clearly present in the north in a way they are not in the south. Names invoking goddesses are essentially absent from the Hebrew corpus.

The limits must be stated with equal firmness. Names are conservative: a person is named once, by parents, often after a relative, and the name then persists for a lifetime and recurs in later generations, so the onomasticon reflects naming convention with a lag of decades and possibly of centuries. A Yahwistic name does not exclude the worship of anything else, as the Elephantine community demonstrates conclusively, since its members bore thoroughly Yahwistic names while contributing to Eshem-Bethel. Names compounded with El are ambiguous, because El functions both as the generic word for god and as the name of a specific deity. The corpus is skewed toward the literate and the administrative, which is to say toward exactly the register that the ostraca show was uniformly Yahwistic. And the absence of goddess-names may reflect a convention about what names are made of rather than the absence of goddess-worship, since naming practices in many cultures draw on a restricted subset of the divine world.

What the onomasticon establishes is that YHWH was the national god and that his worship was near-universal in the sense that almost everyone was in some relation to him. It does not establish that his worship was exclusive, and it was never designed to.

#### Monolatry and Monotheism

The distinction that organizes the whole question is between monolatry, the worship of one god without any claim that the others do not exist, and monotheism proper, the assertion that there is only one god and that the others are nothing. These are different positions and the corpus contains both, in a distribution that is chronologically informative.

The first commandment does not deny that other gods exist. It forbids having them before or besides YHWH, which presupposes their availability. Psalm 82 opens with God standing in the divine council and passing judgment among the gods, and concludes by sentencing them to die like men, which is a demotion rather than a denial. Deuteronomy 32:8 in the reading preserved at Qumran and reflected in the Greek has the Most High apportioning the nations according to the number of the divine beings, with YHWH receiving Jacob as his allotted share, which places YHWH as one of a set of national deities under a higher head; the Masoretic reading, sons of Israel, is best explained as a later correction of a theologically awkward text. Jephthah, negotiating with the Ammonites in Judges 11, asks whether the king will not possess what Chemosh his god gives him to possess, and the question is asked in perfect good faith. In 2 Kings 3 the king of Moab, besieged, sacrifices his eldest son on the wall, and great wrath comes upon Israel so that they withdraw; the Israelite narrator reports the efficacy of a Moabite sacrifice to a Moabite god without comment.

The comparative evidence shows that this was the regional norm and that Israel's theology of history was not distinctive. The Mesha Stele, a Moabite royal inscription of around 840, explains Moab's period of subjection to Israel by saying that Chemosh was angry with his land, and explains the recovery by saying that Chemosh restored it and commanded the campaigns; Mesha devotes the population of one captured town to Ashtar-Chemosh under a ban using the same vocabulary the Hebrew texts use, and reports carrying off the vessels of YHWH from Nebo and dragging them before Chemosh. The theological structure of that inscription and of the book of Kings is the same structure. Defeat as the anger of the national god and restoration as his favour is a Levantine convention, not an Israelite insight.

The first unambiguous denial that other gods exist appears in the chapters of Isaiah addressed to a deported community in Babylon. There the formulations are explicit and repeated: I am the first and I am the last, and besides me there is no god; I am YHWH and there is no other; I form light and create darkness, I make weal and create woe. The gods of the nations are not weaker rivals in these chapters. They are manufactured objects, and the polemic against them is a satire on carpentry. This is a different claim from anything earlier in the corpus, and it is made in a specific historical situation.

#### The Exile as Forcing Event

The situation is the obvious candidate for the cause. In the ordinary logic of the ancient Near East, the destruction of a national temple and the deportation of a national population demonstrated the weakness of the national god relative to the god of the conqueror. That inference was available, it was the standard one, and Assyrian and Babylonian royal propaganda made it explicitly. A Judean community in Babylonia in the sixth century faced it directly.

Two responses could preserve the tradition. The first, already available in the prophetic literature and heavily developed by the Deuteronomistic editors, was that the defeat was not YHWH's weakness but his judgment, executed by an instrument he controlled. The second, which follows from the first if it is pressed, is that a god who directs the Babylonian army is not a national god at all but the sole power in history, and that Marduk, in whose city the exiles lived and whose New Year procession they could watch, is not a rival but a fiction. The first response saves the god. The second, taken to its conclusion, abolishes the category of rival gods entirely, and that is what the exilic chapters of Isaiah do.

The reconstruction is a strong one and should still be labelled as a hypothesis rather than a demonstration. What can be established is the distribution: monolatrous and council-presupposing language is early and pervasive, unambiguous monotheistic assertion is exilic and later, and the transition is not gradual across the corpus but concentrated. What cannot be established is the mechanism, and the alternative reading, that a monotheizing minority current existed considerably earlier and that the exile gave it its opportunity rather than creating it, is compatible with the same distribution. Morton Smith's reconstruction of a Yahweh-alone party as a long-running faction is of this second type, and the evidence does not decide between them.

#### The Deuteronomistic Frame Inverted

Return now to the frame with which this began. The Deuteronomistic scheme presents the history of Israel and Judah as a record of apostasy from an original exclusive Yahwism into foreign cults, punctuated by reformers who restore what was lost. The evidence assembled here inverts the direction of that movement almost entirely.

What the texts denounce as foreign was indigenous. Asherah, the standing stones, the high places, the household images, the veneration of the dead, and the local instantiation of the deity are all continuous with the Bronze Age religion of Canaan, from which the Iron Age highland population overwhelmingly derived. There is no moment identifiable in the archaeological record at which a pure Yahwism existed and was subsequently corrupted. The exclusivist position is not the starting point from which the population fell away. It is a programme, developed by a particular current, argued for over centuries, and imposed with only partial success even at the height of its political influence.

The corpus itself, read carefully, concedes this. The reform notices in 2 Kings 18 and 23 are the strongest evidence in the whole Bible for what the religion of Judah actually contained, precisely because they are hostile. Hezekiah is said to have broken up the bronze serpent that Moses had made, because the people were burning incense to it, which is an admission that a relic attributed to Moses himself was a cult object in Jerusalem receiving offerings. Josiah's purge, as inventoried, removed from the temple of YHWH in Jerusalem the vessels made for Baal and Asherah and the host of heaven, the asherah itself, which was taken out to the Kidron and burned, the quarters where women wove for the asherah, and the horses and chariots dedicated to the sun at the temple entrance; outside it he defiled the Topheth in the Hinnom valley and the installations attributed to Solomon for Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Milcom. No editor invents an inventory that embarrassing for the temple of Solomon. Whatever the historicity of the reform as an event, the list is a description of furniture.

And the reform's effect appears to have been limited in exactly the way one would expect of a top-down measure against household practice. The pillar figurines continue to the end. The amulets continue. Jeremiah, writing after Josiah, describes women baking cakes for the Queen of Heaven and reports the refugees in Egypt telling him plainly that they had prospered when they made offerings to her and suffered since they stopped, which is not the speech of a defeated minority. Nadav Naaman and others have argued on both textual and archaeological grounds that the reforms were considerably smaller in scope than the account in Kings suggests, and the material record does not contradict them.

#### The Minority Report

The conclusion follows and should be stated without softening. The religion that the prophets attack was the normal religion of the population of Israel and Judah. It was not a deviation, an importation, or a fringe. It was what people did, in their houses and at their local shrines and at the tombs of their dead, for the entire duration of the monarchies, and there is no period for which the evidence shows otherwise.

This means that the prophetic literature is a minority report. It is the polemic of a party that did not command the practice it demanded, written from inside a society that was not doing what the party wanted, and preserved because that party eventually controlled the editing of the tradition. Read as a description of Israelite religion it is misleading. Read as the argument of one faction against the majority, it becomes intelligible in every particular, including its bitterness, its repetition, and its recourse to the claim that the majority position was foreign, which is the standard move of a reforming minority everywhere and is almost never true.

None of this diminishes the tradition, and it would be a poor reading that took it as debunking. Two things follow that are considerably more interesting than debunking. The first is that the minority report won, decisively and permanently, and that the winning took place under conditions of national catastrophe rather than of political success, which is a genuinely unusual pattern and calls for explanation rather than assumption. The second is that the tradition preserved, inside its own canon, the evidence that condemns its own framing. The inventories of Josiah's purge, Jephthah's concession to Chemosh, the divine council of Psalm 82, the apportionment of Deuteronomy 32, the teraphim in Hosea's list of ordinary furniture: all of these survived the editing that had every motive to remove them. A tradition that suppressed its own past completely would leave no such traces. This one left enough for the reconstruction to be made, which is a fact about the character of its transmission and deserves to be counted in its favour.
