## EXCURSUS IX. Writing, Literacy, and the Manufacture of a Usable Past

Every document discussed in this work exists because somebody paid for it, and not once. A text on papyrus in a Mediterranean climate becomes unreadable within a few generations unless it is recopied; parchment lasts longer and costs the skins of a herd; a tradition held in memory dies with the last person holding it. Survival is not a passive property of a text. It is the cumulative output of a long series of decisions by institutions with budgets, and every one of those decisions was made by a party with an interest.

The corpus available to a historian is not a sample of what was written. It is a sample of what somebody wanted to keep, filtered by what the climate permitted to remain, filtered again by the technological transitions that forced everything worth having to be physically re-manufactured, and filtered a final time by the institutional survival of the parties doing the copying. Each filter has a known bias, and the biases compound in one direction: toward states, temples, and the winners of doctrinal disputes, and away from everything else.

#### The Alphabet as a Workers' Technology

The writing systems of the Bronze Age Near East were institutional monopolies by design. Mature Mesopotamian cuneiform required control of several hundred signs in regular use, many carrying multiple syllabic values and multiple logographic readings, disambiguated by context and by a determinative system that itself had to be learned. Competence took years of formal instruction, which confined it to people whose institutions could support a decade of unproductive training. Writing was a profession, and like most professions it protected its entry.

The alphabet broke that. Instead of a sign for each syllable or word, take a sign for each consonant and derive its sound from the first consonant of the name of the object depicted: a house sign for the first consonant of the word for house, an ox head for the word for ox. Applied to a Semitic language whose morphology is carried by consonants, acrophony yields a working script of roughly two dozen signs. A system requiring years becomes one that can in principle be taught in weeks.

At Serabit el-Khadim, the turquoise mining region of the southwestern Sinai worked by Egyptian expeditions with a substantial Semitic-speaking labour force, Flinders Petrie's excavation early in the twentieth century recovered short inscriptions in a script that was neither hieroglyphic nor any known Semitic writing. Alan Gardiner subsequently proposed the acrophonic key, reading a recurring sequence as an address to the Lady, Baalat, the Semitic name for the goddess the Egyptians worshipped there as Hathor. Not every particular is accepted and the dating has been argued across several centuries. The second body of evidence, found in the 1990s by John and Deborah Darnell in the Wadi el-Hol in the Egyptian Western Desert, consists of short inscriptions cut beside a desert road among graffiti left by travellers and by the personnel who worked and policed the routes, placed in the first half of the second millennium and possibly earlier than the Sinai material.

The alphabet was not invented in a scribal school, by scribes, for scribal purposes. It was invented at the margin of the Egyptian system, by people in visual contact with hieroglyphic writing without being trained in it, who reassigned its signs by the sound of their own words. A technology that lowers the entry cost of a profession is not attractive to that profession, and the scribal establishments of the Late Bronze Age had no reason to abandon a system whose difficulty was the basis of their standing.

#### From Sinai to Byblos to the Aegean

Between the Sinai inscriptions and the mature Phoenician alphabet lies a scatter of short Proto-Canaanite texts on arrowheads, sherds, and small objects from Levantine sites of the Middle and Late Bronze Age, thin, frequently unreadable, and unstable in writing direction and letter form. That is what an unstandardized script looks like: everyone improvising within a shared principle.

Across the Late Bronze Age and into the Iron Age the inventory settles at twenty-two signs, the forms become linear and abstract, and the direction fixes right to left. The result is the Phoenician alphabet, attested monumentally in the royal inscriptions of Byblos, of which the sarcophagus of Ahiram is the best known. Ugarit yielded abecedary tablets, and the letter order they record is substantially the order later carried by Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. That order is arbitrary, and its persistence across three millennia and several language families is evidence of unbroken pedagogical transmission.

The Greeks took the Phoenician script, retained letter names meaningless in Greek and transparent in Semitic, retained the order, and made one alteration: signs for consonants Greek lacked were repurposed to write vowels. Herodotus recorded the tradition that the letters came from Phoenicia and called them Phoenician letters. The date is argued across the ninth and eighth centuries; the mechanism is not in doubt. It was sustained commercial contact, and it moved in the hands of merchants who needed to keep accounts. Wherever the alphabet arrived, it arrived cheap.

#### What the Levant Wrote On

Papyrus was manufactured in Egypt from the pith of the sedge, laid in crossed layers, pressed, dried, and joined into rolls. It was the standard medium for extended writing throughout the eastern Mediterranean, an Egyptian export, and not cheap in the Levant, where it had to be imported. Leather and prepared skins served where durability mattered and became standard for scriptural scrolls. Both are organic, and both are destroyed by moisture, fungal action, and the ordinary microbial activity of soil that is wet for part of the year.

The southern Levant is wet for part of the year. The consequence is absolute and it is the single most distorting fact about the Iron Age Levantine record: every papyrus and every leather document produced in Israel and Judah across the entire monarchic period is gone, with a handful of exceptions preserved in the exceptionally arid caves west of the Dead Sea. Not damaged. Not fragmentary. Gone, without residue. Egypt is the measure of the loss, since rainless conditions preserved papyrus there in enormous quantity and at every social level. Where the climate permits, the documentary record is dense. Where it does not, the record is not thin. It is absent.

What survives instead is the ostracon: a sherd of broken pottery written on in ink, used for the ephemeral and the cheap. Ostraca were free, generated continuously as vessels broke, and were the medium of the receipt, the ration order, the short note, the practice exercise, the thing not worth a sheet of papyrus. Pottery is chemically inert and indestructible, so ostraca survive in precisely the conditions that destroy everything else. The surviving Hebrew epigraphic record therefore consists almost entirely of material its own writers regarded as disposable, while everything they thought worth a durable medium has perished. Arguments running from the character of the surviving inscriptions to the character of Israelite writing culture are arguments from the wastepaper basket to the library.

#### The Bulla and the Ghost of the Archive

A papyrus intended to be kept or sent was rolled, tied with cord, and a lump of soft clay pressed over the cord and stamped with a seal. The lump is a bulla, a security device: the document cannot be opened without breaking the clay. The papyrus decays and disappears, and the bulla, if the building holding the archive burned, is fired by the conflagration into hard ceramic and becomes effectively permanent. The archaeological signature of a destroyed archive is a scatter of hard-fired seal impressions in a burnt layer with no documents at all, their reverse faces carrying the negative impression of what they were pressed against, the fibre pattern of the papyrus and the channel left by the cord.

Excavation in the City of David recovered a group of such bullae from a burnt building of the final Judean period, among them a sealing naming Gemaryahu son of Shaphan, a man the book of Jeremiah places in the royal palace. The inference is direct: these buildings held collections of rolled papyrus documents, in quantity, sealed by named officials. Judah had archives, the archives are gone, and the only surviving evidence for them is the security hardware. This should be held firmly whenever it is claimed that the epigraphic record shows Judah lacked the documentary infrastructure for extended literature. It shows that the relevant medium does not survive in that soil, and it supplies positive evidence that documents on that medium existed in numbers.

#### The Size of the Hebrew Corpus

The surviving Hebrew epigraphic corpus can now be described honestly, and the honest description is that it is small. Counted generously, including seals, stamped handles, single-word jar inscriptions, and illegible fragments, it runs into the thousands of items. Counted as texts carrying more than a formula or a name, it runs to a few hundred. Counted as continuous compositions of any length, it is a list a specialist can hold in memory. Mesopotamia has yielded cuneiform tablets in the hundreds of thousands; the Hebrew material would fit physically into one room.

The Gezer Calendar, a small inscribed limestone tablet, lists agricultural operations through the year in ten short lines; its date is placed by palaeography around the tenth century, its language is disputed as between Hebrew and a neighbouring Canaanite dialect, and its function is unknown. The Samaria ostraca, around a hundred legible dockets from the northern palace complex, record deliveries of wine and oil with regnal years but no king's name, from the first half of the eighth century. The Siloam tunnel inscription describes in six lines the moment when two tunnelling crews driving from opposite ends heard each other and broke through; it is late eighth century on palaeographic grounds and names no king, which is itself a datum about who commissioned display inscriptions in Judah. The Lachish letters are military correspondence of the last months before the Babylonian destruction, of which the best known reports that the writer watches for the signals of Lachish because those of Azekah are no longer visible. The Arad ostraca, over a hundred from the fortress in the eastern Negev, are largely quartermaster's paperwork: orders to Eliashib son of Eshyahu to issue wine, flour, and oil, frequently to a contingent called the Kittim, with correspondence touching a threat from Edom and a reference to the house of YHWH.

The ostracon from Khirbet Qeiyafa, from a fortified site in the Elah valley whose radiocarbon dating places it near the transition from the eleventh century to the tenth, carries five lines of ink on a sherd. Published readings differ so radically that they do not agree on the language, the direction of writing, the word division, or the genre. The honest statement is that the inscription is early, alphabetic, and long enough to be a text rather than a label, and that nobody can read it with confidence. The corpus as a whole is small for climatic rather than cultural reasons, as the bullae demonstrate, but the smallness is a real constraint: any reconstruction of Israelite scribal culture rests on very few objects.

#### Abecedaries and the Archaeology of Instruction

Formal instruction leaves a distinctive archaeological signature, and it is not the signature of accomplished writing. It is the signature of bad writing: one short text copied repeatedly, with errors, by hands of varying competence.

Scribal training in Babylonia proceeded through a standard curriculum of sign lists, then lexical lists of increasing length, then proverbs and short compositions, then the extended literature. Practice tablets survive on which a teacher's model is written on one portion and the student's attempt on another, the student's demonstrably inferior, and excavation at Nippur exposed a residential building whose tablet assemblage consists overwhelmingly of such exercise material, allowing a scribal school to be identified as a physical place. Egypt supplies the parallel: student copies survive on ostraca in quantity, particularly from the workmen's village at Deir el-Medina, and among the texts copied is a composition contrasting the scribe's condition with every manual trade, arguing that the potter is filthy, the smith scorched, the fisherman in danger, and the scribe alone comfortable and free. That text was itself a copying exercise, so the profession's advertisement for itself was the material on which its recruits learned to write.

The Levantine evidence is thinner and consists principally of abecedaries: the alphabet written out in order, often clumsily, on a sherd at Izbet Sartah in an Iron I context, on a stone at Tel Zayit in a tenth-century context, at Kuntillet Ajrud, and elsewhere. Nobody writes out the alphabet except to learn or teach it, so somebody was teaching the sequence, which means the sequence was fixed and transmitted rather than reinvented, and teaching a non-productive skill implies an institution capable of feeding someone who is not farming. It does not follow that schools existed in the Mesopotamian sense; no building in Iron Age Israel or Judah has been securely identified as one, and instruction may equally have been conducted within families as an apprenticeship, which leaves no institutional footprint. The strongest argument for formal training in Judah is therefore the script itself: Hebrew inscriptions of the eighth and seventh centuries show a standardized letter repertoire, consistent stance, and consistent ductus across widely separated sites, and Christopher Rollston has pressed the point that such uniformity is produced by instruction against a norm rather than by informal imitation. The corollary is that the writing in the epigraphic record is the product of trained personnel, which tells us about the trained and nothing whatever about everyone else.

#### Three Literacies

Discussion of ancient literacy is routinely wrecked by the assumption that literacy is one thing a person either has or lacks. It is not, and the distinctions matter more than any rate.

Signature literacy is the ability to write one's own name and recognize it, and perhaps a few other fixed forms. Functional literacy is the ability to read and produce short practical texts within a known genre: a receipt, a ration order, a list, a brief letter following a formula. Compositional literacy is the ability to compose extended prose or verse to a genre standard, to control orthography across a long text, and to copy accurately at length without introducing catastrophic error. That is a different order of accomplishment, requiring years, access to an existing literature, and the institutional support to spend those years, and in any ancient society it was confined to very few people.

These three do not scale together, and evidence for one is not evidence for another. An ostracon written by a junior officer at a desert fort demonstrates functional literacy at the periphery of the state apparatus. It demonstrates nothing about the general population.

For the ancient Mediterranean generally, William Harris argued in the standard treatment that literacy rates were low, that the burden of proof lies with those claiming otherwise, and that even in classical Athens the proportion able to read at any useful level was a minority and probably a small one. Later work has qualified the argument without overturning its central caution. For Iron Age Judah no rate can be established at all: any figure offered is the output of a model whose inputs are estimates of population, of the proportion of the literate leaving recoverable traces, and of the survival rate of those traces, each uncertain by a large factor and multiplying. The rate is unknown. The interesting question is the distribution.

#### The Hands at Arad

The Arad ostraca from the fortress's final phase constitute a closed group: texts from one small installation, over a short period, in a known institutional context. A team including Shira Faigenbaum-Golovin, Arie Shaus, Eli Piasetzky, and Israel Finkelstein applied algorithmic handwriting comparison to a selection of them, treating letter forms as measurable objects and testing whether the observed variation was consistent with a single writer. Their conclusion was that the group required a minimum of six distinct hands.

The finding is a statistical minimum derived from a model, it depends on choices about inclusion and about how letter similarity is quantified, and it has been contested. The direction of the result is what carries the argument and is robust to the details. Arad was not the capital. It was a small garrison at the desert edge of the kingdom and its correspondence was routine supply administration. Six or more writers there means the capacity reached well below the central chancery.

The inference is a floor. It does not tell us that ordinary Judeans were literate; there is no reason to think they were. It tells us that the state's writing capacity was diffused through its officer class rather than concentrated in a handful of court specialists, which is the condition under which extended composition becomes institutionally possible, because it means the state was producing trained writers in numbers rather than singly.

#### Who Fed the Scribes

A scribe produces no food. Someone else's surplus supports him, and the identity of that someone determines what gets written. In the ancient Near East the answer is almost always the palace or the temple, frequently operating as one fiscal system. The book of Jeremiah preserves an account of a scroll dictated to a scribe, read publicly, read again in the chamber of the royal scribe, and then read to the king, who cut and burned it column by column as it was read; whatever its historicity, its assumptions about who writes, where documents are kept, and how they reach a king are the assumptions of a functioning chancery.

The material correlates of Judean administration are substantial from the eighth century. Storage jars stamped on the handle with a royal formula and one of a small set of place names occur in the hundreds from the late eighth century, indicating a centrally organized provisioning system; a different stamp type succeeds them in the seventh; inscribed stone weights in a standard denominational system are recovered in numbers. These are the signatures of a state that measures, records, and audits, and such a state trains people to write.

Literature is a by-product of administration. But the capacity remains the state's or the temple's and is deployed on the priorities of whoever controls it. There is no ancient equivalent of an independent literary sector. A text surviving from antiquity was, at the moment of its production, either useful to an institution or produced by someone that institution was already feeding for other reasons.

#### The Deuteronomistic History as a State Project

The narrative running from Deuteronomy through Kings is the largest sustained prose composition in the Hebrew Bible and the clearest case of institutional literature in the corpus. Its source analysis is treated elsewhere in this work; what concerns the present argument is its character as a funded project.

Every king of Israel and Judah is graded, the criterion is cultic and concerns worship at a single legitimate sanctuary, and it is applied retroactively to periods in which no such requirement demonstrably existed. Between the evaluations sit materials of a different texture: regnal formulae with accession synchronisms and lengths of reign, lists of officials, building notices, and references to further records under the formula of the book of the chronicles of the kings. That material is dry, formulaic, and carries no theological load, which is the profile of chancery extract carried through rather than composed. The scheme culminates: Josiah receives an evaluation exceeding every other king's, placing him above all his predecessors in the completeness of his turning. A narrative built to that climax exists to legitimate the programme of that king, and the natural reading is that a first edition was produced in his reign as the historical charter of a centralizing reform, which is the Josianic edition proposed by Frank Moore Cross.

It continues past Josiah's death in a manner the preceding narrative does not prepare for, through four undistinguished reigns, to the destruction of the temple and the deportation, and closes with a short notice recording that in the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's exile the king of Babylon released him from prison, gave him a seat above the other kings at his court, and provided a daily allowance for the rest of his life. It is a note about rations, and it functions as the smallest possible signal that the Davidic line was not extinguished. The most economical account of the whole is a two-stage composition: a work assembled to justify a reform, then revised after that reform's political framework had been annihilated, the revision's task being to explain the disaster without conceding that the god who commanded the reform had failed. Its solution is the theodicy running through the received text, in which destruction is judgment rather than weakness, executed through an instrument YHWH controlled. Martin Noth's alternative reconstruction of a single exilic author remains a live position.

#### The Chronicler's Method, Documented

The field has one controlled experiment on ancient editorial method. Chronicles reworks Samuel and Kings, or a text closely resembling them, and both source and revision survive, so it is possible to observe rather than infer what a Persian-period editor did to an inherited narrative when he had reason to change it.

Omission of the discreditable: David's adultery with Bathsheba, the murder of Uriah, the rebellion of Absalom, and the succession intrigue are absent entirely, and the David of Chronicles is a liturgical founder who organizes temple personnel and prepares building materials. Nothing signals the omissions, and a reader without access to Samuel would not know there was anything to omit. Excision of a whole subject: the northern kingdom is not narrated, its kings appearing only where their actions touch Judah, so an entire polity with two centuries of history is removed by the expedient of declining to treat it. Correction of an offensive agent: in the older account of the census YHWH incites David to number Israel and then punishes the numbering, and in Chronicles the inciting agent is a satan. The change is one word, and it repairs a theological problem the later period found intolerable.

Repair of a theodicy: Kings presents Manasseh as Judah's worst king and assigns to his reign the guilt that made destruction inevitable, while also recording that he reigned longer than any other Judean king, which is a problem for a scheme in which prosperity tracks fidelity. Chronicles supplies the missing element, taking him to Babylon in fetters, where he humbles himself, prays, is restored, and reforms, so that the long reign is earned.

The value of the list is that it is not hypothetical. It records what an ancient editor actually did with both terms of the comparison in hand, and it specifies what the operations look like: silent omission, agent substitution, explanatory supplementation, and quantitative inflation, all performed without any indication to the reader that anything has changed.

#### A Genre That Cannot Record Defeat

Royal inscriptions are the largest body of contemporary narrative evidence for the ancient Near East, and they are unreliable in a specific and predictable way that is a property of the genre rather than of any king's dishonesty. Their function is not to inform. A royal inscription is addressed to a god, to posterity, and to a successor, and it is frequently deposited where no human being will read it, in a foundation deposit or a wall core. Its purpose is to record that the king discharged the commission his god gave him: extended the borders, defeated the enemies, built the temple, maintained the order of the world. It is a statement that the commission was not discharged, for which the genre has no grammar. The handling of defeat is therefore not denial but restructuring, in recognizable patterns.

The commonest is the substituted objective. Sennacherib's account of his third campaign, preserved on several clay prisms in closely agreeing versions, enumerates the Judean cities taken, the spoil and captives, the tribute exacted, and the confinement of Hezekiah in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage. It does not report the capture of Jerusalem. In a genre that reports captures relentlessly, and in an account reporting the capture of dozens of smaller places in the same campaign, the silence about the campaign's principal objective is the loudest thing in the text. The inscription is not lying; it describes a partial success in language permitting the partial to be read as the whole, and the caged-bird image converts a failure to take a city into a demonstration of the city's helplessness.

The second is the converted outcome. Ramesses II fought a Hittite army under Muwatalli at Kadesh in the fifth year of his reign, was drawn into an ambush, and extricated his forces at heavy cost; the city was not taken and the region remained under Hittite control, as the subsequent treaty between the powers confirms. The Egyptian monumental record, carved at multiple major temples in narrative and poetic versions with extensive reliefs, presents the engagement as a personal triumph in which the king, deserted by his troops and surrounded, called on Amun and broke the enemy alone. A clear victory does not require five temples.

Against these stands a genre that behaves differently and thereby proves the point. The Babylonian chronicle texts are terse, annalistic, and comparatively free of rhetorical elaboration, and they do occasionally record reverses, including an engagement with Egypt in which both sides suffered heavily and the Babylonian king withdrew to refit. The chronicles were not display inscriptions; they appear to have served an internal, probably scholarly and divinatory, purpose for which accuracy about outcomes had a use. Where the audience changes, the reliability changes, which is the clearest available demonstration that the distortion in royal inscriptions is a function of purpose rather than of a general ancient indifference to fact.

#### Erasure as Editorial Policy

Curation extended to the systematic removal of what had been written, and Egypt documents it clearly because monuments are durable enough that erasure leaves a visible scar: the record of the Amarna period was expunged, the city abandoned, the temples of the Aten dismantled and their blocks reused as fill, and the kings of the period omitted from subsequent official king lists, so that the sequence of legitimate rulers passes over them as though they had not reigned. Mesopotamian practice included the reverse operation, the Cyrus cylinder narrating the fall of the previous regime as an act of Marduk who was displeased with Nabonidus and delivered Babylon to Cyrus without a battle. Regime change produces a new archive, and produces it fast. Where a scar remains the operation can be observed; where the medium was papyrus, nothing remains, and the absence is indistinguishable from a text that was never written.

#### Josephus, Client

The most important narrative source for Judean history in the Second Temple and early Roman periods is the work of a man whose position makes every page a problem. Yosef ben Matityahu was born to a priestly family in Jerusalem in the late 30s of the first century, held a command in Galilee at the outbreak of the revolt against Rome, and surrendered at Jotapata in 67 after the town fell, having survived a suicide pact among the defenders by a lot-drawing procedure he describes himself. Brought before Vespasian, he predicted that the general would become emperor. When the prediction was fulfilled two years later he was freed, took the family name of his patrons, and spent the rest of his life in Rome on an imperial pension, writing. Everything he wrote, he wrote as a client of the dynasty that had destroyed his city, for an audience including the men who commanded the destruction. This is not inference: he states that Titus authorized publication of his history of the war and that copies went to the imperial family.

The resulting thesis is exactly what the position requires. The war was not a national uprising but the work of a faction of tyrants, brigands, and fanatics who seized the city and terrorized its inhabitants; the mass of the people were their victims; the priestly and propertied classes, to which the author belonged, opposed the war and were overwhelmed; God had transferred his favour to Rome, so that resistance was not merely futile but impious. And Titus conducted the siege with restraint, sought to preserve the temple, and was thwarted when a soldier hurled a firebrand against his express orders. That last claim is load-bearing, and it is where an independent line bears. A Christian chronicler writing in the early fifth century gives an account in which Titus argued in a council of war that the temple should be destroyed in order to extirpate the religions of the Jews and the Christians, held to be connected. The passage is widely thought to derive from the lost portion of Tacitus's Histories, though the derivation is an inference rather than a demonstration. Its existence establishes that a version of the destruction as deliberate Roman policy circulated, and the version favourable to Titus reaches us from a man on his payroll.

#### War Against Antiquities

The history of the war, written in the 70s, and the twenty books of Jewish Antiquities, completed two decades later under Domitian, cover overlapping ground with different emphases and sometimes different facts. The later work is addressed to a Greek-reading gentile audience and presents the Judean people as ancient, as possessed of a venerable constitution given by a lawgiver comparable to those the Greeks admired, and as philosophically respectable; its treatment of the Judean sects is fuller and more sympathetic, and its account of the Hasmonean and Herodian periods is longer and differently weighted.

The sharpest divergence is between the war narrative and the autobiographical Life, appended to the Antiquities and written partly to answer a rival account by Justus of Tiberias. In the earlier work the author is a general, regularly appointed by the Jerusalem authorities, who fortified Galilee and conducted a competent defence. In the later work he is an envoy sent to restrain the revolt and persuade the hotheads to lay down their arms. These are not compatible self-descriptions, and the change tracks a change in what needed explaining: in the 70s he had to account for himself to Romans as a defeated but honourable opponent, and in the 90s against a fellow Judean's charge that he had led the revolt.

No Jewish community preserved Josephus. He survived because the Church preserved him, beginning with the fourth-century use of his work as an external witness to Christian origins and to the destruction of Jerusalem as divine judgment. The preservation left its mark: the passage in the Antiquities describing Jesus contains material no first-century Judean writer would have written, and the majority position holds that a shorter original notice was expanded by a Christian hand in transmission. The most important single source for Second Temple Judaism reaches us through the copying effort of the party with the strongest interest in one particular reading of it, and the copying is detectable in the text.

#### The Codex and the Extinction of What Was Not Recopied

Between roughly the second and the fifth centuries the standard physical form of the book in the Mediterranean world changed, and the change functioned as a filter on the entire inherited literature. The scroll, a continuous roll of papyrus or prepared skin unwound as it is read, had been the literary book form for millennia. The codex, sheets folded, stacked, and bound along one edge, developed from the wax tablet and the parchment notebook and was initially a form for notes and ephemera. The papyrological evidence from Egypt, where alone the quantities support statistics, shows the codex a small minority of literary manuscripts in the second century, growing through the third, reaching parity in the fourth, and dominant thereafter; Colin Roberts and Theodore Skeat's study remains the standard account. They also identified an asymmetry that has not been satisfactorily explained: among surviving Christian literary manuscripts the codex is preferred overwhelmingly from the earliest period, in sharp contrast to the general literary population of the same date. Explanations have been offered in terms of cost, portability, capacity, ease of reference, and a wish for a form distinct from the synagogue scroll, and none commands agreement.

The consequence for survival is the point of substance. The transition was a physical re-manufacture of the entire body of literature anyone wished to keep. Every work that continued to be read had to be copied from scroll to codex at the cost of the writing material and the scribal labour, and every work not copied ceased to exist as soon as its remaining scrolls decayed, which in a Mediterranean climate meant within a few generations. The third and fourth centuries are therefore the great extinction event for ancient literature, and the surviving corpus is to a first approximation the list of works that some institution in that window judged worth the expense. There is no list of what did not make the cut. The new medium compounded the effect, since parchment is durable and expensive and a large book consumes the hides of a herd; the great fourth-century biblical codices, of which Sinaiticus and Vaticanus survive, represent a capital outlay only a wealthy institution could make, and their existence is evidence of patronage at imperial scale for Christian scripture after Constantine.

Two further bottlenecks followed. In the Byzantine world of the ninth and tenth centuries the standard book hand shifted from majuscule to minuscule and works were transliterated into the new hand; what was not transliterated largely perished, so that for many classical Greek authors the entire surviving tradition descends from a single minuscule copy of that period.

Capacity permitted the four gospels in one volume and eventually the whole of scripture between two covers, which made the boundary of a canon a physical rather than a merely conceptual matter: a book has a first page and a last, and binding is an act of inclusion and exclusion. Random access permitted systematic cross-reference, indexing, and commentary keyed to location, and the apparatus of biblical scholarship in both the Christian and later the Jewish traditions is built on capacities the scroll does not offer.

#### The Masoretic Apparatus as Error Correction

The Jewish tradition solved a different problem, and its solution is the most sophisticated system of textual quality control produced in the ancient or medieval world. The problem was drift. Manuscript evidence from the Judean desert shows that in the late Second Temple period several text types of the Hebrew scriptures circulated simultaneously, differing in orthography, in wording, and occasionally in the presence or absence of substantial blocks. By the second century of the common era the picture had changed: manuscripts from the Bar Kokhba period caves agree closely with the text later received, indicating that standardization had occurred within a comparatively short interval and probably through the authority of a particular circle rather than by gradual convergence.

Standardizing a consonantal text does not solve the transmission problem. Hebrew consonantal writing does not encode vowels, and vocalization carries much of the grammar, so a text fixed in its consonants can still be read in more than one way, and copyists still err. The Masoretic enterprise, developed principally at Tiberias between roughly the seventh and tenth centuries with parallel systems in Babylonia and elsewhere in Palestine, addressed both problems with a layered apparatus. The first layer is vocalization: points above, below, and within the consonants encoding the vowels. The second is the accentual system, a set of signs performing three functions at once. They mark the stressed syllable; they encode the syntactic division of the verse into a hierarchy of clauses, functioning as a complete parsing notation; and they specify the melodic pattern for public chanting. Syntax and performance are the same data, which is an unusually economical piece of engineering.

The third layer is the Masorah proper, and it is the error-detecting part. Marginal notes record that a given word occurs a specified number of times in the Bible, or occurs in this form only here, or occurs twice with one spelling and three times with another. Fuller lists appear at the ends of books, together with counts of the verses, words, and letters of each book and the identification of its middle verse and middle letter. The function of these counts is not devotional. A count is a checksum. A copyist who omits a line by eye-skip or duplicates one produces a text whose totals no longer match the recorded totals, and the error becomes detectable without collation against another manuscript. The fourth layer handles cases where the tradition knew the written text to be problematic and refused to change it: the ketiv and qere apparatus records that a word is written one way and read another, preserving both, and scribal peculiarities are preserved likewise, letters oversized or undersized, letters suspended above the line, dots placed over words, an inverted letter marking a passage's boundaries. Each is an anomaly a rational copyist would normalize, and each was retained across a millennium because the tradition's rule was that the text is not to be improved.

The great Tiberian codices are the products of this system: the codex associated with the ben Asher family and long kept at Aleppo, which lost the majority of its Torah in the twentieth century, and the complete codex now in St Petersburg, dated by its colophon to the first decade of the eleventh century, which serves as the base of the standard modern critical editions. These are large parchment books with colophons naming scribe, vocalizer, and patron, commissioned by wealthy individuals and communities, and their survival is the survival of luxury goods. The Masoretic text is remarkably well transmitted and the apparatus is why; and an elaborate error-detection system is direct evidence that the community building it knew, correctly, that texts drift.

#### The Refusal to Write

Against everything said so far stands a tradition that made a doctrine of not writing, and its history is the most instructive case in this whole history, because it shows a community deciding what the medium of its authority would be and then being overruled by circumstance.

The rabbinic movement held that revelation at Sinai comprised two Torahs, one written and one oral, and that the oral Torah was to be transmitted by recitation from teacher to student and not committed to writing. The principle is stated in the tradition's own texts as a rule that what was given orally may not be transmitted in writing and what was given in writing may not be transmitted orally. It was not a practical preference but a boundary condition on the tradition's identity, and it did several things at once. It made the tradition inseparable from persons, since to learn the oral Torah one had to attach oneself to a sage, which placed interpretive authority in a living institution rather than in a document anyone might acquire. It maintained flexibility, since an unwritten tradition can be adjusted in transmission in ways a written one cannot. And it drew a line against outsiders at a period when the written scriptures were being expounded with increasing confidence by a Christian movement that claimed them; a body of interpretation existing only in the mouths of its own scholars could not be appropriated in the same way.

The academies employed the tanna, a professional reciter whose function was to hold and reproduce the received formulations exactly, a living reference work consulted in debate. The material was shaped for memorization: the Mishnah's language is terse, formulaic, and rhythmically patterned, with fixed structures repeated across tractates, numbered lists, and disputes reduced to the minimum needed to identify each position. It is mnemonic engineering, not literary awkwardness.

The policy did not hold. The Mishnah was compiled under the patriarch Judah around the turn of the third century, and whether that compilation was written at the time or fixed orally and written later is genuinely disputed and probably not resolvable. Around it accumulated the Tosefta, the legal midrashim, and then the two Talmuds, and by the geonic period the Babylonian Talmud existed as a written text, copied and cited. The corpus a doctrine forbade to be written became within a few centuries the largest written literature produced by any ancient religious community. Oral transmission requires a chain of teachers and students in continuous contact, which requires a stable centre with the resources to maintain academies. As the demographic centre dispersed across two empires and then the whole span of the Islamic world, the chain could not be maintained, and communities in the western Mediterranean could not send every student to Babylonia. What they could receive was a letter, and the geonic responsa system was built on exactly that. Once the authoritative answer travels in writing, the authoritative tradition follows it.

The oldest complete manuscript of the Babylonian Talmud is a fourteenth-century codex, some eight hundred years after the text's substantial completion, and the earlier evidence consists of fragments, many recovered from the storeroom of a Cairo synagogue. The Palestinian Talmud fared considerably worse: displaced in authority by the Babylonian, it was copied far less and survives complete in a single medieval manuscript. A text that loses institutional sponsorship does not survive by its quality.

#### The Control Group: Archives Nobody Selected

Everything described so far concerns selected material. The historian's most valuable evidence comes from the few cases where the filter failed and material survived without being selected at all. The Cairo Geniza is the purest case: Jewish practice forbids destroying writings containing the divine name, so disused documents were deposited in a storeroom of the Ben Ezra synagogue in Fustat rather than discarded, and because the criterion was the presence of Hebrew script rather than the value of the contents, the accumulation was indiscriminate, holding court records, marriage contracts, children's exercises, and shopping lists alongside biblical manuscripts. Among the recoveries were the Hebrew original of a book known for centuries only in Greek translation, and the liturgical poetry of Yannai, which had vanished entirely from the transmitted tradition. A whole poet was recovered from a rubbish room. The Nag Hammadi codices preserve in Coptic a literature otherwise surviving only as quotations in the works written to refute it, and the rubbish mounds of Oxyrhynchus preserve the discarded paper of a provincial town across centuries. In every case the mechanism of preservation is indifferent to content, and in every case the recovered material contains things the transmitted tradition had lost, mostly things it would not have chosen to keep. Where an unselected archive can be compared with the selected tradition, the differences measure the filter. Where none exists, the filter is still operating and its effects are invisible.

#### The Economics of Survival

A text survives from antiquity if and only if some institution, or a chain of institutions, found it worth the cost of copying at every point across many centuries, in a medium requiring the operation to be repeated indefinitely. The cost was substantial: writing material, and the maintained subsistence of a trained specialist for the weeks or months a copy required. No ancient or medieval institution incurred that cost at random.

Three consequences follow. Survival correlates with institutional favour, not with quality, representativeness, or truth; a mediocre work useful to a monastery outlived a good one that was not, and the surviving corpus over-represents the concerns of temples, royal chanceries, churches, monasteries, rabbinic academies, and later madrasas, while under-representing everything those institutions did not care about, which includes almost the whole of ordinary life. Second, the losers of every argument are underrepresented in inverse proportion to how thoroughly they lost, because the copying was done by the winners: Marcion's teaching is known chiefly through Tertullian's refutation, Celsus's attack on Christianity through Origen's reply quoting it in order to answer it, and the Sadducean position from Pharisaic and Christian reports, since no Sadducee's own account of Sadducean doctrine exists. In each case the historian holds the case for the prosecution and reconstructs the defence from the quotations the prosecutor found it useful to include. Third, the appropriate default before any ancient text is to ask three questions prior to asking whether it is true. Who paid for the writing. Who paid for the copying, repeatedly, and why. And what did they need this text to accomplish.

None of this licenses the conclusion that ancient texts are worthless as evidence, which would be an error of the same order as taking them at face value. A document saying what its sponsor needed it to say is weak evidence for its own claims and may be strong evidence for what the sponsor needed. A document saying something contrary to its transmitters' interest, and surviving anyway, is worth more than a great deal of confirming material, because the mechanism that should have removed it did not. An administrative record produced for internal use is worth more than a display inscription produced for an audience. An incidental detail serving no purpose in the argument it sits inside is worth more than the argument. And convergence between two sources that had no contact with each other is worth more than any amount of internal consistency within one tradition.

#### What This Means for the Corpus

The corpus this work treats consists, in the main, of documents produced by, or preserved by, institutions with a direct stake in what they said.

The Hebrew Bible reaches us because a Judean religious establishment, and then a rabbinic movement, maintained a copying tradition across two and a half millennia at very considerable cost, and because a Christian church independently maintained a parallel tradition for its own reasons. Both had positions. The Deuteronomistic History was produced by a royal scribal establishment for a reform programme and then revised by the survivors of that programme's failure. Chronicles was produced by a Second Temple establishment whose institutional priorities are visible on every page. The prophetic books were preserved by the party whose position they advocate. The Greek and Roman material on Judean affairs was produced by outsiders for outsiders, and the chief Judean historian of the period wrote in Rome on a Flavian pension. The rabbinic corpus was produced by a movement that was, for much of the period, a minority within its own community, and it was written down in defiance of its own stated policy because dispersion made oral transmission impossible. The early Islamic sources for the first century of the conquests were compiled substantially later, in a milieu with active political and doctrinal stakes in the account.

None of this is a reason to despair of the history. It is the ordinary condition of ancient history everywhere and it is manageable by the criteria set out above. But it is a reason to refuse two habits common in writing about this material. The first is treating a text's antiquity as a proxy for its reliability, when the royal inscriptions demonstrate that a contemporary document produced for display is among the least reliable classes of evidence in existence. The second is treating the absence of evidence for a claim as symmetrical with the absence of evidence against it, when the filters described here operate asymmetrically and predictably, removing the records of the poor, the illiterate, the defeated, the heterodox, and the merely uninteresting at a far higher rate than they remove the records of states and temples.

What the surviving record documents, with great richness, is what powerful institutions in the ancient Levant and Mediterranean wanted written down and kept. That is a genuine and valuable object of knowledge, and it happens to be a different object from the one most readers assume they are being handed. Reading the corpus well begins with holding the two apart.
