## EXCURSUS X. The Jewish Thread Through the Christian and Islamic Centuries

A history of Judaism that follows the sources rather than the subject will lose its subject somewhere in the second century and not recover it. The reason is structural. After 70 the Jewish communities of the Roman and Persian worlds stopped producing the kind of evidence that historians of empires use: no more royal annals, no more national historiography, no Josephus after Josephus, no political narrative because there was no longer a polity to narrate. What the imperial sources supply in its place is legislation, which records Jews only as a problem to be managed, and Christian polemic, which records them only as a foil. Follow those and the account slides, almost without noticing, into a history of Christianity in which Jews appear as objects of policy.

The slide is a serious distortion, because the period from 70 to 750 is not a gap in Jewish history. It is the period in which almost everything that would afterwards be recognizable as Judaism was constructed. The synagogue as a monumental institution, the fixed consonantal text and then the fixed vocalization of the Bible, the liturgy and its poetry, the calendar, the entire system of rabbinic law in two great compilations, the doctrine that made legal life under foreign sovereignty coherent, and the network of academies and legal correspondence that would govern Jewish practice from Spain to Iran: all of these were made in these centuries, by communities that had no state, no army, no capital city, and, for most of the period, no legal standing better than tolerated subordination.

#### The Shape of the Gap

Two things make the reconstruction hard and one makes it possible.

The first difficulty is that the rabbinic sources are almost useless as chronicle. They are legal and exegetical compilations, not histories. They preserve names, sayings, and disputes attributed to named sages across several generations, but they order the material by topic rather than by time, they attribute freely, and they contain narrative only as illustration. A date extracted from them is an inference from a chain of attributions, and the chain is not documentary. The second difficulty is that the rabbis wrote about themselves and their circle and are correspondingly silent about the great majority of Jews who were not in that circle.

What makes reconstruction possible is that this period, uniquely in Jewish antiquity, supplies a substantial material record. Late antique synagogues survive in numbers, with their inscriptions, their donors, their languages, and their art. Burial complexes supply demography and geographic reach. Papyri and, later, the Cairo Geniza supply documents nobody selected. Imperial law codes supply the state's view in the state's own words. Read against the rabbinic corpus rather than through it, this material yields a picture that is considerably more interesting than the one the texts alone would give, and in several respects contradicts it.

#### After Seventy: Yavneh and What Can Be Known

The standard account has Yohanan ben Zakkai smuggled out of besieged Jerusalem in a coffin, obtaining from Vespasian permission to establish a school at Yavneh on the coastal plain, and there reconstituting Jewish religious authority around Torah study and prayer in place of the destroyed temple cult. The account is told in several rabbinic versions that differ in detail, and it is the founding narrative of rabbinic Judaism.

It is also a later account, composed by the movement whose legitimacy it establishes, and its picture of an orderly transfer of authority is not supportable as it stands. What can reasonably be said is narrower. A circle of sages did gather at Yavneh in the decades after the destruction; the office of patriarch emerged from that circle, associated with the house of Gamaliel; and a body of legal tradition was consolidated there that the later movement regarded as its foundation. What did not happen was a general recognition of that circle's authority by the Jewish population, in Palestine or anywhere else. The evidence for such recognition in the first two centuries after 70 is thin to absent outside the movement's own literature.

The genuinely decisive development is easier to state and harder to see, because it happened by default. The temple was not rebuilt. Sacrifice, which had been the central act of Israelite religion for as long as there had been an Israelite religion, simply stopped, and the priesthood lost the institution that made it a priesthood. Every subsequent form of Judaism is a response to that termination, and the rabbinic response, that study of the law and prayer substitute for the offerings, eventually prevailed because no competitor with an institutional base survived.

#### Bar Kokhba and the Closing of Judaea

The second rupture was worse than the first and is less often given its weight. Between 132 and 135 a revolt under Shimon bar Kosiba, whom his supporters called Bar Kokhba, established an independent administration over part of Judaea, minted its own coinage overstruck on Roman issues, dated documents by the years of the redemption of Israel, and was destroyed by a Roman campaign that required the transfer of substantial forces and the personal attention of Hadrian.

The documentary evidence is exceptional because it is contemporary and it was not transmitted. Caves in the Judean desert have yielded letters, contracts, and administrative papers of the revolt period, including correspondence issued in bar Kosiba's name as nasi, written in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek. They show a functioning administration allocating land, requisitioning supplies, and enforcing observance, and they show a trilingual population.

The aftermath reshaped the geography of Jewish life permanently. Judaea was devastated. Jerusalem was refounded as the Roman colony Aelia Capitolina and Jews were forbidden to enter it, a prohibition maintained in principle for five centuries. The province was renamed Syria Palaestina. The centre of Jewish population and institutional life shifted north into Galilee and the Golan, where it remained, and the second great centre, in Babylonia, grew in relative importance from this point onward. Every subsequent development in this essay is downstream of that displacement.

#### How Small the Rabbinic Movement Was

The rabbinic literature presents a world in which rabbis are the natural leaders of Jewish communities and their rulings the operative law. The material record does not corroborate this for the second, third, or much of the fourth century, and the discrepancy is one of the most productive findings in the study of the period.

Synagogue inscriptions from late antique Palestine and the diaspora name donors, officers, and benefactors in large numbers. The recurring titles are those of the Greek-speaking civic world: the head of the synagogue, the elder, the father or mother of the synagogue, the archon. Priests are named, and priestly identity clearly retained prestige long after the temple. Rabbis are named comparatively rarely, and where the title appears it does not obviously carry authority over the community's affairs. The people paying for the buildings were not, in general, identifying themselves as rabbis or as the clients of rabbis.

Seth Schwartz has argued from this and related evidence that the rabbinic movement was a small and socially marginal group for its first two or three centuries, and that its transformation into the leadership of Jewish society occurred later, in a landscape reshaped by the Christianization of the empire and by the pressure that put on Jewish communal self-definition. The argument has been contested in its stronger forms, and the alternative view holds that rabbinic influence was real but diffuse and simply not the sort of thing that leaves epigraphic traces. The evidence does not settle it. What the evidence does settle is that a straightforward reading of the rabbinic corpus as a description of Jewish society is not available.

#### The Patriarchate and Its Abolition

Between the second century and the fifth, Jewish Palestine possessed a recognized head, the nasi or patriarch, whose office is documented from both sides: in the rabbinic sources, which treat the patriarchal house as the apex of the movement, and in Roman law and Latin and Greek correspondence, which treat it as an official channel to a subject population.

The house claimed descent from Hillel and, through him, from David. Its greatest figure, Judah ha-Nasi, active around the turn of the third century, is remembered as the compiler of the Mishnah, as a man of substantial wealth, and as being on good terms with Roman power. By the fourth century the patriarch held recognized honorific rank in the imperial hierarchy, was addressed by emperors in terms reserved for high officials, and was permitted to levy a contribution from Jewish communities across the diaspora and to send agents to collect it. That fiscal privilege is the clearest index of the office's real position: the Roman state licensed a Jewish authority to tax Jews internationally, which no purely honorific dignity would have carried. The Antiochene rhetorician Libanius corresponded with a patriarch, which places the office within the ordinary social world of provincial notables.

The office was extinguished in the early fifth century. In 415 the patriarch Gamaliel VI was stripped of his honorary rank for offences including the construction of new synagogues and the exercise of jurisdiction over Christians. Within about fifteen years the office had ceased, and a constitution of 429 addresses the situation after the cessation of the patriarchs and redirects the diaspora contribution into the imperial treasury. Whether the line failed biologically or was suppressed is not recoverable from the sources. The consequence is clear: the one centralized Jewish authority recognized by the Roman state disappeared, and nothing replaced it in the west.

#### The Galilean Academies and the Unfinished Talmud

The intellectual centres of Palestinian Judaism in this period were Tiberias, on the western shore of the lake, which became the principal seat; Sepphoris, refounded as Diocaesarea, a Hellenized Galilean city with a substantial Jewish population; Caesarea on the coast, which was also a centre of Christian scholarship, so that Origen and later Eusebius worked in a city with a functioning Jewish academy; and Lydda in the south.

The product of these centres is the Talmud Yerushalmi, the Palestinian or Jerusalem Talmud, which despite its name was compiled principally in Tiberias. It is a commentary on the Mishnah, built of the discussions of Palestinian sages across roughly two centuries, and its redaction is generally placed in the late fourth or early fifth century. Its language is Galilean Jewish Aramaic carrying a heavy load of Greek and Latin loanwords, which is itself evidence about the linguistic world its authors inhabited.

It is unfinished, and the manner of its incompleteness is informative. It treats the agricultural order in full, because those laws applied in the land, where the Babylonian compilation largely ignores them; it has no treatment of the order dealing with temple offerings; and in places it simply stops, breaking off without the closure the material invites. The usual explanation connects this to the deteriorating conditions of the fifth century, and specifically to the collapse of the patriarchate and the institutional support it represented. The explanation is plausible and is not demonstrable. What is demonstrable is the consequence for transmission: displaced in authority by the Babylonian compilation, the Yerushalmi was copied far less, and it survives complete in a single medieval manuscript. A text whose institutions fail does not survive on merit.

#### Babylonia: Sura, Pumbedita, Nehardea

The Jewish community of Babylonia was older than the Roman one and had never been part of the Roman world. It descended from the deportations of the sixth century before the common era, it had never wholly returned, and by the third century of the common era it was large, agriculturally rooted, and organized. It lived first under Parthian and then, from 224, under Sassanid rule, in an empire whose state religion was Zoroastrian and whose treatment of religious minorities varied sharply with the ruler and with the fortunes of war against Rome. Periods of relative freedom alternated with episodes of restriction and violence, reported in both Jewish and Syriac Christian sources and concentrated in the fifth century.

The academies are the institution the tradition remembers. Sura was founded, in the tradition's account, by Abba Arikha, known as Rav, on his return from study in Palestine early in the third century. Nehardea was the seat of his contemporary Samuel, and was destroyed in the disorders of the mid-third century, its function passing to Pumbedita. These three names, with Sura and Pumbedita as the enduring pair, organize Babylonian Jewish intellectual history for the next seven hundred years.

The relationship between the two Jewish centres was continuous and asymmetric. Students and sages travelled between Palestine and Babylonia in both directions, traditions were carried and cited across the distance, and the Babylonian compilation preserves a great deal of Palestinian material. But Babylonia was outside Roman jurisdiction, and as conditions in Palestine deteriorated under Christian rule the balance moved decisively east.

#### The Law of the Kingdom Is Law

One legal principle, attributed in the Babylonian Talmud to Samuel of Nehardea, did more to make diaspora existence workable than any other single ruling: dina de-malkhuta dina, the law of the kingdom is law.

The principle holds that the civil law of the state under which Jews live is valid and binding within Jewish law itself, in matters such as taxation, property transfer, and the enforcement of contracts. It is not a counsel of prudence or an accommodation to force. It is a rule of Jewish law that incorporates the sovereign's law into Jewish law, and it therefore resolves what would otherwise be a permanent conflict of jurisdictions for a community holding a complete legal system while living under someone else's government.

Its scope was and remained contested. It was generally held not to extend to ritual or family law, and not to legitimate arbitrary confiscation as opposed to regular taxation, so it functioned as a boundary rather than a surrender. Its effect was to allow a Jewish community to be simultaneously a self-governing legal body and a law-abiding subject population, which is the position every diaspora community occupied for the next fifteen centuries.

#### The Exilarch

The Sassanid empire recognized a head of the Jewish community, the resh galuta or exilarch, who claimed Davidic descent through the line of the deported Judean kings and held a formal rank at the Persian court.

The office was not primarily scholarly. The exilarch collected taxes on the state's behalf, appointed judges and market officials, exercised jurisdiction in civil matters, and represented the community to the crown. Its relationship with the academies was frequently tense, since the exilarch's authority was political and hereditary while the heads of the academies claimed authority by learning, and the Talmud preserves traces of the friction.

The comparison with the Roman patriarchate is instructive in both directions. Both offices were dynastic, both claimed Davidic descent, and both were recognized by an imperial state that found a single addressable authority convenient. But the patriarchate was abolished within four centuries, while the exilarchate survived the Sassanid collapse, was continued under the caliphate, and persisted for centuries longer. The difference is not in the Jewish institutions. It is in the states.

#### The Babylonian Talmud

The Bavli is the largest and most consequential work of the period, and its character follows from how it was made. It is arranged as a commentary on the Mishnah, but the commentary form is a container for something else: an extended, dialectical, and often digressive record of argument, in which positions are stated, challenged, defended, and frequently left unresolved, and in which legal analysis is interleaved with narrative, medicine, dream interpretation, magic, folklore, and material drawn from the surrounding Persian world.

Its composition ran from the third century to roughly the sixth in the named amoraic layer, and the anonymous argumentative stratum that frames and drives the discussions is generally held to be later, the work of the redactors of the sixth and seventh centuries, whose contribution is the dialectical texture that gives the work its character. Its language is Jewish Babylonian Aramaic with a Middle Persian loan vocabulary, and the loans are evidence of the community's embeddedness: terms for administration, dress, food, and law come from the surrounding society.

Its later dominance was not automatic. Two Talmuds existed, and the Babylonian prevailed because the geonim of Sura and Pumbedita, answering legal questions from communities across the Islamic world, answered them out of the Bavli, so that the network of legal correspondence carried one compilation and not the other. The result is that the whole of subsequent rabbinic Judaism descends from the tradition of one of the two centres.

#### The Synagogue Becomes Monumental

The most striking fact in the archaeology of late antique Judaism is that the great age of synagogue building coincides with the period of legal disability, and the two records point in opposite directions.

Synagogues existed before 70, and are attested in the diaspora considerably earlier. But the monumental synagogue, a substantial public building with a decorated facade, columns, mosaic floors, and a permanent architectural focus for the Torah scroll, is a phenomenon of the fourth to the sixth centuries. In Galilee and the Golan they survive in numbers. The Galilean type, with a monumental facade of dressed limestone oriented toward Jerusalem, is represented at Capernaum, Chorazin, Meiron, and Baram; the Capernaum building, long dated early, is now generally placed in the fourth or fifth century on the evidence beneath its floors. The Golan has yielded dozens of sites, at Qatzrin, Ein Nashut, Umm el-Qanatir, and elsewhere, built in local basalt.

The inference is direct. Communities that build in stone are not communities in flight. Whatever the codes were legislating, Jewish villages in Byzantine Palestine had the resources, the confidence, and in practice the permission to erect substantial public buildings, and they did so in the century when new synagogue construction was formally prohibited. The gap between law and practice is as wide here as anywhere in the period.

#### Helios in the Sanctuary

The mosaic floors of these buildings pose a problem for any simple account of Jewish aniconism, and the problem should be stated in its full strength rather than managed.

At Beth Alpha, in the Beth Shean valley, a sixth-century pavement excavated by Eleazar Sukenik carries three panels in a naive, vigorous, provincial style. The lowest shows the binding of Isaac, with the figures labelled in Hebrew. The uppermost shows a Torah shrine flanked by menorot, lions, and ritual objects. Between them is a circular zodiac, the twelve signs named in Hebrew and rendered as human and animal figures, with the four seasons personified as female busts in the corners and, at the centre, the sun god driving a four-horse chariot across a starry ground. The artisans signed their work in Greek and Aramaic. At Hammat Tiberias a considerably earlier and far finer pavement carries the same composition, the zodiac and the charioteer sun, with Greek dedicatory inscriptions naming donors including one connected with the patriarchal household. At Sepphoris the scheme recurs with a variation that shows the tension was felt: the sun's place is occupied by a chariot and a radiant disk, with no human figure.

Three observations follow. The scheme was not marginal or clandestine; it occupies the centre of the floor in the principal room of the building, it was paid for by named donors, and it recurs at multiple sites across several centuries. Its meaning is genuinely unresolved, with readings ranging from a calendar of the liturgical year through an assertion of divine governance of the cosmos to the borrowing of a prestigious late antique visual convention with no doctrinal content. And it did not last: at Naaran near Jericho the zodiac figures were carefully defaced, in what is most economically explained as a later Jewish reaction against images. Aniconism in Judaism was not a constant. It was a position that won, after a period in which it did not hold, and the Palestinian Talmud itself preserves a notice to the effect that in a certain generation figures began to be depicted on walls and pavements and the sages did not prevent it.

#### Dura-Europos

The most extreme case is not in Palestine and survives by accident. At Dura-Europos, a garrison town on the Euphrates, the synagogue stood against the western city wall. When the Sassanid siege came in the middle of the third century the defenders packed the buildings along that wall with earth to strengthen it. The city fell and was abandoned, and the fill preserved what it buried.

Excavation in the early 1930s exposed a hall whose walls were covered, from dado to ceiling, with figural paintings of biblical scenes: Moses at the burning bush and at the sea, the infancy of Moses, the ark among the Philistines, the anointing of David, Ezekiel in the valley of dry bones, Esther and Mordecai before Ahasuerus. An Aramaic dedicatory inscription dates the building's refurbishment to the 240s. The paintings are in the visual idiom of the Roman east, and human figures including the hand of God appear without evident inhibition.

The building was not the work of a heterodox fringe. It was the synagogue of an ordinary provincial Jewish community, it stood a short distance from a Christian house-church and a temple of Mithras in the same street, and its inscriptions are unremarkable. Any account of Jewish visual practice in late antiquity that treats figural narrative painting as impossible has to explain Dura, and the honest position is that the rule against images was understood variously and applied variously in different places and periods.

#### Beth Shearim

South of the Galilean hills, at Beth Shearim, a rock-cut necropolis of catacombs was excavated across several seasons under Benjamin Mazar and Nahman Avigad. It contains hundreds of burials, and it is the single best source for the geographic and linguistic reach of the Jewish world in late antiquity.

The tradition associates the site with the burial of Judah ha-Nasi, and the presence of the patriarchal household is the likeliest explanation for what followed: burial there became desirable, and bodies were brought from a very long way. The inscriptions name the dead and often their cities, and those cities include Palmyra, Antioch, Beirut, Byblos, Tyre, and Sidon, together with places further afield. Jews of the Syrian and Phoenician coast, and beyond it, were transporting their dead to a hillside in lower Galilee for burial in the land.

The languages are the second finding, and the more disconcerting. The great majority of the inscriptions are in Greek. Hebrew and Aramaic occur, and Palmyrene occurs, but Greek is the working language of the epigraphy, in a Jewish cemetery in the Galilee, in the centuries of the Mishnah and the Yerushalmi. The decoration is the third: alongside menorot and Jewish ritual symbols, the sarcophagi and catacomb walls carry figural and animal ornament in the common repertoire of Roman funerary art, including motifs of Greek mythological derivation. Burial in the land, in Greek, under a carved lion, was an entirely ordinary thing for a Jew of the third century to want.

#### Piyyut

The liturgical poetry of Byzantine Palestine is the least known major literature of the period and the one that most directly registers the experience of the communities that produced it.

Piyyut is Hebrew liturgical verse composed for insertion into the fixed prayers, particularly on festivals and special sabbaths. It emerges as a developed art in Palestine, probably from the fifth century, and its earliest named practitioner is Yose ben Yose, associated with compositions for the Day of Atonement. Its two great figures are Yannai, of the sixth century, who composed cycles keyed to the triennial Torah reading of the Palestinian rite, and Eleazar ben Killir, of the sixth or seventh, whose enormously influential work is written in a dense, allusive, and deliberately difficult Hebrew that coins words freely and presumes an audience able to follow midrashic reference at speed.

Three features are worth registering. Piyyut is among the earliest literatures anywhere to make systematic use of end rhyme, alongside alphabetical acrostics and acrostics spelling the poet's name, which is how authorship is recovered at all. It presumes a congregation for which Hebrew was a living liturgical language and allusion a shared competence, which qualifies the picture the Greek epigraphy gives. And it carries polemic: anti-Christian argument appears in these poems, which makes them one of the very few places where the Jewish side of the confrontation with Christianity in the Byzantine period can be heard directly rather than through Christian report. Yannai's work was almost entirely lost, and was recovered in the twentieth century from the Cairo Geniza.

#### The Masoretes of Tiberias

The final Palestinian achievement of the period is the fixing of the biblical text, and it belongs to the eighth to tenth centuries, which is to say to Galilee under Muslim rule rather than Christian.

The consonantal text had been stable since roughly the second century. What the Masoretes added was everything else: a full system of vowel points, a system of accents encoding stress, syntax, and cantillation together, and an apparatus of marginal notes and counts by which errors in copying could be detected. Competing systems developed in Babylonia and elsewhere in Palestine; the Tiberian system prevailed. The work is associated above all with two families, ben Asher and ben Naphtali, whose differences in minute detail were themselves recorded and compared.

The two great products of the school are the codex associated with Aaron ben Moses ben Asher, kept for centuries at Aleppo and mutilated in the twentieth, and the complete codex now in St Petersburg, dated by its colophon to the first decade of the eleventh century, which supplies the base text of modern critical editions. The relationship of the Masoretes to the Karaite movement, which was strong in the region and placed exceptional weight on the precise text of scripture, has been argued and is not settled; that the environment was one in which textual precision had become a matter of contention is not in doubt.

#### The Legal Descent: Theodosian Code Book Sixteen

The Christianization of the Roman empire changed the legal position of the Jews slowly, unevenly, and in one direction. The record is preserved principally in the sixteenth book of the Theodosian Code, promulgated in 438, whose eighth title collects the constitutions concerning Jews, and it should be read with two things held in mind at once: the trend and the floor beneath it.

The trend runs from Constantine onward. Conversion to Judaism was prohibited and penalties attached to those who assisted it. Jews were forbidden to circumcise slaves and then to own Christian slaves at all, which in an agrarian economy of estates worked by slave and coloni labour was an economic disability of the first order and not a symbolic one. Marriage between Jews and Christians was prohibited and assimilated to adultery. Jews were progressively excluded from the imperial service, from the administration, and from military office, while remaining liable to the expensive obligations of municipal councillors, a combination that removed the honours and retained the burdens. Construction of new synagogues was forbidden. Jewish jurisdiction over Christians was curtailed, and the patriarchate was demoted and then extinguished.

The floor is stated in the code in its own words. A constitution of the 390s declares plainly that the Jewish sect is prohibited by no law, and the principle is not a dead letter: the code also protects synagogues from seizure and from burning, orders restitution or compensation where they had been taken, and forbids the disturbance of Jews at their sabbath. The Roman state in its Christian phase was pursuing two policies at once, degradation and protection, and it pursued both because both followed from the same theology. Judaism was permitted, uniquely among non-Christian religions after the suppression of public paganism, and it was permitted on terms designed to make its inferiority visible.

That the prohibitions were repeated is the standard evidence that they were not obeyed. The ban on new synagogues coexists with the greatest synagogue-building period in Jewish history, and the two facts have to be held together rather than resolved.

#### Justinian and Novella 146

Under Justinian the direction hardened and the state's ambition widened. The Justinianic Code retained the accumulated disabilities and added to them: Jews were barred from giving testimony against Christians in many circumstances, and imperial legislation reached into the timing of Passover in relation to Easter. The Samaritan revolts of 484 and 529 were suppressed with a ferocity that effectively destroyed the Samaritan community as a significant population, which is worth registering precisely because it shows what the state was capable of doing to a religious minority it decided to end, and did not do to the Jews.

The most remarkable single document is the constitution of 553 known as Novella 146. It was issued, according to its own preamble, in response to a dispute within a Jewish community over the language of scriptural reading. The emperor's response was to legislate on the internal liturgical practice of the synagogue: Jews might read the scriptures in Greek, and the Septuagint was commended, with the version of Aquila permitted as an alternative; and the deuterosis, the second tradition, was prohibited.

Two things about this are extraordinary. The first is the object of the prohibition. The deuterosis is most plausibly the oral tradition, the Mishnah and the interpretive apparatus around it, and the emperor is therefore attempting to legislate the rabbinic tradition out of Jewish worship, on the ground that it obscures the scriptural text in which, on the Christian reading, Christ is foretold. The second is the reason given for permitting Greek at all, which is not tolerance but the hope that Jews reading the Septuagint would be brought to the Christian understanding of their own books. The law is an instrument of conversion dressed as a liturgical concession, and there is no evidence that it had any effect whatever on what happened in synagogues.

#### Augustine and the Doctrine of Witness

The intellectual settlement that governed western Christian practice toward Jews for a millennium was formulated by Augustine, and it should be stated exactly, because it is neither the tolerance its defenders claim nor the simple hostility its critics assume.

Augustine's argument, developed in the Contra Faustum and given its classic form in the City of God, turns on a verse of Psalm 59: slay them not, lest my people forget. The Jews, he argues, are not to be killed or forcibly converted. They are to be preserved, dispersed among the nations, and kept in a subordinate condition. The reason is evidentiary. The Jews carry the scriptures that, on the Christian reading, testify to Christ, and they carry them without accepting that reading. Their possession of those books is therefore proof to any pagan that Christians did not forge them, since the very people who reject Christian claims preserve the texts on which those claims rest. And their dispersion and subjection is itself a further testimony, the visible sign of what befell them for the rejection.

The doctrine's effect was protective, and its premise was degrading, and the two are inseparable: the protection is conditional on the subjection, because a Jewish community that flourished would not testify to what the doctrine required it to testify. It underwrote the papal position, restated repeatedly across the Middle Ages, that Jews were not to be forcibly baptized, killed, or disturbed in their observance. It also supplied the theological reason why they should never be permitted to prosper or hold authority. Both halves came from the same argument, and both were enforced.

#### Visigothic Spain

The harshest legislation of the period was produced in the Visigothic kingdom, and it is the necessary background to what happened in 711.

The sequence begins with the conversion of the Visigothic monarchy from Arian to Catholic Christianity under Reccared at the end of the sixth century, which fused the crown and the Catholic episcopate into a single legislating body meeting in the councils of Toledo. Around 613 King Sisebut ordered the Jews of the kingdom to accept baptism or leave. The order was carried out sufficiently to create a large population of forced converts, and it was criticized within the church, by Isidore of Seville among others, on the ground that faith cannot be compelled, though not on the ground that the goal was wrong.

What followed is the trap that forced conversion always creates. The Fourth Council of Toledo in 633 ruled that no one should be converted by force in future, and in the same breath ruled that those already baptized must remain Christians, that their children were to be taken from them and raised by Christians, and that relapse was to be punished. Subsequent kings and councils escalated across the seventh century: the legal code of Recceswinth carried extensive anti-Jewish titles, later kings tightened the provisions, and in 694 the Seventeenth Council of Toledo, at the instance of King Egica, declared that the Jews of Spain had conspired with their coreligionists overseas against the kingdom and decreed that they be reduced to slavery, their property confiscated, and their children removed at the age of seven to be raised as Christians.

Whether that final decree was executed in full across the kingdom is unclear, and the seventeen years between it and the Muslim landing are short. But the legal situation of Spanish Jewry on the eve of 711 was, on the statute book, enslavement. Arabic and later Christian sources report that as the conquering army moved north it left Jewish inhabitants to garrison captured cities, at Cordoba and Toledo among others, which is what a small army does with a population it has reason to trust. The later Christian legend that the Jews betrayed the cities is polemic, and the reports of garrison duty come from sources with their own interests. The documented fact is the legislation, and it is sufficient to explain why the conquest was not resisted by the people it liberated.

#### Six Hundred and Fourteen

In 614, during the great Sassanid offensive of Khusrau II, a Persian army under Shahrbaraz took Jerusalem. The episode that followed is the one moment in these seven centuries when Jews acted as an armed political force in their own land, and it is among the most poorly evidenced things in this essay.

The sources are all interested. Christian accounts, including a narrative attributed to a monk of the Judean desert, describe massacre of the city's Christians, with the killing concentrated at a reservoir outside the walls, and assign a leading role to Jewish participants. The Armenian history attributed to Sebeos reports Jewish support for the Persians. Jewish evidence is not documentary at all but apocalyptic: a Hebrew text of roughly this period anticipates a messianic deliverance and names a figure who appears in the later tradition as having led a brief Jewish administration in Jerusalem. Whether such an administration existed, and for how long, cannot be established from the material available, and the casualty figures in the Christian accounts are of the inflated kind treated elsewhere in this work.

What is reasonably clear is the shape of the outcome. Jewish hopes attached to the Persian conquest; the Persians, needing to govern a population that was overwhelmingly Christian, reversed course within a few years and withdrew whatever privileges had been extended; and when Heraclius recovered the city in 630 the reprisal was severe. Christian sources report a massacre and an expulsion, and a general edict of forced baptism is attributed to Heraclius in the early 630s, though its scope and even its promulgation are disputed. Eight years later the question was moot.

#### Six Hundred and Thirty-Eight

Jerusalem passed to Muslim control around 638, in the campaigns that followed the death of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and carried Syria and Palestine out of Roman rule within a decade. The document known as the Pact of Umar, which purports to record the terms granted to the conquered, is in its received form considerably later than the conquest and cannot be used as a transcript of what was agreed; the general shape of the arrangement, however, is not in doubt.

For the Jews the immediate and enormous change was residence. The prohibition on Jewish habitation in Jerusalem, imposed after 135 and maintained in principle throughout the Christian centuries, ended. Jews returned to live in the city, and the tradition of the Mourners of Zion, communities settling in Jerusalem to lament the temple and await its restoration, belongs to the early Islamic period. The temple platform, which under Christian rule had been left deliberately ruined and used as a dump as a visible demonstration of the prophecy of desolation, was cleared and built upon: the Dome of the Rock was completed in the early 690s under Abd al-Malik, its foundation inscription still carrying a date that a later caliph altered only in the name of the builder.

The change of regime was not liberation in a modern sense and should not be described as one. It was the replacement of one subordinating order by another with different terms. But the terms differed in ways that mattered, and the most consequential was that the new order had no doctrinal requirement that Jews be visibly humiliated in order to bear witness against themselves.

#### The Dhimma

The legal framework was the dhimma, the covenant of protection extended to the People of the Book, ahl al-kitab, in return for the payment of a tax and the acceptance of subordinate political status. Its scriptural basis is the verse of Sūrat al-Tawbah instructing that those who have been given the Book pay the jizya from a position of submission, and the wider Qur'anic treatment of Jews and Christians is not uniform: alongside sharp polemic stand the verses of Sūrat al-Baqarah and Sūrat al-Māʾidah promising reward to those who believe among the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians, and the verses of Sūrat Āl ʿImrān distinguishing an upright portion of the People of the Book. Judaism was recognized as a revealed religion with prophets in common, Musa (AS), Dawud (AS), and Ibrahim (AS) among them, which is a different relation from the one Christian theology assigned it.

In practice the dhimma meant this. Jews and Christians paid the jizya, a poll tax on adult free males with exemptions for women, children, the poor, and the incapable, and they were exempt from military service. They governed themselves in matters of personal status and internal law through their own courts and authorities. They were secure in life and property and in the practice of their religion. And they were subordinate: restrictions on new places of worship, on riding certain animals, on dress, on public religious display, and on holding authority over Muslims were articulated in the legal tradition and enforced episodically, with enormous variation by ruler and region. Non-Muslim testimony against Muslims was restricted in most schools.

The system was stable, legally defined, and predictable, which was its great practical advantage over the Byzantine arrangement, and it was a system of institutionalized inequality, which is its permanent character. Periods of severity occurred, notably under the caliph al-Mutawakkil in the ninth century, who revived and enforced discriminatory regulations that had lapsed. Neither the stability nor the inequality should be omitted from an account of it.

#### The Geonic Period and the Karaite Challenge

The conquests placed the two great Jewish centres, Palestine and Babylonia, inside a single polity for the first time in a thousand years, and with them the Jewish communities of Egypt, North Africa, Spain, and Iran. The consequence was the geonic period.

The geonim, heads of the academies of Sura and Pumbedita, became the effective legislative authority for Jews across the caliphate. The mechanism was the responsum: a community anywhere from Qayrawan to Khurasan wrote to a gaon with a legal question, the question was discussed in the academy, and a reply went back and was preserved and copied. Thousands survive, many recovered from the Cairo Geniza. The responsa network did three things at once. It made the Babylonian Talmud the operative law everywhere, because the answers were derived from it. It bound geographically scattered communities into a single legal system without any coercive apparatus whatever. And it converted an oral tradition into a written one, permanently. In the course of the following centuries the academies themselves relocated to the new Abbasid capital at Baghdad, following the centre of political and commercial gravity.

Against this consolidation came the first great internal challenge. The Karaite movement rejected the authority of the oral tradition and held that law must be derived from scripture alone. The traditional account traces it to Anan ben David in the eighth century, but Karaism as a coherent movement is better placed in the ninth and tenth, with figures such as Benjamin al-Nahawandi and Daniel al-Qumisi, and the linear descent from Anan is a later simplification. Its consequences were substantial and largely intellectual. It forced the rabbinic side to articulate and defend the theory of the oral law explicitly, which it had never had to do. And it drove both parties into intensive study of the biblical text itself, of Hebrew grammar, and of systematic exegesis, in a competition that produced much of the foundational work in all three fields.

#### Merchants and a New Written Language

Two developments of the eighth and ninth centuries indicate how thoroughly Jewish life had been reoriented, and both are visible from outside the community.

The first is commercial. The Abbasid postmaster and geographer Ibn Khurradadhbih, writing in the middle of the ninth century, describes a body of Jewish merchants he calls the Radhanites who travelled by four routes between the Frankish lands and China, by sea through the Mediterranean and the Red Sea and overland through Central Asia. He notes that they spoke Arabic, Persian, Greek, Frankish, Andalusi, and Slavic, and he lists their goods in both directions. The account is brief and its details have been argued over, including whether the Radhanites were an organized association or a category of trader. What it establishes is that a Muslim official in Baghdad regarded Jewish long-distance merchants as a recognized and describable feature of Eurasian commerce, operating across the frontier between the Islamic and Christian worlds at a period when little else crossed it.

The second is linguistic, and it is the deeper change. Jews across the caliphate adopted Arabic as their spoken and then their written language, writing it in Hebrew characters. Judaeo-Arabic became the ordinary vehicle for law, philosophy, grammar, medicine, exegesis, and correspondence, and the Bible itself was translated into it. The pattern is the one this community had followed before, with Aramaic and then with Greek: the language of the surrounding society is taken up completely, and the tradition is carried in it. What the adoption of Arabic made possible was participation in the intellectual life of the most advanced culture in the world at that moment, and the results are visible from the tenth century onward.

#### A Comparative Assessment

The comparison between Jewish conditions under Byzantine Christian and under early Islamic rule has been made polemically in both directions for two centuries, and both polemics are constructions of the modern period serving modern arguments. The honest assessment has to hold several things together.

Under Christian Rome, Judaism retained legal recognition throughout, which is more than paganism retained after Theodosius and more than dissenting Christian communities retained at various points. Jewish communities continued to exist, to own property, to litigate, to maintain their own courts in internal matters, and, as the archaeology shows unambiguously, to build. The state protected synagogues from mob attack in law and sometimes in fact. That floor was real and it should not be omitted.

But the trend was unmistakably downward across four centuries, the disabilities accumulated and were not reversed, the one recognized Jewish authority was abolished, the emperor legislated on the content of synagogue worship, and forced baptism appeared at the edges under Heraclius and at the centre in Visigothic Spain. Underlying all of it was a theology that assigned Jewish existence a function, witness to a rejection, and required Jewish subordination as the visible content of that witness. The framework had no place for Jewish flourishing even in principle.

Under early Islamic rule the trajectory in the century after the conquest ran the other way, and the evidence is institutional rather than rhetorical. Jerusalem was reopened to Jewish residence after five hundred years. The Babylonian academies operated with caliphal recognition, the exilarchate continued as a formal office, and the geonic responsa system built a legal network of a scale and reach that had never existed. Jews participated in the commerce and, shortly afterwards, in the intellectual life of the caliphate at a level Byzantine law had made structurally impossible. The demographic centre of world Jewry lay inside the Islamic world and would remain there for centuries.

The subordination, however, was real, formalized, and enforced. The jizya was not merely a tax but a mark of status, and the legal literature is explicit that it should be experienced as such. Discriminatory regulations on worship, dress, and public conduct existed in law and were enforced when a ruler chose to enforce them, which some did severely. Non-Muslims could not hold authority over Muslims, and their testimony was restricted. Conditions varied enormously by place and by reign, and the variation is the most important single fact about them.

The accurate summary is therefore not that one order was tolerant and the other persecuting. It is that both were systems of legally defined religious subordination, that the Islamic system was more stable, more clearly specified, and less totalizing in its demands, and that the Christian system was uniquely constrained by a doctrine which required the subordinated community to survive. The Jewish communities of the period understood both, negotiated with both, and by the end of the period had moved decisively into the orbit of the one that offered more room.

#### What Stood in 750

Set the ledger at the middle of the eighth century and the achievement is visible in a way it is not from inside any of the individual centuries.

A people that had lost its temple, its capital, its political existence, and finally the right to live in its own holy city had, in the intervening seven centuries and without a state at any point, produced a complete and portable legal system in two great compilations; a doctrine, dina de-malkhuta dina, that made lawful life under foreign sovereignty coherent rather than merely tolerable; a fixed and progressively perfected scriptural text with an apparatus of transmission unmatched anywhere; a liturgy with a poetic tradition of its own; an institutional structure of academies, courts, and legal correspondence capable of governing practice across five thousand kilometres without any power of enforcement; and a body of communities from Spain to Iran that recognized one another as a single people.

None of it was produced by a government. All of it was produced under two empires that regarded the community as theologically superseded and politically subordinate, and that legislated accordingly. The material record shows the communities building, decorating, burying their dead at expense, and arguing with one another, throughout. That is the thread the imperial and ecclesiastical sources cannot show, because they were not written to show it, and it is the reason it has to be followed separately.

# PART THREE · APPARATUS

## APPENDIX A · Master Chronology

A chronology is a chain of inferences, and its strength is the strength of its weakest link, not the confidence of its published figures. The dates below are therefore given with the ground they stand on stated in the third column, and that column is the point of the tables. A date resting on a computed eclipse and a date resting on a genealogical notice composed centuries after the event are both printed in Arabic numerals, and the numerals conceal the difference; the Attestation column restores it.

Four kinds of ground carry the span. Astronomical: a recorded celestial event whose date can be computed backward, fixing a point absolutely. Documentary: a king list, an eponym list, a chronicle series, a dated legal or ration tablet, each supplying relative sequence and, once tied to an astronomical fix, absolute position. Stratigraphic and radiometric: a destruction layer, a ceramic horizon, a set of radiocarbon determinations on short-lived samples. And the biblical text itself, which supplies regnal totals and synchronisms between the two kingdoms, and which is internally inconsistent in ways no reconstruction has fully resolved.

The consequence is a gradient of precision. Bronze Age dates are approximate and marked so throughout: the second millennium floats within a window of roughly a century and a half, and no date before the ninth century BCE here should be read as more than a period assignment. From the mid ninth century the Assyrian record supplies firm synchronisms; from 747 BCE the chronology is essentially secure; from the Persian period it is firm to the year and often to the day.

### The Anchors

Five fixed points and one unresolved dispute do most of the load-bearing work.

The **Bur-Sagale eclipse** is the hinge of Near Eastern chronology. The Assyrian eponym list, a year-by-year register naming the official after whom each year was designated, records under the eponymy of Bur-Sagale, governor of Guzana, that in the month Simanu the sun made an eclipse. The only solar eclipse visible in Assyria matching the record is that of 15 June 763 BCE. Because the eponym list is continuous for the ninth to seventh centuries, a single computed date converts the entire relative sequence into absolute years, and every Assyrian king with whom an Israelite or Judean king interacts is thereby dated.

**Ptolemy's Canon**, a king list transmitted with the astronomical works of Claudius Ptolemy, gives regnal years for Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian, and Roman rulers beginning with Nabonassar in 747 BCE, cross-checked at many points by dated astronomical observations recorded in cuneiform. From 747 BCE forward the sequence of reigns in Mesopotamia, and later in the Hellenistic and Roman east, is not seriously in doubt.

The **Babylonian Chronicle series** supplies dated campaign narratives in terse annalistic form. The most important entry for this history is in Chronicle 5 (BM 21946): in the seventh year of the king of Akkad, in the month Kislev, he mustered his troops, marched to Hatti-land, encamped against the city of Judah, and on the second day of Adar seized the city and captured its king. That converts to 15 or 16 March 597 BCE and is the only day-precise date in the history of the Judean monarchy.

The **Sothic dating** of Egyptian chronology is the major unresolved question of the second millennium. The method uses recorded heliacal risings of Sirius, notably in Papyrus Ebers and in a papyrus from Illahun, to fix Egyptian regnal years absolutely. The difficulty is that the observation's date depends on the latitude of the observing station, which is nowhere stated: Memphis, Thebes, and Elephantine yield answers differing by decades, and a serious body of scholarship now questions whether the Ebers text is a Sothic observation at all. New Kingdom dates are given here on the conventional low chronology, subject to adjustment.

The **Mesopotamian high, middle, and low chronology problem** is the corresponding difficulty further east. The Venus Tablet of Ammisaduqa records risings and settings of Venus over a reign, and the observations repeat on a cycle, so they permit several solutions separated by fixed intervals. The fall of Babylon at the end of Hammurabi's dynasty is placed at 1651 BCE on the high chronology, 1595 on the middle, and 1531 on the low, with an ultra-low solution near 1499 also defended. Middle chronology remains the publishing convention and is used here; dendrochronological and radiocarbon work has tended to favour lower solutions, and the question is open.

| Anchor | Fixes | Attestation |
|---|---|---|
| 15 June 763 BCE | Absolute position of the Assyrian eponym list | Solar eclipse recorded in the eponymy of Bur-Sagale; astronomical fix |
| 747 BCE onward | Reign lengths, Babylon to Rome | Ptolemy's Canon, cross-checked by dated cuneiform observations |
| 15/16 March 597 BCE | First deportation from Jerusalem | Babylonian Chronicle 5 (BM 21946), 2 Adar of Nebuchadnezzar's year 7 |
| 12 October 539 BCE | Persian capture of Babylon | Nabonidus Chronicle, 16 Tashritu |
| Second millennium Egypt | New Kingdom regnal years | Sothic method; observation latitude unknown; disputed |
| Second millennium Mesopotamia | Old Babylonian and later sequence | Venus Tablet of Ammisaduqa; high/middle/low; disputed |
| 51/52 CE | Pauline chronology | Delphi inscription of Claudius naming Gallio proconsul of Achaia |

### I · The Middle Bronze Age, c. 2000 to 1550 BCE

Every date here is approximate and most are period assignments rather than years. Nothing in the patriarchal material is externally dated, and no individual named in it appears in any contemporary document. What can be dated is the world the narratives describe: the collapse of a redistributive state in southern Mesopotamia, the westward drift of Amorite groups, the fortification of Canaanite towns, and the arrival of an Asiatic population in the eastern Nile delta. The stratigraphy of Tell el-Dab'a is the strongest chronological control on the Egyptian side; the Mari archive is the strongest for the social grammar of the Syrian steppe.

### II · The New Kingdom and the Late Bronze Levant, c. 1550 to 1200 BCE

Egypt supplies the framework and the Levant is documented from outside. The Amarna correspondence gives a dense, dated section of Levantine politics in the fourteenth century; the Karnak topographical lists give toponyms; the garrison at Beth-Shean gives stratified imperial presence. The chronology is internally consistent and floats as a block against absolute time, on the conventional low chronology here. The Israelite material has no independent anchor in this period: the two candidate Exodus dates, an early fifteenth-century figure derived from the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 and a thirteenth-century figure derived from the store-city name at Exodus 1:11, are both textual inferences and neither is externally attested.

### III · The Collapse and Iron I, c. 1200 to 1000 BCE

The Late Bronze system ends across the eastern Mediterranean within roughly a generation, and the Levant enters two centuries with almost no written documentation at all. This is the darkest stretch of the whole span for absolute dating. Settlement archaeology carries the period: several hundred small unwalled highland villages appear in the central hill country, Philistine material culture with Aegean affinities appears on the coastal plain, and the great Canaanite cities either end violently or shrink. Attributing any particular destruction to any particular agent is beyond the evidence. Dates in this section are era assignments derived from ceramic sequence and a growing but still contested body of radiocarbon determinations.

### IV · The Monarchy and the Iron IIA Problem, c. 1000 to 930 BCE

This is the most contested century in the archaeology of the region, and the contest is chronological rather than evidential. The same monumental buildings at Megiddo, Hazor, and Gezer are assigned to the tenth century on the conventional chronology and to the ninth on the Low Chronology, a shift of roughly seventy to eighty years that moves them from a united monarchy to the Omride kingdom. Radiocarbon programmes at Megiddo, Tel Rehov, and elsewhere have narrowed the gap without closing it. The circularity should be named plainly: 1 Kings 9:15 was used to date the strata, and the strata are now cited to corroborate the verse. No inscription of David or Solomon has ever been found, and the earliest external reference to the dynasty is a century and a half later.

### V · The Divided Monarchy to the Fall of Samaria, c. 930 to 720 BCE

From this point the chronology hardens quickly, because Assyria begins to record Israelite and Judean kings by name and the eponym list dates the Assyrian side absolutely. The Kurkh Monolith, the Black Obelisk, the Tell al-Rimah stele, and the annals of Tiglath-pileser III and Sargon II supply a series of synchronisms against which the biblical regnal figures can be tested. They do not agree perfectly. The internal biblical synchronisms between the two kingdoms accumulate error, and every reconstruction requires coregencies, dual reckoning systems, or both, none of which the text states. Regnal dates below follow the common reconstruction and carry an uncertainty of a few years each.

### VI · Judah Alone: Assyria, Egypt, Babylon, c. 720 to 586 BCE

This is the best-attested stretch of the Iron Age. Sennacherib's campaign of 701 is documented by three independent classes of evidence that converge: the royal prisms, the palace reliefs from Nineveh, and the excavated siege works at Lachish. The Babylonian Chronicle series then carries the Neo-Babylonian period with year-by-year precision. The one significant remaining uncertainty is the year of Jerusalem's destruction, where 587 and 586 are both seriously defended and the choice turns on whether Zedekiah's regnal years are counted by accession or non-accession reckoning and whether the year begins in Nisan or Tishri.

### VII · Exile and the Persian Province, 586 to 332 BCE

The Persian period is well dated at the imperial level and poorly documented at the provincial level. Ptolemy's Canon and the Babylonian business archives give the reigns to the year; Yehud itself produces coins, seal impressions, and one excavated administrative centre at Ramat Rahel, but no narrative source outside the biblical books. The Elephantine papyri are the exception and the most valuable documentary body of the period for Jewish history, because they are dated to the day and were written by the community they describe.

### VIII · Hellenistic and Hasmonean, 332 to 63 BCE

Seleucid Era dating, running from 312/311 BCE, makes this the first period in which local documents and coins carry an explicit era count rather than a regnal year, which is why 1 Maccabees can be checked against Babylonian and Seleucid sources with some confidence. The Maccabean dates are secure to the year. Internal Hasmonean chronology depends chiefly on Josephus, whose reign lengths are usable but not independent of one another.

### IX · Rome and the Herodian Dynasty, 63 BCE to 6 CE

Roman consular dating makes this period firm. The one significant uncertainty is the date of Herod's death, which is fixed by a lunar eclipse Josephus reports shortly before it and a Passover shortly after. The eclipse of 13 March 4 BCE is the standard identification and is reinforced by the reign lengths of his sons reckoned from that year; a minority case for 1 BCE rests on the total eclipse of 10 January of that year. The 4 BCE date is used here and is an inference from an astronomical datum plus a narrative interval, not a documentary date.

| 31 BCE | Battle of Actium; earthquake in Judea in Herod's year 7 | Josephus; a crack in the stepped cistern at Qumran has been connected to it, disputed |
| 22-10/9 BCE | Construction of Caesarea Maritima and the harbour Sebastos | Josephus; underwater survey has recovered hydraulic concrete with Italian volcanic ash |
| 20/19 BCE | Temple Mount expansion begun, Herod's year 18 | Josephus; the Herodian ashlar courses and the masonry seam are directly observable |
| 13 March 4 BCE | Lunar eclipse; Herod dies shortly after | Astronomical fix plus narrative interval; the 1 BCE alternative is defended by a minority; disputed |
| 4 BCE | Revolts after Herod's death; Varus intervenes from Syria | Josephus; no inscription from Judea names Varus and no destruction horizon of this year is confirmed at Sepphoris |
| 4 BCE | Territory divided; Archelaus, Antipas, Philip | Josephus |
| 6 CE | Archelaus deposed; Judea annexed as a province | Josephus |
| 6 CE | Census of Quirinius; the revolt of Judas the Galilean | Josephus; the Lukan synchronism with Herod's reign is a standing chronological problem |

### X · Roman Judaea and the Jesus Movement, 6 to 66 CE

The framework here is Roman and secure; the internal chronology of the Jesus movement is not. Pilate's prefecture is dated by Josephus and confirmed as to office and province by the dedicatory inscription from Caesarea. The crucifixion is placed in 30 or 33 CE on the basis of the gospel Passover notices combined with the prefecture, and neither year can be excluded. Pauline chronology, by contrast, has a genuine external anchor in the Delphi inscription, which dates Gallio's proconsulship of Achaia and thereby fixes one point in Paul's movements to within a year.

| Date | Event | Attestation |
|---|---|---|
| c. 18-20 CE | Antipas founds Tiberias | Josephus; the city's foundation coinage |
| 26-36 CE | Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judaea | Josephus; the Pilate Stone from the Caesarea theatre, discovered 1961, names him prefect of Judaea |
| c. 28-29 CE | Ministry of John the Baptist begins | Luke 3:1 gives year 15 of Tiberius; the reckoning basis is disputed |
| c. 28-32 CE | Execution of John the Baptist by Antipas | Josephus, who connects it to Antipas's later defeat by Aretas IV |
| 30 or 33 CE | Crucifixion of Jesus under Pilate | Gospel Passover notices within Pilate's prefecture; Tacitus confirms the execution under Pilate; the year is disputed |
| 36 CE | Antipas defeated by Aretas IV of Nabatea | Josephus |
| 39/40 CE | Philo's embassy to Gaius; the Alexandrian crisis | Philo, Embassy to Gaius; In Flaccum |
| 40-41 CE | Caligula orders his statue erected in the temple; his death ends the crisis | Josephus and Philo |
| 41-44 CE | Agrippa I rules Judea as king | Josephus; his coinage |
| c. 48-50 CE | The Jerusalem council on Gentile admission | Acts 15 and Galatians 2, which are not straightforwardly reconcilable |
| 49 CE | Claudius expels Jews from Rome | Suetonius; Acts 18:2; the date rests on Orosius and is disputed |
| 51/52 CE | Gallio proconsul of Achaia; Paul in Corinth | Delphi inscription of Claudius; the anchor of Pauline chronology |
| c. 62 CE | Execution of James the brother of Jesus | Josephus, Antiquities 20.200 |
| 19 July 64 CE | Great Fire of Rome; the Neronian persecution follows | Tacitus, Annals 15; Suetonius |
| c. 64-68 CE | Deaths of Peter and Paul traditionally placed in this window | Later Christian tradition; not documented in a contemporary source |

### XI · The Revolts, 66 to 136 CE

Josephus supplies a day-precise narrative for the first revolt, and because he was a participant and later a client of the Flavians his chronology is detailed and his interpretation is interested. The material record corroborates the outline at several points: the collapsed ashlars on the street beneath Robinson's Arch, the ash horizon in the Jewish Quarter, and the complete Roman siege system at Masada. The Bar Kokhba revolt is documented by dated legal papyri from the Judean desert caves, which is unusual and valuable, since they are administrative rather than narrative and were not composed to be read by posterity.

| Date | Event | Attestation |
|---|---|---|
| 66 CE | Revolt begins; the Roman garrison in Jerusalem destroyed | Josephus |
| November 66 CE | Cestius Gallus defeated at Beth Horon | Josephus |
| 67 CE | Galilean campaign; Jotapata falls; Josephus surrenders | Josephus; siege debris and ballista stones at Yodfat |
| 67 CE | Gamla falls | Josephus; the breach, ballista stones, and arrowheads are excavated |
| 68 CE | Qumran destroyed | Coins and iron arrowheads; no evidence of a massacre |
| 69 CE | Vespasian proclaimed emperor | Roman imperial record |
| August/September 70 CE | Jerusalem taken; the temple burned | Josephus, who dates the burning to the tenth of the month Loos; rabbinic tradition places it on the ninth of Ab |
| 70s CE | The fiscus Judaicus imposed | Roman fiscal record; the tax is documented in papyri from Egypt |
| 73 or 74 CE | Masada falls | Josephus; the year turns on the start of Silva's governorship; the mass suicide is not archaeologically confirmed |
| after 81 CE | Arch of Titus erected under Domitian | The monument itself; posthumous, not contemporary |
| 96 CE | Nerva reforms the Jewish tax | Coinage: FISCI IVDAICI CALVMNIA SVBLATA |
| c. 70-130 CE | Rabbinic reorganization at Yavneh | Rabbinic sources only; the "Council of Jamnia" as a single dated event is a modern construct and is not attested |

| 132-135/136 CE | Bar Kokhba revolt | Cassius Dio; coinage overstruck on Roman issues; dated legal documents from Nahal Hever, including the Babatha archive |
| 135 CE | Betar falls | Rabbinic tradition places it on the ninth of Ab; the siege works at Khirbet el-Yahud are visible |
| after 136 CE | Judea renamed Syria Palaestina | Roman administrative usage; attested epigraphically |

### XII · Rabbinic Consolidation and the Roman Crisis, 136 to 324 CE

The second and third centuries are firmly dated on the Roman side and loosely on the Jewish side. The rabbinic corpus does not date itself: the Mishnah carries no colophon, no year, and no editorial statement, and its conventional date of about 200 CE is an inference from the generations of named authorities it contains and from its attribution to Judah ha-Nasi. Dura-Europos supplies the one hard archaeological date of the period for Jewish material culture, since the synagogue's dedicatory inscriptions are dated and the city's destruction gives a terminus.

| Date | Event | Attestation |
|---|---|---|
| c. 200 CE | Redaction of the Mishnah under Judah ha-Nasi | Rabbinic tradition; the corpus is undated and the figure is an inference |
| 212 CE | Constitutio Antoniniana; citizenship extended | Roman legal record; the Giessen papyrus preserves a copy |
| 224 CE | Ardashir I defeats Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan; Sassanid dynasty | Sassanid and later Islamic historiography; Ardashir's rock reliefs |
| 226 CE | Ardashir crowned at Ctesiphon | Sassanid record |
| c. 220s-250s CE | Rise of the Babylonian academies at Sura and Nehardea | Talmudic tradition only |
| 244/245 CE | Dura-Europos synagogue rebuilt and painted | Dated Aramaic dedicatory inscriptions in the building |
| 249-251 CE | Decius; the universal sacrifice edict | Roman legal record; the libelli certificates survive on papyrus from Egypt |
| 256/257 CE | Dura-Europos falls to the Sassanids; the synagogue is sealed in a rampart | Destruction stratigraphy; the burial in the siege embankment preserved the paintings |
| 260 CE | Valerian captured by Shapur I at Edessa | Shapur's trilingual inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam; the rock reliefs |
| 284 CE | Accession of Diocletian | Roman imperial record; the Era of Martyrs is counted from this year |
| February 303 CE | The Great Persecution begins | Eusebius; Lactantius; Roman legal record |
| c. 3rd-4th c. CE | Beth Shearim necropolis in use as a diaspora burial centre | Excavated catacombs; Greek, Hebrew, Aramaic, and Palmyrene inscriptions |
| 28 October 312 CE | Milvian Bridge | Roman historiography; consular dating |
| 313 CE | Toleration agreed at Milan | Lactantius and Eusebius preserve the rescript |

### XIII · The Christian Empire, 324 to 602 CE

Late Roman and Byzantine dating is firm: consular years, indiction cycles, imperial regnal years, and conciliar acts all cross-check. Jewish chronology in this period is again inferential, since the Jerusalem and Babylonian Talmuds are undated compilations whose closing horizons are estimated from the last authorities named. The Justinianic plague is the one point where a documentary date and a biological one can be compared, since ancient DNA from sixth-century burials has confirmed the pathogen independently of the chroniclers.

|---|---|---|

| 335 CE | Dedication of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre | Eusebius, Life of Constantine |
| 361-363 CE | Julian; the pagan restoration | Roman historiography; Julian's own works |
| 363 CE | Julian's project to rebuild the Jerusalem temple halted | Ammianus Marcellinus reports fire; a regional earthquake of 18/19 May 363 is separately attested |
| 26 June 363 CE | Julian dies on campaign in Mesopotamia | Ammianus Marcellinus |
| 27 February 380 CE | Edict of Thessalonica | Codex Theodosianus 16.1.2 |

| 451 CE | Council of Chalcedon; the Christological schism | Conciliar acts |

| 529 CE | Samaritan revolt under Julianus ben Sabar | Procopius; Byzantine chronicles |
| 537 CE | Hagia Sophia dedicated | Procopius, Buildings |
| 541 CE | Plague reaches Pelusium; Constantinople 542 | Procopius, Wars 2.22-23; Yersinia pestis DNA recovered from sixth-century burials confirms the pathogen |
| 552 CE | Battle of Taginae; Totila defeated | Procopius |
| 553 CE | Second Council of Constantinople; Novella 146 on synagogue reading | Conciliar acts; the Novella itself |
| 554 CE | Pragmatic Sanction; Italy reorganized and ruined | Imperial legislation |

| c. 500-600 CE | Babylonian Talmud reaches its closing horizon; saboraic additions later | Inferred from named generations; the compilation is undated |

### XIV · The Last War, Islam, and the Caliphates, 602 to 762 CE

Two chronological systems now run in parallel and must be converted between: the Byzantine year, dated by imperial regnal year, indiction, and the world era, and the Hijri year, a purely lunar count of 354 or 355 days beginning in 622 CE and therefore drifting against the solar calendar by about eleven days annually. Conversions of Hijri to Julian years are exact where a month and day are given and approximate where only the year is. The early Islamic narrative sources are ninth-century compilations of earlier material, so their dates are transmitted rather than contemporary; the documentary controls are coins, papyri, and building inscriptions, of which the Dome of the Rock inscription is the most important because it dates itself.

## APPENDIX B · Gazetteer of Sites

Ancient toponyms and modern place names correspond by inference, and the inference varies enormously in strength. A handful of identifications are secured by an inscription found at the site naming the site: Gezer by its boundary stones, Gibeon by its inscribed jar handles, Ekron by its royal dedicatory block, Dan by a bilingual dedication. Most rest instead on a convergence of Arabic or Hebrew toponymic survival, the itineraries of ancient sources, and a plausible occupational sequence, which is usually sufficient and occasionally wrong. A number are genuinely contested, and a few of the most famous places in the tradition have no accepted location at all. Where an identification is disputed, the entry says so.

Occupation periods are given where they bear on the volumes; they are ranges of attested settlement, not statements about continuity, and a gap in the record is sometimes a real abandonment and sometimes a limit of excavation. Tell names are given in the customary transliteration.

### A

**Ai** · et-Tell, north of Jerusalem, is the traditional identification. Excavated by Judith Marquet-Krause and later by Joseph Callaway, it proves to be a substantial Early Bronze city, abandoned for roughly a millennium, then reoccupied as a small unwalled Iron I village. There is no Late Bronze town to be destroyed, which is the central archaeological problem for Joshua 8; Khirbet el-Maqatir has been proposed as an alternative and is not generally accepted.

**Alexandria** · Egypt. Ptolemaic foundation and the largest Jewish diaspora community of antiquity, the milieu of the Septuagint translation and of Philo. The pogrom of 38 CE and the Kitos War destruction are both attested textually. The ancient city is largely submerged or built over, so its archaeology is thin relative to its documentary importance.

**Antioch on the Orontes** · Antakya, Turkey. Seleucid capital, then capital of Roman Syria and the third city of the empire, with a large Jewish population and the base from which the Gentile mission was launched. Most of the ancient city lies beneath the modern town and under river alluvium.

**Aphek** · Tel Afek, at the springs of the Yarkon. A Late Bronze Egyptian governor's residency was excavated here, along with cuneiform and Ugaritic texts. It is the staging point of the Philistine victory of 1 Samuel 4. Herod refounded the site as Antipatris.

**Arad** · Tel Arad, in the eastern Negev. A large Early Bronze II city on the lower mound, thereafter unoccupied, with a separate Iron Age fortress on the upper mound. The fortress contained a sanctuary with a broad room, a niche, and two incense altars, and produced the Arad ostraca, which mention the house of YHWH. The phasing of the sanctuary and the date of its decommissioning are disputed.

**Ashdod** · Tel Ashdod, coastal plain. One of the Philistine pentapolis cities, with a full Philistine ceramic sequence. Fragments of a victory stele of Sargon II were recovered here, corroborating the Assyrian campaign of 712 BCE against the city.

**Ashkelon** · Tel Ashqelon, on the coast. Named in the Middle Bronze Execration Texts and on the Merneptah Stele. The Middle Bronze rampart carries an arched mudbrick gate, and a small silver calf figurine came from a sanctuary of that phase. Philistine occupation follows; the city was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar in 604 BCE.

**Assur** · Qal'at Sherqat on the Tigris. The original Assyrian capital and the cult centre of the god Ashur, excavated by Walter Andrae before the First World War. An inscribed cubical die used to draw the eponym year by lot was recovered here.

**Avaris** · Tell el-Dab'a, eastern Nile delta, excavated by Manfred Bietak from 1966. A large Asiatic population with Levantine material culture and burial practice is attested from the Middle Bronze Age, and the site becomes the Hyksos capital of the Fifteenth Dynasty. A later palatial precinct at Ezbet Helmi produced wall paintings in Minoan technique and style.

**Azekah** · Tell Zakariya, in the Shephelah overlooking the Elah valley. It is named in Lachish Letter 4, where the writer reports that he can no longer see the signal fires of Azekah, and again at Jeremiah 34:7 as one of the last fortified towns holding out.

### B

**Babylon** · near Hillah, Iraq. Excavated by Robert Koldewey from 1899. The Ishtar Gate, the Processional Way, and the palace complex are the principal remains, with the gate reconstructed in Berlin. The Hanging Gardens are unattested at the site. Judean exiles are documented in the Babylonian legal and ration record rather than in the monumental one.

**Baghdad** · Madinat al-Salam, founded on the Tigris by al-Mansur in 762 CE as the Abbasid capital. The Round City with its four equidistant gates is described in detail by the chroniclers and has not been recovered archaeologically beneath the later city.

**Beersheba** · Tel Sheva, some four kilometres east of the modern city of Beersheba, which is a separate settlement. The mound carries a planned Iron II town with a peripheral street, a deep well outside the gate, and a dismantled four-horned altar whose ashlars were found reused in a later wall. The Iron II town was destroyed in the late eighth century. Bronze Age occupation is slight, which bears on the patriarchal narratives set here.

**Betar** · Khirbet el-Yahud, near Battir southwest of Jerusalem. The last stronghold of the Bar Kokhba revolt. A Roman siege wall and camp remains are visible on the ground, and rabbinic tradition places the fall on the ninth of Ab.

**Beth Alpha** · in the Beth-Shean valley. A sixth-century CE synagogue whose mosaic floor carries the Binding of Isaac, a zodiac wheel with Helios in a chariot, and a Torah shrine, with an inscription naming the artisans Marianos and his son Hanina.

**Beth Horon** · Upper and Lower Beth Horon, Beit Ur el-Foqa and Beit Ur et-Tahta, on the ascent from the coastal plain to the Benjamin plateau. The pass is narrow and steep and was repeatedly the site of ambushes, including the destruction of Cestius Gallus's column in November 66 CE.

**Bethel** · traditionally Beitin, north of Jerusalem, excavated by W. F. Albright and James Kelso. The identification is contested, with el-Bireh proposed as an alternative. The site was the southern royal sanctuary of the northern kingdom after the division.

**Bethlehem** · Beit Lahm, south of Jerusalem. Iron Age occupation is modest and largely inaccessible beneath the modern town; a bulla reading Bethlehem was recovered in the Jerusalem excavations. The Church of the Nativity was founded under Constantine and rebuilt under Justinian.

**Beth-Shean** · Tel Beth-Shean, at the junction of the Jezreel and Jordan valleys, with the Roman and Byzantine city of Scythopolis spread below the mound. An Egyptian garrison town through the Late Bronze Age, with governor's residencies and royal stelae of Seti I and Ramesses II recovered on site.

**Beth Shearim** · Sheikh Abreiq, western Lower Galilee. A necropolis of rock-cut catacombs used from the second to the fourth century CE, with several hundred inscriptions in Greek, Hebrew, Aramaic, and Palmyrene. Tradition associates the burial of Judah ha-Nasi with the site.

**Beth-Zur** · Khirbet et-Tubeiqa, on the road between Jerusalem and Hebron. A Hellenistic fortress guarding the southern approach, with a large stratified coin series useful for dating the Maccabean campaigns.
