**John of Nikiu** · Coptic bishop's *Chronicle*, composed in the late seventh century in Greek or Coptic and surviving only in a Ge'ez translation made in 1602 from an Arabic intermediary. It is the fullest local account of the Arab conquest of Egypt. The double translation and the thousand-year transmission gap are not a footnote; names and numbers in it cannot be pressed. Tier 4.

**Theophanes the Confessor** · Byzantine *Chronicle*, composed around 815 CE and covering 284 to 813. It is the principal Greek narrative for the Persian war, the conquests, and the Arab sieges of Constantinople, and it preserves eastern material otherwise lost. He wrote roughly two centuries after the events of 610 to 630 for which he is most often cited. Tier 4.

**Gregory of Tours** · *Decem Libri Historiarum*, written in the 570s and 580s, the sole substantial narrative for Clovis and the early Merovingians, composed some ninety years after the conversion by a bishop making an argument to living kings about how to treat bishops. Tier 4.

**Madaba Map** · Mosaic floor map of the Holy Land in a church at Madaba in Jordan, sixth century CE, showing Jerusalem in detail with its colonnaded cardo and the Holy Sepulchre complex. It is a contemporary depiction of the Byzantine city's plan and has been repeatedly confirmed by excavation. Tier 1.

### VIII · Arabic and Islamic Sources

**The Qur'an** · The scripture of Islam, in Arabic, understood by Muslims as revelation received by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ between 610 and 632 CE. Early manuscript witnesses include the Sana'a palimpsest and other hijazi-script folios whose radiocarbon determinations fall within the first century of Islam, establishing an early written transmission of the consonantal text. Its material concerning Ibrahim (AS), Musa (AS), and Isa (AS) is theological address rather than chronicle and is used here as such. Tier 1 for the early manuscript witnesses; Tier 3 as canonical text.

**Sirat Rasul Allah of Ibn Ishaq, in the recension of Ibn Hisham** · The foundational biography of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, composed by Ibn Ishaq, who died around 767 CE, surviving principally through the edited recension of Ibn Hisham, who died around 833, with further material in al-Tabari's quotations from a different transmitter. It contains the Constitution of Medina, which many scholars regard as an early document embedded in a later frame. It is a compilation made more than a century after the events, reaching us through an editor who states that he has omitted material. Tier 4.

**al-Tabari** · *Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk*, the History of Prophets and Kings, by Abu Ja'far al-Tabari, who died in 923 CE. The largest and most important Arabic chronicle for the period, arranged annalistically and built by reproducing earlier accounts with their chains of transmitters, often placing contradictory versions side by side without adjudicating. That method is his great virtue as a source, because it preserves the disagreement. He is the reason the Rashidun, Umayyad, and Abbasid narratives have any detailed shape. Tier 4.

**al-Baladhuri** · *Kitab Futuh al-Buldan*, the Book of the Conquests of the Lands, and the *Ansab al-Ashraf*, by al-Baladhuri, who died around 892 CE. The *Futuh* organizes the conquests region by region and preserves the terms of the surrender treaties and the taxation arrangements imposed, which makes it the principal source for the administrative shape of the conquest as distinct from its battles. Tier 4.

**Dome of the Rock inscriptions** · Mosaic bands running some two hundred and forty metres around the inner and outer faces of the octagonal arcade, gold on blue, in Arabic Kufic, with a foundation date corresponding to 691 or 692 CE and the name of al-Walid later substituted for Abd al-Malik in one place, the alteration visible. The texts are largely Qur'anic and address the nature of Isa (AS) directly. They are the earliest securely dated monumental Arabic inscriptions of any length and a control on the Qur'anic text's early form. Tier 1.

**Hammat Gader inscription of Mu'awiya** · Greek inscription from the bath complex at Hammat Gader recording restoration under Abdallah Mu'awiya, commander of the faithful, with a date in the 660s CE. It is a contemporary epigraphic attestation of the caliphal title, in Greek, in a public bath that continued to function. Tier 1.

**Treaty of Tudmir** · The surrender agreement of 713 CE between Abd al-Aziz ibn Musa and the Visigothic lord Theodemir of the southeastern Iberian region thereafter called Tudmir, guaranteeing his people their lives, churches, and property against payment. The text survives only in later Arabic geographical and historical compilations, with variations in wording, and not in a contemporary document. It is the fullest surviving specimen of the conquest-era capitulation formula. Tier 4 as transmitted.

### IX · Numismatics

Coins are struck by an authority, dated by its reckoning, and distributed to be handled, which makes them the most systematically political of small objects and the best surviving evidence for what a regime wished to assert about itself. They also travel, so a find-spot is weaker evidence than a die-study.

| Issue | Date | Legends and types | What it establishes | Tier |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Yehud coinage | 4th c. BCE | Tiny silver, palaeo-Hebrew *YHD*; some naming a governor | A minting authority in the Persian province | 1 |
| Hasmonean prutot | c. 135 to 37 BCE | Yehohanan and Yehonatan the High Priest and the *heber* of the Jews; cornucopiae, anchor, star; Jannaeus bilingual with Greek royal title | A priestly regime taking a royal title, aniconic in practice | 1 |
| Herodian bronze | 40 BCE onward | Greek legends, anchor, tripod, helmet, no portrait of Herod | Deliberate avoidance of the human image in a Hellenizing kingship | 1 |
| Prefectural bronze | 6 to 66 CE | Palm, ears of barley, and under Pilate the lituus and simpulum of Roman cult | Roman administration and a prefect testing local sensibility | 1 |
| First revolt silver | 66 to 70 CE | *Shekel of Israel*, year 1 to 5, *Jerusalem the Holy*, chalice and pomegranates, palaeo-Hebrew | A sovereign silver coinage, the strongest single assertion of independence | 1 |
| Judaea Capta | 71 CE onward | *IVDAEA CAPTA*, palm tree, mourning woman, bound captive | The Flavian use of the victory as dynastic legitimation, minted for decades | 1 |
| Bar Kokhba coinage | 132 to 135 CE | *Shimon*, *Eleazar the Priest*, *For the Freedom of Jerusalem*, temple facade, lulav and etrog | A revolutionary administration, its year-count, its priestly partner, and its temple programme, struck over Roman coins | 1 |
| Arab-Sasanian and Arab-Byzantine | c. 640 to 690 CE | Sasanian bust and fire altar with Arabic marginal *bismillah*; imitation Byzantine types | Deliberate monetary continuity during the conquests | 1 |
| Abd al-Malik reform | 77 AH, 696 to 697 CE | Purely epigraphic gold and silver, no image, Qur'anic and confessional legends | A decisive break to an aniconic, doctrinally explicit imperial coinage | 1 |
| Tyrian shekel | to 1st c. CE | Melqart head, eagle, high silver purity | The accepted currency of the temple tax, and the reason money-changers were needed | 1 |

### X · Papyri

**Zenon archive** · Greek papyri of the mid third century BCE from the estate manager of Apollonios, finance minister of Ptolemy II, including correspondence generated on a journey through Palestine and Transjordan. It names the Tobiad family in Ammanitis and documents grain, slaves, and estate business, and it is the best documentary evidence for Ptolemaic administration of the region. Tier 1.

**Nash Papyrus and the Oxyrhynchus corpus** · The Nash Papyrus is a single Hebrew sheet from Egypt, second or first century BCE, carrying the Decalogue in a form mixing the Exodus and Deuteronomy versions followed by the Shema; before 1947 it was the oldest known Hebrew biblical manuscript by roughly a millennium. The Oxyrhynchus papyri, many thousands of Greek documentary and literary texts from the rubbish mounds of a provincial Egyptian town, are the standing control on ordinary life and include some of the earliest Christian manuscript fragments. Tier 1.

**Decian libelli** · Some forty-odd Greek certificates on papyrus from Egypt, all dated to 250 CE, in which a named individual attests before the local commission that he has always sacrificed to the gods and has now sacrificed, poured libation, and tasted the offerings in their presence, with the commissioners countersigning. Every surviving example is issued to a person presenting as a conforming sacrificer. They establish that the Decian measure was a universal loyalty requirement administered as paperwork, not a search for Christians. Tier 1.

**Nessana papyri** · Greek and Arabic documents of the sixth and seventh centuries from a town in the western Negev, including tax demands issued by the new Arab administration in the 650s alongside continuing Greek civic and ecclesiastical paperwork. They establish administrative continuity across the conquest: the tax machinery and its Greek-speaking personnel were absorbed rather than replaced. Tier 1.

**PERF 558** · Bilingual Greek and Arabic papyrus receipt from Egypt for sheep requisitioned for the Arab garrison, dated in both the Greek indiction and the Arabic year twenty-two. It is the earliest dated Arabic document known and the earliest surviving use of the hijri reckoning, converting to 643 CE, and it shows the conquest administration issuing receipts in both languages from the outset. Tier 1.

**Elephantine, Wadi Daliyeh, and Babatha** · Treated above under Persian sources and under Hebrew and Jewish texts respectively, and belonging equally to this class. Together with the material listed here they constitute nearly the whole surviving documentary record of Jewish life outside literary transmission before the Geniza, and every one of them survives because it lay in a desert. Nothing comparable survives from the monarchic Levant, and the absence is a fact about rainfall rather than about literacy.

---

## APPENDIX D · Dramatis Personae

The register below is organized by period, and alphabetically within each period. Dates are regnal or floruit unless marked otherwise, and they carry the precision the evidence carries: approximate for the second millennium, firm from the mid ninth century BCE, and firm to the year from the Persian period onward.

The register marks two classes of person wherever the distinction is live. Some are attested only in canonical text: the patriarchs, Moses, Joshua, the judges, Saul, and most of the early monarchy have left no contemporary document, inscription, or securely identified object, and their historicity is an inference from a text composed centuries later. Others are attested externally: Omri, Ahab, Jehu, Menahem, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Hoshea, Jehoiachin, Sanballat, Herod, Pilate, and Shimon ben Kosiba appear in inscriptions, archives, coins, or documents of their own lifetime or nearly so, and for them the account can be checked. Where existence is genuinely at issue the entry says so; where it is not, the entry does not manufacture doubt. Figures known only as a name in a genealogy are omitted.

### I · Patriarchal and Exodus Figures

Everyone here is attested in canonical text alone. No contemporary document names any of them and no excavated object has been securely connected to any of them, which is what the second-millennium record would lead one to expect. The narratives are read in this work for the social and legal world they presuppose, which is checkable, and not for the biography of individuals, which is not.

**Aaron** · Brother of Moses and eponym of the priestly line claiming descent from him. The Aaronid claim to exclusive priesthood is contested across the Pentateuch's sources and reflects a later argument over cultic authority.

**Abraham** (Abram) · The founding patriarch, migrating from Ur by way of Harran to Canaan. Which Ur is meant is disputed, and the narrative's repeated returns to Harran sit more comfortably with a northern origin than with the Sumerian city.

**Balaam son of Beor** · Mesopotamian seer hired to curse Israel and made to bless instead. Uniquely in this section he is attested externally, in the Deir Alla plaster inscription of around 800 BCE, which names him as a seer of the gods in a wholly non-Israelite context.

**Caleb** · One of the two scouts who returned a favourable report from Canaan, and later the recipient of Hebron. His designation as a Kenizzite marks him as an incorporated outsider, which the tradition preserves rather than smooths.

**Esau** (Edom) · Jacob's elder twin, and the eponymous ancestor assigned to Edom. The relationship narrated between the brothers encodes the later relationship between the two polities.

**Hagar** · Egyptian slave of Sarah and mother of Ishmael, expelled into the wilderness of Beersheba. In Islamic tradition she is central to the sacred history of Mecca, a development belonging to a different corpus and a different register.

**Isaac** · The second patriarch, whose narratives concentrate on wells, treaties, and grazing rights around Gerar and Beersheba. He is the least developed of the three and carries the fewest independent traditions.

**Ishmael** · Son of Abraham and Hagar, ancestor of the northern Arabian tribes in the biblical schema and, in Islamic tradition, of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ through the line settled at Mecca. Ibrahim (AS) and Isma'il (AS) are the Qur'anic forms.

**Jacob** (Israel) · The third patriarch, whose narratives run through Harran, kinship marriage, boundary treaty, and a change of name. He is the eponym of the people and the point at which family history becomes national history in the text's own scheme.

**Jethro** (Reuel, Hobab) · Midianite priest and father-in-law of Moses. The variation in his name across sources is a clear sign of independent traditions combined, and the narrative's crediting of an outsider with the judicial structure at Exodus 18 is striking.

**Joseph** · Son of Jacob sold into Egypt and rising to administer the grain supply during famine. The Egyptian court detail is broadly accurate for the period but not specific enough to date it, and no Egyptian source names a Semitic vizier answering to the account.

**Joshua son of Nun** · Successor to Moses and commander of the entry into Canaan. The archaeology of the sites his campaigns name does not support a single rapid conquest, which is treated at length in the volumes and in Excursus IV.

**Korah** · Levite leader of a revolt against the authority of Moses and Aaron, swallowed by the earth. The episode is a priestly-succession dispute in narrative form.

**Leah and Rachel** · Sisters and wives of Jacob, and the ancestresses to whom the tribal divisions are assigned. The division of tribes between them is a genealogical map of later political alignments.

**Miriam** · Sister of Moses and Aaron, called a prophetess, leader of the song at the sea. The Song of the Sea attributed to her circle is on linguistic grounds among the oldest poetry in the Hebrew Bible.

**Moses** · Central figure of the Exodus and Sinai narratives, lawgiver and intermediary. He is attested in no Egyptian document; his name is Egyptian in form, which is the strongest single argument for an authentic Egyptian element in the tradition. Musa (AS) in the Qur'an.

**Pharaoh of the oppression and Pharaoh of the Exodus** · Unnamed in the biblical text, which is the central obstacle to dating the events. Ramesses II is the conventional candidate on the strength of the store-city name at Exodus 1:11, which is an inference from a toponym rather than an attestation.

**Sarah** (Sarai) · Wife of Abraham and mother of Isaac. The wife-sister episodes attached to her were long read against Nuzi practice; that reading is no longer sustained.

**Zipporah** · Midianite wife of Moses, whose act of circumcision at the lodging place preserves one of the strangest and evidently oldest fragments in the Pentateuch.

### II · The Judges and the Early Monarchy

Attestation remains textual throughout. The Tel Dan Stele supplies the earliest external reference to the house of David, roughly a century and a half after his conventional dates; no inscription of David or Solomon has ever been found, and the architecture once assigned to Solomon is at the centre of the Iron IIA chronology dispute.

**Abiathar** · Priest of the line of Eli who survived Saul's massacre at Nob, served David, backed Adonijah, and was banished by Solomon. His fall marks the consolidation of the Zadokite priesthood.

**Abimelech son of Gideon** · Killed his brothers and ruled Shechem for three years before dying at Thebez. The episode is the tradition's own critique of monarchy, placed before the monarchy exists.

**Abner** · Saul's army commander and the maker of Ish-bosheth's short kingship, murdered by Joab. His defection to David is the hinge of the northern succession.

**Absalom** · Son of David whose revolt drove his father from Jerusalem and who died caught in a tree. The revolt narrative is among the most sophisticated political writing in the Hebrew Bible.

**Ahithophel** · David's counsellor who went over to Absalom and hanged himself when his advice was rejected. His counsel is described as being like an oracle of God.

**Barak** · Commander of the tribal levy against Sisera, acting under Deborah. The Song of Judges 5 and the prose of Judges 4 differ in detail, and the Song is the older text.

**Bathsheba** · Wife of Uriah the Hittite, taken by David, and mother of Solomon. Her manoeuvring at the succession in 1 Kings 1 makes her the decisive actor in the transfer of the throne.

**David** · c. 1010 to 970 BCE on the conventional dating. King of Judah at Hebron and then of a united kingdom at Jerusalem. His existence as a dynastic founder is supported by the Tel Dan Stele's house of David and possibly by the disputed line 31 of the Mesha Stele; the extent of the kingdom attributed to him is not externally attested.

**Deborah** · Prophetess and judge under whose authority the northern coalition fought Sisera, and the only woman in the book to hold the office in her own right.

**Eli** · Priest at Shiloh, whose sons' conduct and whose own death frame the loss of the ark. The eleventh-century destruction horizon at Khirbet Seilun is consistent with the tradition of Shiloh's fall without dating it to an event.

**Gideon** (Jerubbaal) · Judge who broke the Midianite raids by a night attack, then declined kingship while accepting its substance. The camels of the raiding narrative are an updating layer: domesticated camels are not attested in the southern Levant before the last third of the tenth century.

**Hiram of Tyre** · Contemporary of David and Solomon, supplier of timber and craftsmen. He is known only through the biblical text and through Josephus's citation of Menander of Ephesus, which is not an independent witness since Menander survives only in Josephus.

**Ish-bosheth** (Eshbaal) · Son of Saul, installed at Mahanaim by Abner and assassinated. The two forms of his name preserve a scribal substitution of bosheth, shame, for the element baal.

**Jephthah** · Gileadite commander who defeated the Ammonites and sacrificed his daughter in fulfilment of a vow. The narrative's refusal to soften the outcome is unusual.

**Joab** · David's army commander through the whole reign, killer of Abner, Absalom, and Amasa, executed by Solomon. He is the most consistently drawn figure in the succession narrative.

**Jonathan** · Son of Saul, whose raid at Michmash broke the Philistine position and whose friendship with David the narrative uses to legitimate the transfer of the throne.

**Michal** · Daughter of Saul and wife of David, given away and reclaimed. Her childlessness closes the possibility of a Saulide claim through her.

**Nathan** · Court prophet who confronted David over Bathsheba and secured Solomon's succession. The dynastic oracle of 2 Samuel 7 is placed in his mouth and is the constitutional charter of the Davidic house.

**Samson** · Danite strongman whose exploits against the Philistines are individual and unstrategic. The cycle preserves the border friction of the Shephelah more reliably than it preserves a person.

**Samuel** · Prophet, judge, and kingmaker, who anointed Saul and then rejected him. The books bearing his name present the monarchy as a concession, which is a theological position rather than a report.

**Saul** · c. 1020 BCE. First king, of Benjamin, who died with his sons at Gilboa. Attested only in the biblical text; the fortress at Tell el-Ful long identified as his citadel rests on both a contested site identification and a contested interpretation.

**Sheshonq I** · c. 945 to 924 BCE. Libyan founder of the Egyptian Twenty-second Dynasty, whose Levantine campaign is recorded on the Bubastite Portal and identified with the Shishak of 1 Kings 14. He is the earliest figure in the biblical narrative for whom a contemporary external record survives.

**Solomon** · c. 970 to 931 BCE on the conventional dating. Builder of the temple, organizer of a corvée, and partner of Tyre. No contemporary attestation of any kind exists, and the buildings once assigned to him at Megiddo, Hazor, and Gezer are dated a century later on the Low Chronology.

**Zadok** · Priest under David and Solomon, whose line supplied the Jerusalem high priesthood thereafter. His origins are obscure, and the proposal that he was a Jebusite priest incorporated at the conquest of the city is a hypothesis.

### III · The Divided Monarchy

From Omri onward the record becomes external and checkable. The tables give the two royal lines with the evidence outside the biblical text where it exists. Dates follow the conventional reconstruction and carry the uncertainty of overlapping coregencies.
