| Ahaziah | 841 | Killed in Jehu's coup. Probably the restored king of the house of David of the Tel Dan Stele |
| Athaliah | c. 841 to 835 | Queen regnant, of the Omride house; killed in a priestly coup. Text only |
| Joash (Jehoash) | c. 835 to 796 | Temple repairs; paid off Hazael. Text only |
| Amaziah | c. 796 to 767 | Defeated by Israel at Beth-Shemesh. Text only |
| Uzziah (Azariah) | c. 792 to 740 | Long reign; struck with a skin disease and secluded. A later Aramaic reburial plaque is known but is Second Temple, not contemporary |
| Jotham | c. 750 to 732 | Coregency with Uzziah. Seals naming a Jotham are known and unattributed |
| Ahaz | c. 732 to 716 | Submitted to Assyria in the Syro-Ephraimite crisis. Named as Jehoahaz of Judah in the inscriptions of Tiglath-pileser III |
| Hezekiah | c. 716 to 687 | Centralization, the Broad Wall, the Siloam tunnel, the revolt of 701. Named repeatedly on the Sennacherib prisms; bullae bearing his name are known |
| Manasseh | c. 687 to 642 | Fifty-five years of Assyrian vassalage and recovery. Named as a tributary in the inscriptions of Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal |
| Amon | c. 642 to 640 | Assassinated by his servants. Text only |
| Josiah | c. 640 to 609 | The Deuteronomic reform; killed at Megiddo by Necho II. Text only, though the reform horizon is archaeologically visible |
| Jehoahaz | 609 | Three months; deposed by Necho II and taken to Egypt. Text only |
| Jehoiakim | c. 609 to 598 | Egyptian then Babylonian vassal; burned Jeremiah's scroll. Bullae of his officials are known |
| Jehoiachin | 598 to 597 | Three months; deported. Named in Babylonian Chronicle 5 and in the Babylon ration tablets as Yaʼu-kinu king of the land of Yahudu |
| Zedekiah | 597 to 586 | Last king; blinded and deported after the final revolt. Text only; the destruction is fully attested archaeologically |
| Gedaliah | 586 | Governor, not king, appointed at Mizpah and assassinated. A seal impression naming a Gedalyahu who is over the house is known from Lachish |

**Other figures of the period**

**Ben-Hadad** · The name of more than one Aramean king of Damascus in the ninth and eighth centuries, which is a standing source of confusion in the biblical narrative. A Bar-Hadad son of Hazael appears on the Zakkur Stele.

**Elijah** · Ninth century. Prophet of the Omride period and opponent of the Tyrian Baal cult, associated with Carmel and Horeb. Text only; no installation on Carmel is connected to him.

**Elisha** · Ninth century. Successor to Elijah, and a political actor with a hand in the accession of both Hazael and Jehu. Text only.

**Hazael** · c. 842 to 800 BCE. King of Aram-Damascus, called a son of nobody in Assyrian sources, that is, a usurper. Named in Assyrian inscriptions; the Tel Dan Stele is generally attributed to him and the siege trench at Tell es-Safi to his campaign.

**Jezebel** · Ninth century. Sidonian princess, wife of Ahab, patron of the Tyrian Baal cult and mother of Athaliah. The seal sometimes attributed to her is unprovenanced and the attribution is disputed.

**Mesha** · Ninth century. King of Moab, who revolted against Israel and left the fullest Moabite royal inscription. Attested in his own words on the stele from Dhiban and named at 2 Kings 3.

**Necho II** · 610 to 595 BCE. Pharaoh who marched to support the Assyrian remnant, killed Josiah at Megiddo, deposed Jehoahaz, and was defeated at Carchemish in 605. Attested in Egyptian and Babylonian records.

**Rezin** · Died 732 BCE. Last king of Aram-Damascus, coalition partner of Pekah against Judah, killed when Tiglath-pileser III took the city. Named in Assyrian inscriptions.

**Tirhakah** (Taharqa) · 690 to 664 BCE. Kushite pharaoh named at 2 Kings 19 as advancing against Sennacherib. The chronology of his appearance in that narrative is a known difficulty.

### IV · The Writing Prophets

These are attested as authors of collections rather than as documented persons. The books are composite, the superscriptions editorial, and in several cases the figure and the book named for him stand at some distance. Dates are those of the earliest stratum.

| Prophet | Earliest stratum | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Amos | mid 8th c. BCE | Judean herdsman preaching in the north under Jeroboam II; earliest of the writing prophets and the sharpest on wealth stratification and state failure |
| Hosea | mid to late 8th c. | Northern prophet whose marriage is the sustained figure for the covenant; the principal witness to religious practice in the north before its fall |
| Isaiah of Jerusalem | c. 740 to 700 | Judean prophet from the Syro-Ephraimite crisis through Sennacherib's campaign, with access to the court; roughly the first thirty-nine chapters |
| Micah | late 8th c. | Judean prophet of the Shephelah, contemporary with Isaiah; his threat against Jerusalem is still recalled a century later at Jeremiah 26 |
| Zephaniah | late 7th c. | Active before Josiah's reform, with a royal genealogy in his superscription |
| Nahum | late 7th c. | A single sustained oracle on the fall of Nineveh, which occurred in 612 BCE |
| Habakkuk | late 7th c. | Complaint against divine tolerance of violence; read at Qumran as a coded prophecy of the community's own crisis |
| Jeremiah | c. 626 to 585 | Counselled submission to Babylon and was treated as a traitor; several men named in his book appear on bullae from Jerusalem |
| Ezekiel | from 593 | Priest deported in 597 who prophesied among the exiles, with a visionary programme for a restored temple |
| Obadiah | 6th c. | The shortest book, an oracle against Edom for its conduct at the fall of Jerusalem |
| Deutero-Isaiah | 6th c. | Anonymous exilic author of Isaiah 40 to 55, who names Cyrus and writes the fullest monotheistic argument in the Hebrew Bible; the division is a scholarly reconstruction, not a manuscript fact |
| Haggai | 520 | Prophet of the temple rebuilding under Zerubbabel, precisely dated in his own text |
| Zechariah | from 520 | Contemporary of Haggai; the second half of the book is later and separate |
| Malachi | 5th c. | The name means my messenger and may be a title; addresses cultic negligence and intermarriage in the restored community |
| Joel | disputed | Dated across four centuries; the locust plague framing the book supplies no anchor |
| Jonah | Persian period | A didactic narrative about an eighth-century figure named at 2 Kings 14, and the least biographical of the collection |
| Daniel | final form mid 2nd c. | Set in the sixth century; chapter 11 tracks the Antiochene crisis in detail before losing accuracy at the point of composition, which is the standard dating argument |

### V · Assyrian, Babylonian, and Persian Monarchs

All are attested in contemporary records, and their chronology is fixed by the eponym lists and Ptolemy's Canon rather than by the biblical text.

| Ruler | Dates BCE | Significance for this history |
|---|---|---|
| Ashurnasirpal II | 883 to 859 | Rebuilt Assyrian power and moved the capital to Calah; the deportation apparatus takes shape |
| Shalmaneser III | 858 to 824 | Fought the Levantine coalition at Qarqar in 853 and received Jehu's tribute in 841 |
| Adad-nirari III | 810 to 783 | Campaigned against Damascus, relieving pressure on Israel; names Jehoash of Samaria |
| Tiglath-pileser III | 745 to 727 | Reorganized the empire into provinces; annexed Damascus and Galilee and made Judah a vassal |
| Shalmaneser V | 727 to 722 | Besieged Samaria; the Babylonian Chronicle records that he ravaged it |
| Sargon II | 722 to 705 | Claimed the conquest of Samaria and the deportation; took Ashdod in 712 |
| Sennacherib | 705 to 681 | The campaign of 701 against Judah; destroyed Lachish; did not take Jerusalem |
| Esarhaddon | 681 to 669 | Invaded Egypt; lists Manasseh among tributary kings |
| Ashurbanipal | 669 to c. 631 | Sacked Thebes; assembled the Nineveh library; the empire fractures after him |
| Nabopolassar | 626 to 605 | Founded the Neo-Babylonian dynasty and destroyed Nineveh in 612 with Median allies |
| Necho II | 610 to 595 | Egyptian, listed here for the sequence: killed Josiah and lost Carchemish in 605 |
| Nebuchadnezzar II | 605 to 562 | Took Jerusalem in 597 and destroyed it in 586; the deportations |
| Amel-Marduk | 562 to 560 | The Evil-merodach of 2 Kings 25, who released Jehoiachin from prison |
| Neriglissar | 560 to 556 | Short reign between usurpations |
| Nabonidus | 556 to 539 | Promoted the moon god Sin, rebuilt Harran, and spent a decade at Tayma |
| Belshazzar | regent c. 553 to 543 | Crown prince and regent, not king; the Daniel narrative's title for him is inaccurate but his existence is documented |
| Cyrus II | 559 to 530 | Took Babylon in 539; the policy of restoring local cults and populations |
| Cambyses II | 530 to 522 | Conquered Egypt in 525, bringing Elephantine into Persian service |
| Darius I | 522 to 486 | Reorganized the empire; the Behistun inscription; the temple completed in his sixth year |
| Xerxes I | 486 to 465 | The Greek wars; the Ahasuerus of Esther on the usual identification |
| Artaxerxes I | 465 to 424 | The missions of Ezra and Nehemiah fall in his reign on the conventional reconstruction |
| Darius II | 423 to 405 | Reigning at the time of the Elephantine correspondence |
| Artaxerxes II | 405 to 359 | Longest Achaemenid reign; the alternative dating of Ezra places him here |
| Artaxerxes III | 359 to 338 | Reconquered Egypt; a punitive action in Palestine is reported in later sources |
| Darius III | 336 to 330 | Defeated by Alexander at Issus and Gaugamela; the end of the Achaemenid empire |

### VI · Persian-Period Judah

**Bagavahya** (Bagohi) · Governor of Judah around 407 BCE, addressed by the Elephantine community in its petition to rebuild the temple of Yahu. Attested in the Elephantine papyri, which is his only record.

**Ezra** · Fifth century. Priest and scribe sent from Babylon with a royal commission to enforce the law, and the figure through whom the Torah becomes the community's constitution. Attested in canonical text alone, and his date relative to Nehemiah is disputed.

**Geshem the Arab** · Fifth century. Opponent of Nehemiah, probably a Qedarite ruler; a Geshem king of Qedar is named on silver bowls from Tell el-Maskhuta, and the identification is likely but not certain.

**Jeshua ben Jozadak** · Late sixth century. High priest of the return, paired with Zerubbabel in the rebuilding. Text only.

**Nehemiah** · Governor of Judah from around 445 BCE, cupbearer to Artaxerxes I, who rebuilt the wall and imposed a social and marital settlement. His memoir is the closest thing to a first-person political document in the Hebrew Bible; he is not attested externally.

**Sanballat** · Governor of Samaria, contemporary of Nehemiah. Externally attested: named in the Elephantine petition of 407 BCE, whose writers address his sons, and the name recurs among the Samarian governors of the Wadi Daliyeh papyri, indicating a dynasty.

**Sheshbazzar** · Sixth century. Prince of Judah entrusted with the temple vessels and named as laying the foundation. His relation to Zerubbabel is unresolved in the text itself.

**Tobiah the Ammonite** · Fifth century. Opponent of Nehemiah with connections inside the Jerusalem priesthood. The Tobiad family appears later in the Zenon papyri and at Iraq al-Amir, indicating a long-lived Transjordanian house.

**Zerubbabel** · Late sixth century. Grandson of Jehoiachin, Persian-appointed governor of Yehud, and the focus of Haggai's and Zechariah's expectation. He disappears from the record without explanation, which has invited much speculation and supports none of it.

### VII · Hellenistic and Hasmonean

**Alcimus** · High priest 162 to 159 BCE. Seleucid appointee opposed by the Maccabean party; his death is reported while he was demolishing a temple wall.

**Alexander III of Macedon** · 336 to 323 BCE. Ended the Achaemenid empire and brought the Levant into the Greek world. The tradition of his visit to Jerusalem in Josephus is legendary.

**Alexander Jannaeus** · 103 to 76 BCE. Hasmonean king and high priest whose reign combined the greatest territorial expansion with civil war against the Pharisees, including the crucifixion of eight hundred opponents. His coins carry a Hebrew priestly title and a Greek royal one; the Nahum Pesher appears to refer to the crucifixions.

**Antiochus III** · 223 to 187 BCE. Took Palestine from the Ptolemies at Panion in 200 BCE and granted Jerusalem a charter of privileges; defeated by Rome at Magnesia, whose indemnity drove Seleucid fiscal desperation.

**Antiochus IV Epiphanes** · 175 to 164 BCE. Plundered the temple, banned the ancestral law, and installed a foreign cult in the sanctuary, precipitating the Maccabean revolt.

**Antiochus VII Sidetes** · 138 to 129 BCE. Last Seleucid king to campaign effectively in Judaea; besieged Jerusalem under John Hyrcanus and imposed terms.

**Aristobulus I** · 104 to 103 BCE. First Hasmonean to take the royal title outright, according to Josephus.

**Aristobulus II** · 67 to 63 BCE. Rival of his brother Hyrcanus II; their appeal to Pompey brought Roman arbitration and then Roman rule.

**Demetrius I Soter** · 162 to 150 BCE. Seleucid king whose general Bacchides defeated and killed Judas Maccabeus.

**Hyrcanus II** · High priest 76 to 40 BCE, ethnarch from 47. The passive elder brother through whom Antipater and then Herod exercised power; mutilated by Antigonus to disqualify him from the priesthood.

**Jason** · High priest 175 to 172 BCE. Bought the office and established a gymnasium in Jerusalem, the opening move of the Hellenizing programme.

**John Hyrcanus I** · 135 to 104 BCE. Expanded the Hasmonean state, destroyed the Gerizim temple, and annexed Idumea with forced circumcision. The Gerizim destruction horizon is archaeologically attested.

**Jonathan Apphus** · 160 to 143 BCE. Converted the insurgency into a recognized office by accepting the high priesthood from a Seleucid claimant. A leading candidate for the Wicked Priest of the Qumran texts, which remains an argument.

**Judas Maccabeus** · Died 160 BCE. Commander of the revolt, who retook and rededicated the temple. Attested in 1 and 2 Maccabees and in Josephus; no contemporary document names him.

**Mattathias** · Died 166 or 165 BCE. Priest of Modein whose refusal to sacrifice began the revolt.

**Menelaus** · High priest 172 to 162 BCE. Outbid Jason, was not of the high-priestly line, presided over the desecration, and was executed by the Seleucids.

**Onias III** · High priest to 175 BCE. Deposed and later murdered at Daphne; his removal is the pivot of the crisis in 2 Maccabees.

**Onias IV** · Second century. Fled to Egypt and founded the temple at Leontopolis, the only Jewish sacrificial temple of the period besides Elephantine.

**Ptolemy I Soter** · 305 to 282 BCE. Took Palestine into the Ptolemaic sphere, where it remained for a century.

**Ptolemy II Philadelphus** · 283 to 246 BCE. Under whom the Septuagint translation of the Pentateuch is traditionally placed; the Zenon papyri come from his administration.

**Salome Alexandra** · 76 to 67 BCE. Widow of Jannaeus and sole Hasmonean queen regnant, who reversed her husband's policy and governed with Pharisee support.

**Simon Thassi** · 142 to 135 BCE. Last surviving brother, under whom the Seleucid yoke was formally lifted and the office of leader and high priest was made hereditary by popular decree.

### VIII · Herodian and Roman

Roman officials are attested epigraphically and numismatically in a way earlier figures are not; the Herodians are documented by Josephus and by their own extensive building and coinage.

**Agrippa I** · 41 to 44 CE. Grandson of Herod, raised in Rome, who briefly reunited the whole kingdom under a client king. Coins and the Acts 12 account of his death agree on the shape of his reign.

**Agrippa II** · Died c. 92 or 100 CE. Last of the line, given custody of the temple and the right to appoint high priests; sided with Rome in the revolt.

**Antipater the Idumean** · Died 43 BCE. Father of Herod, who made the family indispensable to Rome by backing Julius Caesar at the right moment and was appointed procurator of Judaea.

**Archelaus** · 4 BCE to 6 CE. Ethnarch of Judaea, deposed by Augustus after complaints from both Jews and Samaritans, which converted the territory into a Roman province.

**Berenice** · Born 28 CE. Daughter of Agrippa I, present at Paul's hearing in Acts 25, and later the mistress of Titus, whose relationship Rome would not accept.

**Caiaphas** · High priest 18 to 36 CE. Presided over the trial of Jesus; his eighteen years are the longest tenure of the prefectural period and indicate a working partnership with Rome. An ossuary inscribed with a form of the name Qayafa is generally though not universally connected with his family.

**Cestius Gallus** · Legate of Syria, whose column was destroyed at Beth Horon in November 66 CE, the defeat that made the revolt general.

**Gessius Florus** · Procurator 64 to 66 CE. His seizure of temple funds triggered the revolt; Josephus, who has an interest, presents him as the sole proximate cause.

**Herod the Great** · 37 to 4 BCE. Idumean client king, builder of the temple platform, Caesarea, Masada, and Herodium, and a dynast who executed three of his own sons. Attested by the buildings, the coinage, and Josephus; the identification of the Herodium mausoleum as his tomb is disputed.

**Herod Antipas** · 4 BCE to 39 CE. Tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, founder of Tiberias, executioner of John the Baptist, exiled by Caligula.

**Herod Philip** · 4 BCE to 34 CE. Tetrarch of the northeastern territories, who refounded Banias as Caesarea Philippi. His coinage carries imperial portraits, which the Judaean Herodians avoided.

**John of Gischala** · Leader of one of the rebel factions in besieged Jerusalem, and Josephus's principal personal enemy in his account of Galilee.

**Josephus** · 37 to c. 100 CE. Commander in Galilee, prisoner, then Flavian client and historian, whose four works are the indispensable source for the period and the account of a party to the events.

**Julius Caesar** · Confirmed Jewish privileges in a series of decrees Josephus preserves, which are the foundation of the community's legal standing in the empire.

**Menahem ben Judah** · Sicarii leader who seized Masada's armoury in 66 CE and was killed in Jerusalem by rival rebels, an early sign of the factionalism that destroyed the revolt.

**Pompey the Great** · Entered Jerusalem in 63 BCE, ended Hasmonean independence, and walked into the Holy of Holies, an act that Roman and Jewish sources both record and read very differently.

**Pontius Pilate** · Prefect of Judaea 26 to 36 CE. Attested contemporarily by the Caesarea stele, which gives his title as praefectus, and by his aniconic bronze coinage bearing Roman cult implements. Removed after a violent action against Samaritans.

**Quirinius** · Legate of Syria, who conducted the census of 6 CE on the annexation of Judaea. Reconciling this census with the Lukan nativity chronology is a long-standing and unresolved difficulty.

**Simon bar Giora** · Rebel commander who held much of Jerusalem in the final siege, was taken to Rome for the triumph, and was executed at its close.

**Tineius Rufus** · Governor of Judaea at the outbreak of the Bar Kokhba revolt in 132 CE, named in rabbinic sources as Turnus Rufus.

**Titus** · 79 to 81 CE. Commanded the siege and destruction of Jerusalem in 70 and celebrated the triumph commemorated on his arch.

**Sextus Julius Severus** · Recalled from Britain to command against Bar Kokhba, and the general credited by Cassius Dio with the attritional method that ended the revolt.

**Shimon ben Kosiba** (Bar Kokhba) · Died 135 CE. Leader of the second revolt, styled prince of Israel. Externally attested in his own administrative letters from Nahal Hever and on his overstruck coinage, which give his real name, his title, his officials, and his year-count. Rabbinic sources call him Bar Koziba, son of the lie.

**Vespasian** · 69 to 79 CE. Commanded in Galilee, was proclaimed emperor while the war continued, and instituted the Fiscus Judaicus, redirecting the temple tax to Jupiter Capitolinus.

**Roman emperors bearing directly on the narrative**

| Emperor | Reign | Bearing |
|---|---|---|
| Augustus | 27 BCE to 14 CE | Confirmed Herod, deposed Archelaus, annexed Judaea |
| Tiberius | 14 to 37 | Pilate's prefecture; the execution of Jesus |
| Caligula | 37 to 41 | Ordered his statue set up in the temple; the order lapsed at his death |
| Claudius | 41 to 54 | Restored Agrippa I; the expulsion from Rome reported by Suetonius |
| Nero | 54 to 68 | The fire of 64 and the persecution; the revolt begins in his reign |
| Trajan | 98 to 117 | The diaspora revolt of 115 to 117 during the Parthian campaign |
| Hadrian | 117 to 138 | Refounded Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina; the Bar Kokhba war; the province renamed Syria Palaestina |
| Antoninus Pius | 138 to 161 | Relaxed the circumcision ban for Jews while retaining it for others |
| Septimius Severus | 193 to 211 | Severan detente; the patriarchate consolidates |
| Caracalla | 211 to 217 | The Antonine Constitution of 212 extended citizenship across the empire |
| Decius | 249 to 251 | The universal sacrifice edict of 250; the libelli |
| Valerian | 253 to 260 | Renewed persecution; captured by Shapur I in 260 |
| Diocletian | 284 to 305 | The tetrarchy; the persecution from 303 |
| Constantine I | 306 to 337 | Legalization, Nicaea, and the building programme in Jerusalem |
| Julian | 361 to 363 | Attempted pagan restoration and the abandoned rebuilding of the temple |
| Theodosius I | 379 to 395 | Nicene Christianity established as the religion of the state |
| Theodosius II | 408 to 450 | The Theodosian Code; abolition of the patriarchate around 425 |
| Justinian I | 527 to 565 | The legal codification, Novella 146, the reconquests, and the plague |
| Heraclius | 610 to 641 | Defeated Persia in 628 and lost the Levant to the Arab armies within a decade |

### IX · The Jesus Movement and the Apostolic Generation

Only Jesus and James are mentioned by any non-Christian writer of antiquity, in both cases briefly. The rest are attested within the movement's own literature: for the seven undisputed Pauline letters a named author writing in the 50s CE to communities he founded, and for the Gospels and Acts anonymous composition a generation or more later.

**Ananias and Sapphira** · Members of the Jerusalem community whose deaths at Acts 5 follow their withholding of property, the sharpest surviving indication of how the common fund was enforced.

**Apollos** · Alexandrian Jewish teacher active at Ephesus and Corinth, and the leader of a Corinthian faction Paul is at pains to accommodate rather than denounce.

**Barnabas** · Cypriot Levite who introduced Paul to the Jerusalem community and travelled with him until they separated over Mark.

**James the brother of Jesus** · Died 62 CE. Leader of the Jerusalem community and the decisive voice at the Jerusalem council. Josephus records his execution by the high priest Ananus II during an interregnum between governors, the strongest external attestation for any figure in this section.

**James son of Zebedee** · Died c. 44 CE. Executed by Agrippa I, the first of the twelve to be killed.

**Jesus of Nazareth** · c. 4 BCE to c. 30 or 33 CE. Galilean teacher and healer executed by crucifixion under Pontius Pilate on a charge framed as sedition. Tacitus, Josephus, and Suetonius refer to him or his followers within a century; his existence is not seriously contested, and almost everything else is reconstructed from confessional sources.

**John the Baptist** · Died c. 28 to 30 CE. Wilderness preacher offering a baptism of repentance, executed by Herod Antipas. Josephus describes him independently of the Gospels and gives a political motive, a rare case of genuine external corroboration for the movement's setting.

**John son of Zebedee** · One of the twelve, associated by later tradition with the Fourth Gospel and with Ephesus. The identification of the apostle with the evangelist is traditional and disputed.

**Judas Iscariot** · The disciple who handed Jesus over. The two accounts of his death in Matthew and Acts are irreconcilable in detail.

**Luke** · Author of the Gospel and Acts on the traditional attribution, writing around 80 to 90 CE. His interest in provincial administration supplies incidental detail of real value; his chronology is not always reliable.

**Mary Magdalene** · Follower from Galilee named first among the women at the crucifixion and the tomb in every Gospel that lists them, which is the strongest structural feature of the resurrection accounts.

**Mary the mother of Jesus** · Named in all four Gospels and in Acts. Maryam in the Qur'an, which devotes a sura to her and treats Isa (AS) as her son and a prophet.

**Paul of Tarsus** · c. 5 to c. 65 CE. Pharisee, persecutor, then apostle to the Gentiles, whose letters are the earliest Christian documents and whose decision to admit Gentiles without circumcision determined the movement's future. His appearance before Gallio at Corinth, fixed by the Delphi inscription to 51 or 52 CE, anchors the whole chronology.

**Peter** (Simon, Cephas) · Fisherman of Capernaum, leader of the twelve, and pivotal in the admission of Gentiles. Tradition places his death in Rome under Nero; the archaeology beneath St Peter's is consistent with an early cult of his memory and identifies no remains.

**Priscilla and Aquila** · Jewish couple expelled from Rome under Claudius, tentmakers and Paul's co-workers at Corinth and Ephesus, and the clearest evidence for the movement's spread through trade networks and household workshops.

**Stephen** · Died c. 34 CE. Hellenist member of the Jerusalem community, stoned after a speech attacking the temple, whose death precipitated the first dispersal.

### X · The Rabbinic Sages

Attestation here is internal to the rabbinic corpus, redacted long after the earliest figures lived and preserving their sayings in a form shaped by the transmission. Dates are approximate throughout. Beth Shearim and the Galilean synagogue inscriptions supply material context but name none of the sages.

**Abba Arikha** (Rav) · Died c. 247 CE. Babylonian amora who studied under Judah ha-Nasi and founded the academy at Sura, transferring Palestinian learning to Babylonia.

**Abaye** · Died c. 339 CE. Babylonian amora of Pumbedita, whose sustained disputes with Rava are the model of Talmudic argument.

**Elisha ben Abuyah** · Second century. Tanna who abandoned the tradition and is referred to in the sources as Aher, the other, a designation the corpus preserves rather than erases.

**Gamaliel I** · First half of the first century. Pharisaic leader named at Acts 5 as counselling restraint toward the movement, and in rabbinic tradition as a grandson of Hillel.

**Gamaliel II** · Active c. 80 to 120 CE. Patriarch at Yavneh who consolidated the authority of the academy, sometimes coercively, and led the delegation to Rome.

**Hillel** · Late first century BCE. Babylonian-born sage whose school stood against that of Shammai and generally prevailed. The prosbul attributed to him, preserving debts across the sabbatical year, is a model of legal adaptation.

**Ishmael ben Elisha** · Died c. 135 CE. Tanna and formulator of thirteen hermeneutic rules, standing against Akiva's method of deriving law from every textual particle.

**Johanan bar Nappaha** · Died c. 279 CE. Palestinian amora of Tiberias, the dominant figure of the Jerusalem Talmud.

**Judah bar Ilai** · Second century. Tanna of the generation after Bar Kokhba, frequently cited in the Mishnah.

**Judah ha-Nasi** · c. 135 to c. 217 CE. Patriarch under whom the Mishnah was redacted, and a wealthy aristocrat with recognized standing before Rome. The Talmudic legend of his friendship with an emperor named Antoninus symbolizes the detente rather than reporting it.

**Meir** · Second century. Tanna whose anonymous rulings form a large part of the Mishnah, and a student of Elisha ben Abuyah after the latter's apostasy.

**Rabbah bar Nahmani** · Died c. 330 CE. Babylonian amora of Pumbedita, known for dialectical method.

**Rava** · Died 352 CE. Babylonian amora of Mahoza, whose rulings against Abaye are almost always followed.

**Rav Ashi** · Died c. 427 CE. Head of the academy at Sura and traditionally credited with the principal redaction of the Babylonian Talmud, a process that plainly continued after him.

**Rav Huna** · Died c. 297 CE. Head of Sura after Rav, under whom the Babylonian academies reached institutional maturity.

**Ravina** · Two figures of the name, the later dying around 500 CE, associated with the closing of the Babylonian Talmud.

**Shammai** · Late first century BCE. Contemporary of Hillel and head of the rival school, consistently the stricter of the two.

**Shimon bar Yohai** · Second century. Tanna of the post-revolt generation, remembered for hostility to Rome and, from the thirteenth century onward, attached to the Zohar by a much later tradition.

**Simeon ben Gamaliel II** · Second century. Patriarch of the generation after Bar Kokhba and father of Judah ha-Nasi.

**Tarfon** · Late first and early second century. Tanna of Lydda, frequently the foil to Akiva in the Mishnah.

**Yohanan ben Zakkai** · First century. The pivotal figure of the transition, who according to tradition left besieged Jerusalem and obtained Roman permission to establish a school at Yavneh. The escape narrative exists in several irreconcilable versions and is a foundation legend as much as a report.

**Akiva ben Joseph** · Died c. 135 CE. The most influential tanna, whose exegetical method and organization of oral law underlie the Mishnah, and who reportedly acclaimed Shimon ben Kosiba as the messiah. Executed by the Romans after the revolt.

### XI · Late Antique Churchmen and Theologians

**Ambrose** · c. 339 to 397 CE. Bishop of Milan who compelled Theodosius I to public penance and, in the Callinicum affair, pressed him not to require the rebuilding of a burned synagogue, an early instance of episcopal pressure on the imperial protection of Jews.

**Arius** · c. 256 to 336 CE. Alexandrian presbyter whose position on the Son's relation to the Father precipitated Nicaea, and whose name attached to the Germanic churches long after the theological dispute had moved on.

**Athanasius** · c. 296 to 373 CE. Bishop of Alexandria, exiled repeatedly, the most persistent defender of the Nicene formula.

**Augustine of Hippo** · 354 to 430 CE. Bishop and theologian whose *City of God*, written after the sack of Rome in 410, decoupled the church's fortunes from the empire's, and whose doctrine of Jewish witness became the standard rationale for tolerated Jewish existence in the Latin west.

**Cyprian** · Died 258 CE. Bishop of Carthage whose correspondence is the fullest evidence for how the Decian requirement was administered and for the crisis over readmitting those who complied.

**Cyril of Alexandria** · Died 444 CE. Architect of the condemnation of Nestorius and of the Theotokos formula, and a political operator of the first order.

**Eusebius of Caesarea** · c. 260 to 339 CE. Bishop, historian, and biographer of Constantine, whose preservation of earlier sources makes him indispensable and whose selection of them makes him a partisan.

**Gregory of Tours** · 538 to 594 CE. Bishop and author of the sole substantial narrative of the early Merovingians.

**Helena** · Died c. 330 CE. Mother of Constantine, whose journey to Palestine is associated with the identification of the sites of the Nativity and the Sepulchre and with the imperial building programme that made pilgrimage an economy.

**Ignatius of Antioch** · Died c. 108 CE. Bishop whose letters written on the way to execution in Rome are the earliest evidence for the monarchical episcopate.

**Irenaeus** · Died c. 202 CE. Bishop of Lyon, whose refutation of the gnostic systems preserves most of what is known about them from outside their own texts.

**Jerome** · c. 347 to 420 CE. Translator of the Vulgate from the Hebrew rather than the Greek, resident at Bethlehem, and a correspondent with Jewish teachers whose readings he cites.

**John Chrysostom** · c. 349 to 407 CE. Preacher at Antioch whose eight homilies against Judaizing Christians are the most influential hostile texts of the period, directed in the first instance at his own congregation's attendance at the synagogue.

**Justin Martyr** · c. 100 to 165 CE. Apologist whose *Dialogue with Trypho* is the earliest sustained Christian argument addressed to a Jewish interlocutor.

**Leo I** · Bishop of Rome 440 to 461 CE. His Tome supplied the christological formula adopted at Chalcedon, and his primacy claims are a landmark in the rise of the Roman see.

**Melito of Sardis** · Died c. 180 CE. Bishop whose Paschal homily is the earliest surviving text charging the Jewish people collectively with deicide, delivered in a city with one of the largest synagogues of the empire.

**Nestorius** · Died c. 451 CE. Patriarch of Constantinople condemned at Ephesus in 431 for refusing the term Theotokos; the eastern churches that carry his name largely predate his dispute.

**Origen** · c. 185 to 254 CE. Alexandrian and then Caesarean scholar whose Hexapla set six versions of the Hebrew scriptures in parallel columns, the most ambitious textual project of antiquity.

**Sophronius** · Died c. 638 CE. Patriarch of Jerusalem whose sermons record the approach of the Arab armies in real time, and who surrendered the city to Umar.

**Tertullian** · c. 155 to c. 220 CE. Carthaginian apologist, the first substantial Christian writer in Latin, and the source of a great deal of the west's early legal vocabulary for the faith.

### XII · Sassanid Rulers

| Ruler | Reign CE | Bearing |
|---|---|---|
| Ardashir I | 224 to 242 | Overthrew the Parthians and founded a centralized state with an established Zoroastrian priesthood |
| Shapur I | 240 to 270 | Defeated three Roman emperors and captured Valerian in 260; deported populations into Mesopotamia |
| Shapur II | 309 to 379 | Long reign of war with Rome; persecution of Christians as a suspected Roman fifth column, while the Jewish academies were largely undisturbed |
| Yazdegerd I | 399 to 420 | A period of tolerance, remembered favourably in Jewish and Christian sources alike |
| Kavad I | 488 to 531 | The Mazdakite movement and its suppression; renewed war with Byzantium |
| Khosrow I | 531 to 579 | Administrative and fiscal reform; the high point of Sassanid power |
| Khosrow II | 590 to 628 | Took Jerusalem in 614 and Egypt in 619, then lost everything to Heraclius and was deposed and killed |
| Yazdegerd III | 632 to 651 | Last king; defeated at al-Qadisiyyah and Nihavand and killed in flight, ending the empire |

### XIII · The Early Islamic Caliphs and Commanders

For the caliphs and commanders the narrative sources are ninth and tenth century compilations. The contemporary attestation is epigraphic, numismatic, and papyrological: PERF 558, the Nessana papyri, the Hammat Gader inscription of Mu'awiya, the Dome of the Rock inscriptions, and the transitional coinages.

**Muhammad ﷺ** · c. 570 to 632 CE. The Prophet of Islam, who received the revelation of the Qur'an, established the community at Medina after the Hijra of 622, and unified the Arabian tribes under it. The *Doctrina Jacobi* of around 634 to 640 carries the earliest datable non-Muslim notice of a prophet arisen among the Arabs.

**Abu Bakr** · Caliph 632 to 634. Suppressed the tribal secessions of the Ridda wars, held the community together at the succession, and launched the first campaigns north.

**Umar ibn al-Khattab** · Caliph 634 to 644. Under him the Levant, Egypt, and Iraq were taken; he established the garrison cities and the *diwan* stipend register and accepted the surrender of Jerusalem. The Pact of Umar named for him is a later legal document rather than his text.

**Uthman ibn Affan** · Caliph 644 to 656. Presided over the standardization of the Qur'anic text and over resentment of his kinsmen's appointments; his murder opened the first civil war.

**Ali ibn Abi Talib** · Caliph 656 to 661. Cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet ﷺ, whose caliphate was consumed by the first fitna and ended in his assassination at Kufa. The dispute over his claim is the origin of the enduring division in the community.

**Mu'awiya I** · Caliph 661 to 680. Governor of Syria and then founder of the Umayyad dynasty at Damascus, builder of the first Arab fleet. Attested contemporarily in the Hammat Gader inscription and in early papyri.

**Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan** · Caliph 685 to 705. Reunified the caliphate after the second civil war, built the Dome of the Rock, arabized the administration, and issued the purely epigraphic reformed coinage of 77 AH. He is the best contemporarily attested figure of the early caliphate.

**al-Walid I** · Caliph 705 to 715. Built the Umayyad Mosque at Damascus and presided over the conquests of Spain and Transoxiana.

**Sulayman** · Caliph 715 to 717. Ordered the great expedition against Constantinople that failed in 717 to 718.

**Umar II** (Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz) · Caliph 717 to 720. Remembered for fiscal reform and for regularizing the position of non-Arab converts, whose treatment was the Umayyads' structural weakness.

**Hisham** · Caliph 724 to 743. Long reign of consolidation; the pressures that produced the Abbasid movement matured under him.

**Marwan II** · Caliph 744 to 750. Last Umayyad caliph, defeated at the Zab and killed in Egypt.

**Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah** · Caliph 750 to 754. First Abbasid caliph, proclaimed at Kufa.

**al-Mansur** · Caliph 754 to 775. Consolidated the dynasty, eliminated Abu Muslim, and founded Baghdad as Madinat al-Salam in 762, the terminus of this work.

**Abu Muslim** · Died 755. Organizer of the Abbasid revolution in Khurasan and commander of its armies, executed by al-Mansur once the dynasty was secure.

**Abd al-Rahman I** · Died 788. Umayyad survivor who escaped the massacre of his family and established an independent emirate at Cordoba in 756.

**Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi** · Died 732. Governor of al-Andalus, killed in the engagement between Poitiers and Tours.

**Abd al-Aziz ibn Musa** · Died 716. Son of Musa ibn Nusayr and governor of al-Andalus, party to the Treaty of Tudmir of 713.

**Amr ibn al-As** · Died c. 664. Commander of the conquest of Egypt and founder of Fustat.

**Khalid ibn al-Walid** · Died c. 642. Principal field commander of the early conquests, decisive at Yarmuk in 636, dismissed by Umar at the height of his reputation.

**Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik** · Commander of the land forces at the siege of Constantinople in 717 to 718.

**Musa ibn Nusayr** · Died c. 716. Governor of Ifriqiya who authorized and then joined the invasion of Iberia.

**Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas** · Died c. 674. Commander at al-Qadisiyyah, the battle that broke the Sassanid field army, and founder of Kufa.

**Tariq ibn Ziyad** · Commander of the crossing into Iberia in 711 and of the defeat of Roderic, and the man from whose name Gibraltar derives.

---

## APPENDIX E · Glossary of Technical Terms

Terms are given in the original script where one is standard, unpointed for Hebrew and Aramaic, followed by transliteration. Derivations are supplied where they are secure and are marked as disputed where they are not. A number of the words below have acquired settled English meanings that their sources will not support, and in those cases the entry says what the word does and does not carry.

**aggadah and halakhah** · Hebrew אגדה and הלכה. The two registers of rabbinic material. Halakhah, from the root h-l-k, to walk, is the legal and normative material: what one is to do. Aggadah, from the root n-g-d in the hiphil, to tell, is everything else: narrative, homily, parable, ethical reflection, and speculation. The two are interwoven throughout the Talmuds rather than separated, and the distinction is analytical rather than editorial.

**amoraim** · See tannaim and amoraim.

**amphictyony** · From Greek ἀμφικτυονία, from amphiktyones, those dwelling around. In Greek practice, a league of neighbouring states maintaining a shared sanctuary in rotation, the Delphic league the standard case. Martin Noth proposed in 1930 that premonarchic Israel was organized as a twelve-tribe sacral league of this kind around a central shrine. The model is abandoned and should not be used: there is no evidence for the rotating maintenance obligation that constitutes the Greek institution, no trace of the associated apparatus in the Israelite material, and the Greek arrangements drawn on for the analogy are considerably later and structurally dissimilar. The volumes that carry the term in their headings are using it as inherited vocabulary for tribal decentralization, not as a claim about an institution.

**amsar** · Arabic أمصار amṣār, singular miṣr. The garrison towns founded by the early caliphate rather than occupied from the conquered stock: Kufa, Basra, Fustat, and Qayrawan among them. They kept the Arab military population separate from the conquered urban societies, drew stipends from the diwan rather than from land, and became the demographic nuclei from which the new cities grew.

**Apiru, Habiru** · Akkadian ḫapiru or ʿapiru, written in some texts with the Sumerian logogram SA.GAZ; Egyptian ʿpr.w. Attested across the second millennium BCE from Mesopotamia to Anatolia to Egypt, and prominent in the Amarna letters as a chronic disorder in Canaan. The category is social and legal rather than ethnic: people standing outside the settled order of town and land tenure, appearing variously as mercenaries, brigands, dependent labourers, and clients. The proposed connection with Hebrew ʿibrî, Hebrew, is old, attractive, and unresolved; the consonantal correspondence is imperfect and specialists divide on it. The term describes a status a person could enter and leave, which is precisely what an ethnic label does not do.

**asherah** · Hebrew אשרה. The word carries two senses that the texts do not always separate: a goddess, known from the Ugaritic corpus as Athirat and there the consort of El, and a wooden cult object that could be planted, made, set up, and burned. In the blessing formulas from Kuntillet Ajrud and Khirbet el-Qom the word appears with a pronominal suffix, his asherah, and Hebrew does not ordinarily attach such a suffix to a proper name, which is the central grammatical problem in reading those inscriptions. Whether they invoke a goddess, a cult object, or a hypostatized aspect of the deity's own presence is genuinely unresolved.

**berit** · Hebrew ברית, covenant. The derivation is disputed, with proposals from Akkadian birītu, a bond or fetter, from a preposition meaning between, and from a root meaning to eat, on the strength of the covenant meal. The characteristic Hebrew idiom is karat berit, to cut a covenant, which points to a ritual of dividing animals and passing between the parts. In this work the term is read against the Late Bronze suzerain-vassal treaty form rather than against later theological usage.

**bulla** · Latin, a lump or boss; plural bullae. A pellet of clay pressed over the cord binding a rolled papyrus and stamped with a seal, so that the document could not be opened without breaking it. The papyrus perishes and the bulla, if the building holding it burned, is fired into permanent ceramic. A scatter of hard-fired bullae in a destruction layer with no documents is the archaeological signature of an incinerated archive, and their reverse faces preserve the impression of the papyrus fibre and the cord channel.

**casemate wall** · A fortification of two parallel walls joined at intervals by cross-walls, producing a row of chambers that could be filled with rubble for strength or used as storage and dwelling space. Characteristic of Iron IIA fortified sites in the southern Levant, and a datable feature in its own right.

**corvée, mas** · Hebrew מס mas, a levy of forced labour; the English word is from French corvée, ultimately Late Latin corrogata, requisitioned work. The institution is universal in ancient Near Eastern states and is not slavery: it is a periodic labour obligation on free subjects, assessed by household or district. Its imposition on the northern tribes is the stated cause of the secession at 1 Kings 12, where the levy officer is stoned, and the distinction the text draws between mas and mas ʿoved, permanent labour service, marks the difference between an obligation and a condition.

**dhimma** · Arabic ذمّة, protection or obligation of custody. The legal status of the protected non-Muslim communities under Islamic rule, whose members are ahl al-dhimma or dhimmis. In exchange for the jizya and acceptance of certain restrictions, life, property, and the practice of religion were guaranteed by the state. The specific terms varied enormously by time and place, and the systematized code known as the Pact of Umar is a later juristic document rather than a seventh-century text.

**diwan** · Arabic ديوان dīwān, from Persian. Established under Umar as the register of those entitled to a stipend from the conquest revenue, ranked by precedence in Islam and by tribal standing. The word later denotes a government department or chancery, and later still a collected body of poetry. Its original function was fiscal and it is the institutional core of the early caliphal state.

**Documentary Hypothesis** · The source-critical model of the Pentateuch's composition, given its classical form by Julius Wellhausen in the 1870s and 1880s, which distinguishes four continuous documents, the Yahwist J, the Elohist E, the Deuteronomist D, and the Priestly source P, combined by later redactors. The model in that four-source form is no longer the consensus it once was: D and P remain widely used as identifiable and datable strata, while J and E have been extensively reworked, merged, or abandoned in favour of fragmentary and supplementary models. The composite character of the Pentateuch is not in dispute; the shape of the composition is.

**elep** · Hebrew אלף. The word means a thousand and also a clan, kin-group, or the military contingent drawn from one, and the second sense is well attested: Gideon protests that his elep is the poorest in Manasseh, and Micah addresses Bethlehem as little among the alpe of Judah. George Mendenhall proposed in 1958 that the census lists of Numbers were originally muster rolls counting units and men, later misread as thousands and summed on that basis, which reduces the totals to a credible tribal levy. The proposal has real strengths and known weaknesses, and it is discussed in Excursus VIII.

**Erlangen** · The term has no established technical meaning in the historiography or archaeology of the ancient Near East, and it appears nowhere in the volumes of this work. What can be stated is only this: Erlangen is a Bavarian university town, and the phrase Erlangen Programme denotes Felix Klein's proposal of 1872 that a geometry be characterized by the group of transformations under which its propositions remain invariant. Where the phrase is met in methodological discussion it is being used by analogy, to argue that a register of evidence can assert only what survives the transformations proper to it. No such usage occurs in this work, and readers who encounter the word here should not infer a term of art that does not exist.

**ethnarch** · Greek ἐθνάρχης, ruler of a people, from ethnos and archein. A Hellenistic and Roman administrative title standing below king and above a merely civic magistracy, denoting authority over a community defined by descent rather than over a territory. Hyrcanus II held it under Rome, Archelaus held it over Judaea after Herod's death, and the term is used of the head of the Alexandrian Jewish community. The office implies internal jurisdiction under an external sovereign, which is the constitutional shape of Jewish self-government under both Hellenistic and Roman rule.

**Fiscus Judaicus** · Latin, the Jewish treasury. The tax instituted by Vespasian after 70 CE that redirected the annual half-shekel formerly paid to the Jerusalem temple to the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus in Rome. It was levied on all Jews of the empire including women, children, and the elderly, which the temple tax had not been, and it converted a voluntary religious obligation into a punitive and universal poll tax. Its harsh administration under Domitian and its relaxation under Nerva are both attested, the latter on Nerva's coinage.

**four-room house** · The characteristic domestic building of the Iron Age southern Levantine highlands: a broad room across the back with three long spaces before it, the central one frequently unroofed and often flanked by pillars. It appears at the start of Iron I and continues to the end of the monarchy. It was once treated as an ethnic marker of Israelite settlement; it is now generally read as a functional response to a mixed farming and herding economy, and it occurs outside any plausible Israelite territory.

**gerim** · Hebrew גרים, singular ger. A resident alien: a person living permanently among a people not his own, without land rights and therefore economically vulnerable, and grouped in the legal material with the widow and the orphan as objects of protection. The category is legal and residential, not ethnic or confessional, and its later transformation into the technical term for a convert is a post-biblical development that should not be read back into the earlier texts.

**glacis** · A smooth artificial slope of beaten earth, plaster, or stone laid against the base of a fortification to prevent undermining and to make approach difficult. Together with the earthen rampart it is the signature Middle Bronze fortification technique in the southern Levant and a chronological indicator in its own right.

**gôy and ʿam** · Hebrew גוי and עם. Both are rendered nation or people, and they do different work. ʿam denotes a body united by kinship and shared obligation, the group to which one belongs; gôy denotes a political and territorial body, a nation among nations, and in the plural, goyim, it becomes the standard term for the other nations. The distinction is not absolute, since Israel is called a gôy in several passages, but the general tendency is consistent, and the later use of goyim as a term for non-Jews is a narrowing of the plural rather than a separate word.

**hasidim** · Hebrew חסידים, the loyal or devoted, from ḥesed, covenant loyalty. In 1 Maccabees a body of the scrupulous who joined the revolt in defence of the law and withdrew when its aims became dynastic. Their relation to the later Pharisees and to the Qumran community is a matter of long-standing conjecture and is not documented. The term is not connected to the eighteenth-century Hasidic movement except by the shared root.

**herem** · Hebrew חרם. A thing withdrawn from ordinary use and given over wholly to the deity, whether by destruction in war, by exclusion from human benefit, or by dedication to a sanctuary. Applied to a captured city it means total destruction with no plunder taken, which is a fiscal renunciation as much as a religious act. The term is not distinctively Israelite: the Mesha Stele uses its Moabite cognate in exactly the same sense of a town devoted to Ashtar-Chemosh.

**hijra** · Arabic هجرة, migration or severing of ties. The relocation of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and the early community from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, and the epoch from which the Islamic calendar is reckoned. The dating formula AH, anno hegirae, counts lunar years from that point, which is why hijri and Common Era years do not stand in a fixed offset.

**homoousios** · Greek ὁμοούσιος, of the same substance, from homos, same, and ousia, being or substance. The term adopted at Nicaea in 325 CE to define the relation of the Son to the Father, against the position that the Son was of like substance, homoiousios, or a creature. It was contentious precisely because it is not a biblical word and had a suspect history in earlier controversy, and the half-century of dispute that followed Nicaea turned on it.

**Hyksos** · Greek, from Egyptian ḥqꜣw ḫꜣswt, heqau khasut, rulers of foreign lands, a title used of Levantine chiefs from the Middle Kingdom onward and visible on the Beni Hasan painting well before the Fifteenth Dynasty. The gloss shepherd kings, which reaches modern usage through Josephus's citation of Manetho, is a false etymology resting on a confusion with a similar-sounding Egyptian word for herdsmen, and it should not be repeated. The Fifteenth Dynasty rulers of Avaris were an Asiatic dynasty governing Lower Egypt; the excavated evidence at Tell el-Dabʿa points to a long-resident Levantine population taking power rather than to a conquest by invasion.

**isnad** · Arabic إسناد, support. The chain of transmitters prefixed to a report in the Islamic tradition, naming who heard the account from whom back to its origin. The associated science of criticism assesses the reliability and contact of each link. Al-Tabari's practice of preserving competing isnads and their divergent versions side by side is what makes his chronicle usable as evidence of disagreement rather than merely of a settled account.

**jizya** · Arabic جزية. The poll tax levied on adult free non-Muslim men of the protected communities, from which women, children, the elderly, the destitute, and the religious were exempt. In the conquest period it is frequently indistinguishable in the sources from tribute paid by a community as a whole, and the sharply defined juristic institution belongs to a later stage than the surrender treaties themselves. For many provincial populations the initial burden was lighter than the Byzantine or Sassanid assessment it replaced.

**kharaj** · Arabic خراج. The land tax, as distinct from the poll tax. In the early period the two are not consistently separated in the terminology, and the settled distinction between kharaj on land and jizya on persons is a product of later Umayyad and Abbasid fiscal practice. The problem the distinction was invented to solve was structural: conversion removed a convert from the jizya rolls, and if land tax followed the person rather than the field, conversion drained the treasury.

**lmlk** · Hebrew למלך, belonging to the king. The legend on stamped storage-jar handles from late eighth-century Judah, appearing above a two-winged or four-winged emblem and above one of four place names: Hebron, Ziph, Socoh, and mmst, the last unidentified. Over two thousand are known and their distribution concentrates in the sites affected by Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BCE. They demonstrate a centralized system of standardized jars; whether that system was taxation, military provisioning, or the produce of royal estates is argued.

**locus** · See stratum, locus, and tell.

**maiestas** · Latin, from maiestas populi Romani, the majesty of the Roman people; the offence is properly crimen laesae maiestatis, diminishing that majesty. Under the emperors it became the standard charge for treason and covered a wide range of conduct construed as an offence against the ruler's person or standing. The charge framed against a claimant to kingship in a Roman province falls here, and the mocking titulus of the Passion narratives is the charge stated in the form Roman practice required.

**mashiach** · Hebrew משיח, anointed one; Greek christos is its translation. In the Hebrew Bible the term designates a reigning king, a high priest, and in one instance Cyrus of Persia, and it carries no necessary eschatological content. The developed sense of a future deliverer belongs to the Second Temple period, where it is neither singular nor uniform: the Qumran texts appear to expect two anointed figures, one priestly and one royal, and other bodies of literature expect something different again or nothing at all.

**mas** · See corvée, mas.

**mawali** · Arabic موالي, singular mawlā, a word that carries both patron and client. The non-Arab converts to Islam of the Umayyad period, who were attached to Arab tribes as clients and who were in practice excluded from the stipends and status of the conquering Arab aristocracy, and in some places continued to pay taxes from which their conversion should have released them. Their grievance is the principal social engine of the Abbasid revolution, and Khurasan, where they were most numerous, is where it began.

**midrash** · Hebrew מדרש, from the root d-r-sh, to seek or inquire. Both the activity of interpreting scripture and the literary works that result. Halakhic midrash derives legal rulings from the text; aggadic midrash expounds narrative. The method assumes that scripture is inexhaustible and that its gaps and irregularities are invitations rather than defects, which is a hermeneutic position rather than a genre.

**mikveh** · Hebrew מקוה, a gathering of water; plural mikvaot. A stepped immersion pool for ritual purification, requiring water that has reached it by natural flow rather than being drawn and carried. Hundreds have been excavated in Judaea and Galilee from the Hasmonean period onward, at Qumran, on the temple mount approaches, in private houses in Jerusalem, and beside oil and wine presses. Their distribution is one of the most reliable material indicators of Jewish occupation and of the extent of purity observance outside the temple.

**minim** · Hebrew מינים, singular min, literally kinds or species, used in rabbinic literature for sectarians and heretics within the Jewish community. The referent varies by period and context and cannot be reduced to any single group; Jewish Christians are among those meant in some passages and plainly not in others. The benediction against the minim in the Amidah is frequently read as a formal expulsion of Christians from the synagogue, and that reading imports far more precision and far more datability than the evidence supports.

**Mishnah** · Hebrew משנה, from the root sh-n-h, to repeat, hence teaching by repetition. The compilation of rabbinic law redacted under Judah ha-Nasi around 200 CE, arranged in six orders covering agriculture, festivals, women, damages, holy things, and purities. It is topically rather than scripturally organized, which is its methodological innovation, and it records dissenting opinions alongside the accepted ruling. It is the base text on which both Talmuds are built.

**nasi** · Hebrew נשיא, one lifted up, prince. In Ezekiel a term for the ruler of the restored community; in the rabbinic period the title of the patriarch who headed the academy and represented the Jewish population before Rome, an office recognized in imperial law and abolished around 425 CE. Shimon ben Kosiba uses the title on his coinage and in his letters, which is the clearest evidence for what he claimed to be.

**nawûm** · Akkadian, attested at Mari. The steppe and its pastured herds treated as an administrative and taxable category belonging to a settled polity, rather than as a wilderness beyond the state. The term is important because it shows the pastoral and the urban sectors as two parts of one political economy in the Middle Bronze Syrian world, which is the social grammar the patriarchal narratives presuppose.

**ossuary** · A limestone chest for the secondary burial of bones, used in Jerusalem and Judaea roughly from the late first century BCE to the second century CE. The practice was to allow the flesh to decay in a tomb and then to gather the bones into a box, frequently inscribed with the name of the deceased in Hebrew, Aramaic, or Greek. Ossuaries are the largest source of Jewish personal names from the period and the reason the frequency of common names can be calculated.

**ostracon** · Greek ὄστρακον, a potsherd; plural ostraca. A fragment of broken pottery written on in ink and used for what was not worth a sheet of papyrus: receipts, ration orders, short notes, exercises. Because pottery is chemically inert and papyrus is not, ostraca survive in soils that destroy everything else, and the surviving Hebrew epigraphic record consists almost entirely of material its own writers treated as disposable.

**pesher** · Hebrew פשר, interpretation or solution, the word used in Aramaic for the interpretation of a dream in Daniel. The distinctive Qumran commentary method, in which a verse of prophecy is quoted and then applied directly to the community's own circumstances and adversaries, on the premise that the prophet spoke of the end time and that the end time is now. The plural is pesharim.

**piyyut** · Hebrew פיוט, from Greek poiētēs, poet. Liturgical poetry composed for insertion into the synagogue service, developing in Palestine from around the fifth or sixth century CE and becoming a major literary form. It is a principal source for the language, liturgy, and preoccupations of Byzantine-period Jewish communities, whose prose record is thin.

**praefectus and procurator** · Latin. The equestrian governor of Judaea from 6 to 41 CE held the title praefectus, as the Pilate stele from Caesarea confirms; after the province was reconstituted in 44 CE the title was procurator. Tacitus, writing in the second century, calls Pilate a procurator, which is an anachronism produced by using the title current in his own day. The distinction is small and it is a useful control: it shows a first-rate historian retrojecting an administrative term, which is exactly the kind of slip that later sources make routinely.

**publicanus** · Latin, from publicum, public revenue. A member of a company contracting with the Roman state to collect a tax, having bid for the right and taken the difference as profit. The system was applied to the eastern provinces from the late Republic and was progressively replaced under the empire by direct assessment for the major taxes, with tax farming persisting for customs and tolls. The tax collectors of the Gospels are more probably local sub-contractors of customs dues than members of a publican company.

**qahal** · Hebrew קהל, assembly, from a root meaning to summon. The congregation of Israel convened as a body, whether for war, for judgment, or for cult. The Septuagint renders it ekklesia, which is the route by which the word became the standard Greek term for the church, and the older term edah is the Priestly source's preferred alternative.

**religio licita** · Latin, a permitted religion. The phrase occurs in Tertullian's *Apologeticum* and is not a category of Roman law. There was no register of licensed cults, no licensing procedure, and no legal status of the kind the term is usually taken to describe. Judaism's practice was protected in the Roman east by a series of specific decrees and precedents, and Christianity's exposure derived from other causes; explaining either by reference to a licence that did not exist is an error that has passed into general usage and should be resisted.

**Sea Peoples** · The modern collective label for the groups named in Egyptian sources of the late thirteenth and early twelfth centuries BCE as attacking Egypt by land and sea, among them the Peleset, Tjekker, Shekelesh, Denyen, Weshesh, Sherden, and Lukka. The term is a nineteenth-century coinage and is not Egyptian. The groups are named separately and never collectively in the sources, their origins are argued, and the model of a single migratory wave destroying the Bronze Age world has given way to a picture of varied movements within a systemic collapse.

**Septuagint** · Latin septuaginta, seventy, from the tradition in the Letter of Aristeas that seventy-two translators produced the Greek Pentateuch in Alexandria; conventionally abbreviated LXX. The name properly applies to the Pentateuch translation of the third century BCE and is used loosely for the whole Greek corpus, which was produced over centuries by many hands of varying method. Its textual importance is that in several books it reflects a Hebrew text different from the Masoretic one, and Qumran has produced Hebrew manuscripts of that other type.

**Shasu** · Egyptian šꜣsw, from a root associated with wandering. An Egyptian designation for pastoral nomadic groups of the southern Levant, the Negev, and the Transjordan, appearing from the Eighteenth Dynasty onward in topographical lists, frontier reports, and campaign records. Like Apiru the term is a social category rather than a nation. Its interest here is the topographical entry read as the land of the Shasu of Yhw at Soleb and Amarah West, which if correctly read attaches the divine name to a nomadic population south of Canaan in the fourteenth century BCE.

**sicarii** · Latin, dagger-men, from sica, a short curved blade. Josephus's term for a group active in Judaea from the 50s CE who killed prominent collaborators in daylight crowds and disappeared, an assassination technique rather than a doctrine. He distinguishes them from the Zealots, and the modern habit of merging all the revolt factions into one movement flattens a set of distinctions that his narrative maintains.

**sira** · Arabic سيرة, way of going, conduct, and hence a biography. Specifically the biography of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, above all the work of Ibn Ishaq as preserved in Ibn Hisham's recension. The genre is devotional and legal as well as historical, since much of its material exists to establish the occasions and applications of revelation, and it was compiled more than a century after the events it narrates.

**stratum, locus, and tell** · The basic vocabulary of Levantine excavation. A tell, from Arabic tall, a mound, is an artificial hill formed by the accumulated debris of successive settlements on one site, each new town built on the levelled ruins of the last, so that the sequence is vertical and the earliest is deepest. A stratum is a layer of that accumulation representing one occupational phase, conventionally numbered from the top down. A locus is the smallest excavated unit to which finds are assigned: a floor, a pit, a wall, a fill. The chain of inference from locus to stratum to date is where most archaeological disagreement lives, and two excavators can agree on every locus and disagree on the stratigraphy.

**suzerain-vassal treaty** · The dominant Late Bronze Age international treaty form, best known from the Hittite archives at Hattusa. Its elements are a preamble naming the great king, a historical prologue reciting his past benefits to the vassal, stipulations, provision for deposit and periodic public reading, a list of divine witnesses, and blessings and curses. The correspondence between this structure and the covenant material of Exodus and Deuteronomy is close and was worked out in detail from the 1950s. The argument that the correspondence dates the biblical texts to the Late Bronze Age is weakened by the survival of the same form in first-millennium Assyrian loyalty oaths, which the Deuteronomic material also resembles.

**tannaim and amoraim** · Aramaic תנאים and אמוראים. The tannaim, from the root t-n-y, to repeat, corresponding to Hebrew shanah, are the sages of the period ending with the redaction of the Mishnah around 200 CE, and are the authorities cited in it. The amoraim, from a root meaning to say or expound, are their successors, active in Palestine and Babylonia from the third century to roughly the fifth or sixth, whose discussion of the Mishnah constitutes the Gemara of the two Talmuds. The distinction is one of period and function: a tanna is quoted, an amora argues.

**Targum** · Aramaic תרגום, translation. An Aramaic rendering of the Hebrew scriptures for a congregation whose spoken language was Aramaic, delivered orally alongside the reading before being written down. The surviving Targums range from the fairly literal to the extensively expansive, and the expansions are a valuable record of how texts were understood in the synagogue. Fragments of a Targum of Job were found at Qumran, which establishes the practice as pre-70.

**tell** · See stratum, locus, and tell.

**teraphim** · Hebrew תרפים. Household figures of some kind, whose derivation is disputed and unresolved. They appear in the Jacob narrative, where Rachel steals her father's, in the story of Michal disguising David's absence with one, and in Josiah's purge. Their size is inconsistent across the passages. The reading that they functioned as title deeds to an inheritance, once drawn from the Nuzi material, is no longer sustained, and the older suggestion that they were ancestor figures remains a proposal.

**theotokos** · Greek θεοτόκος, God-bearer, from theos and the root of tiktein, to give birth. The title of Mary at issue in the fifth-century controversy: Nestorius preferred Christotokos, Christ-bearer, on the ground that the divine nature was not born, and Cyril of Alexandria maintained that the refusal severed the person of Christ. The Council of Ephesus in 431 affirmed theotokos, and the term's real content is christological rather than Marian, since what is asserted is the unity of the person born.

**Torah** · Hebrew תורה, from the root y-r-h in the hiphil, to point, direct, or instruct, so that the primary sense is instruction rather than law. It denotes a single teaching or ruling, the five books of Moses, the scroll containing them, and by extension the whole content of revealed instruction including its oral transmission. The standard English rendering as Law follows the Septuagint's nomos and narrows the word considerably, and the narrowing has had a long polemical afterlife.

**tributum** · Latin. The direct tax of the Roman provinces, in two forms: tributum soli on land and tributum capitis on persons. Its imposition on Judaea after the annexation of 6 CE required a census of persons and property, and that census was the immediate occasion of the revolt of Judas the Galilean. The tax is the concrete fiscal substance behind the question about the coin in the Gospels, which is a question about the tributum and not about taxation in general.

**umma** · Arabic أمّة. The community, in the specific sense of the body constituted by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ at Medina and defined in the Constitution of Medina as a single community distinguished from other people, a document that includes the Jewish tribes of the settlement within it on stated terms. The word denotes a body defined by adherence rather than by descent or territory, which is the political innovation the early state rested on.

**yahad** · Hebrew יחד, unity, togetherness. The Qumran community's own name for itself in the Community Rule, denoting the body of the covenant into which a member was admitted after a graded probation and from which he could be excluded by a penal code. The term carries the community's central claim: that it was not a party within Israel but the true remnant, ordered as a substitute for a temple it regarded as defiled.

### Archaeological Periods of the Southern Levant

Period names are conventions of the discipline, not events, and the boundaries between them are ceramic and stratigraphic rather than historical. Ranges vary between schemes by decades and, in one case, by considerably more. Terminology differs between excavators, and the period preceding the Middle Bronze is called MB I in the older Albright scheme, and EB IV or Intermediate Bronze in most current work.

| Period | Conventional range | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| MB IIA | c. 2000 to 1800/1750 BCE | Reurbanization of the Levant after the Intermediate Bronze; unfortified or lightly fortified towns; Egyptian Middle Kingdom contact; the Execration Texts |
| MB IIB | c. 1800/1750 to 1650 BCE | Massive earthen ramparts, glacis, and monumental gates at Hazor, Shechem, Lachish, Ashkelon; the peak of Canaanite urbanism |
| MB IIC | c. 1650 to 1550 BCE | Also called MB III; the Hyksos Fifteenth Dynasty at Avaris; ends in widespread destruction |
| LB I | c. 1550 to 1400 BCE | Egyptian New Kingdom control; reduced and unfortified towns; the campaigns of Thutmose III |
| LB IIA | c. 1400 to 1300 BCE | The Amarna correspondence; a system of small city-states under Egyptian supervision |
| LB IIB | c. 1300 to 1200 BCE | Ramesside garrisons at Beth-Shean and elsewhere; the Merneptah Stele at the close |
| Iron IA | c. 1200 to 1150 BCE | Systemic collapse; Philistine monochrome ceramics on the coast; first highland villages |
| Iron IB | c. 1150 to 1000 BCE | The highland settlement wave; four-room houses, collar-rim jars, terracing; Philistine bichrome |
| Iron IIA | c. 1000 to 900/840 BCE | The disputed century. Monumental gates and palaces at Megiddo, Hazor, and Gezer are assigned here on the conventional chronology and to the ninth century on the Low Chronology, which moves them from a united monarchy to the Omride kingdom |
| Iron IIB | c. 900/840 to 700 BCE | Consolidated kingdoms; Samaria and Jerusalem at their height; Assyrian intervention; the lmlk system; ends with the destructions of 722 and 701 |
| Iron IIC | c. 700 to 586 BCE | Judah alone under Assyrian and then Babylonian domination; the Lachish and Arad ostraca; ends with the Babylonian destruction |

## APPENDIX F · Register of Corrections

#### The audit

Every one of the one hundred and six volumes was read line by line against the evidence scheme the work declares for itself. The audit returned eight hundred and forty-five distinct findings. They are itemised below by volume, with the original claim in italic and the correction following.

The findings are of three kinds and the distinction matters for how a reader should weigh them.

**Corrections of fact.** A date, a site identification, a stratum number, an author, a museum, a transliteration, a regnal figure, or a citation that was simply wrong. Where the original text placed the Weidner ration tablets in the Pergamum Museum, or attributed the Sekmem form to the Execration Texts rather than to the Khu-Sobek stele, or inverted the published dating of the earliest domesticated camel remains in the Aravah, the correction is straightforward and the corrected text carries the right value. These are the minority of the findings but they are the ones that most needed fixing.

**Corrections of warrant.** A claim that is defensible but was stated at a confidence the evidence does not carry. This is the largest class by a wide margin. A literary source tiered as contemporary epigraphy; an artifact from three centuries later cited as same-era corroboration; a contested identification stated as settled; a reconstructed inscription quoted as though intact; a round figure from a single hostile source given as precise. In almost every case the historical claim survives and only its grade changes. Excursus V analyses this class systematically, because the pattern in it is more interesting than any of its members.

**Corrections of structure.** Internal contradictions between sections of a single volume, or between volumes; a heading absent where every other volume carries it; a title that drifts between the index and the body; a figure given two different values in two places. These are editorial rather than substantive, and they have been repaired silently in the text as well as recorded here.

#### What the audit did not find

No finding in the register overturns the historical spine of the work. The Omride dynasty, the Assyrian vassalage of both kingdoms, the fall of Samaria, the Sennacherib campaign of 701, the Babylonian destruction of 586, the Persian restoration, the Hasmonean state, the Herodian building programme, the two revolts against Rome, the rabbinic transition, the Christianisation of the empire, the mutual exhaustion of Byzantium and Persia, and the Arab conquests are all abundantly attested and are described in this work accurately.

What the audit found is that confidence was distributed backwards. The scheme was applied most generously exactly where the evidence is thinnest, in the patriarchal and Exodus material, and most conservatively where the evidence is densest, in the Assyrian and Roman periods where genuine contemporary epigraphy is abundant. Correcting that produces a truer confidence curve across the work: under-determined at the beginning, checkable from the ninth century BCE, densely documented from the eighth, and increasingly so thereafter.

#### A note on the sections audited

The register concerns the original sections A through J only. Sections K through N are new to this edition and are not self-audited here; they were written under the corrected discipline set out in Excursus V and in the note on method.
